§ 681. Basis for Liability 

The Texas cases seem very emphatic in declaring that directors of a corporation are trustees for the corporation and for the 

3 HILDEBRAND TEX.CORP.-1 

1

§ Ch. 14 

stockholders collectively. In the case of San Antonio & G. S. 

R. Co. v. San Antonio & G. R. Co.¹ it is said, "Directors of corporations occupy toward them the position of trustees, and their acts in connection with the property of the corporation are controlled by the principles governing other trustees, and the obligations of the trusteeship are made the basis for the ascertainment of what acts on the part of directors will constitute a fraud, and the remedies that may be applied."

Other Texas cases are to the same effect, and in no case is the correctness of that statement of the relationship questioned. 

Other authorities, however, do question the correctness of this statement, and say that it is erroneous to say that a true trusteecestui que relationship is established. 

If by "trustee relationship" is meant that the directors in the performance of their duties on behalf of the corporation stand in a fiduciary relation to it, then the statement is true. But "trustee❞ ordinarily means something else besides this, as a trustee under a will. In that sense, there is a vast difference between the directors of a corporation and a true trustee. It would be more correct to say that the directors of a corporation are the agents of the corporation, standing in a fiduciary relation toward it; or merely to describe their status as "directors of the corporation," which term would mean, as is the actual case, that they compose a class entirely to themselves, with a special set of rules, liabilities, and duties applying to them, which cannot be said to apply to any other relationship. It is not necessary that they be categorically placed under an established type of legal or equity relationship, as so many courts and writers seem to think.

The duties of the directors vary, according to the size and the type of the corporation of which they are the directors, and in accordance with the duties and obligations which the charter of the respective corporation confers upon them. The fiduciary relation in which they are placed as to their corporation imposes upon them the duty to use the authority given them solely for the benefit of the corporation and its stockholders. They are not permitted to appropriate the property of the corporation to their private benefit, nor should they permit others to do so.³ 

If an officer of the corporation is sued for converting money or other property of the company to his own use and benefit, he should be permitted to show that he used the money that he was accused of converting to pay a third party's claim against the company for its conversion of shingles belonging to the party to whom the money was paid. If the directors wrongfully convert assets of the corporation to their own use, and invest such funds in the stock of another corporation, they hold such stock as trustees for the injured corporation.5 Their primary duty is to look out for the best interests of the corporation, whose affairs they regulate and manage, and whose destinies are controlled by them. In this respect the Texas cases are in accord with the unanimous holdings of other jurisdictions."

§ Ch. 14 

The directors of a corporation have a very high degree of responsibility as to the management of the corporation, being expected to exercise an active and vigilant supervision over the affairs of the company. They must be familiar with the provisions and requirements of the charter and by-laws of the corporation, and do their utmost to enforce them. They are supposed to take the usual methods to inform themselves of the true condition of the affairs of the company. Their position is not merely of honor, void of responsibility, and it is an extremely dangerous practice for prominent men to lend their names as directors for the prestige and advertising value that might be derived, upon an understanding that they are not expected to take an active part in the management and supervision. For, as a director, they are expected by law to use due diligence to see that the business of the corporation is properly carried on," and "* it is wholly immaterial where appellant Slayden (director) resided. He accepted and continued to exercise the duties and responsibilities of director of the corporation, and knowingly allowed himself to be held out to the public, including appellee, as one of the governing officers of the corporation, and the mere fact that appellee knew that he resided in New York would not which his interest is adverse to that of the corporation." In this case a resolution by the directors of the corporation declaring that stock held by certain directors of the corporation, who were present and without whom there would not have been a quorum, non-assessable, was held to be void.

According to the decisions in most of the states, if the directors are guilty of negligence in the performance of their duties, as in cases in which the directors of a bank or other corporation fail to hold meetings or exercise supervision over the affairs of the corporation, and if, as a result of their neglect, the funds or property of the corporation are stolen, wasted, or lost, they are liable; for in assuming the duties of the office, even though gratuitously, they are bound to exercise ordinary care and diligence in the discharge of their duties. The Texas authorities, so far as they have had occasion to determine these questions, have followed the almost unbroken line of authority from the other states of the Union. On this question the Supreme Court of Texas in Fidelity & 

Deposit Co. v. Wiseman,¹¹ said: "In this case W. J. Swain, as president of the insurance company, either willingly or by culpable negligence, by which the forged bonds were ostensibly received for the benefit of the company, made the transaction, but, whether willingly or unintentionally, he would be in either case responsible to make good the default."

Of course, the directors are liable to the corporation and to the stockholders for any losses which are caused by fraudulent acts on their part.12 If a director is aware of a fraud which is being practiced on the corporation, it is his duty to acquaint the other officers of the corporation with the facts, and to use reasonable diligence to prevent the consummation of the fraud. If he does not, but remains silent and allows the funds or property of the corporation to be fraudulently diverted, he is thereby guilty of a neglect of duty to the corporation, for which he is liable in damages, even though he himself did not make any profit from the transaction.

Ch. § 682 

 § 682. Test for Determining Liability 

Texas has decided no case where it became necessary for the court to state exactly what degree of care is required of a director. In Anderson v. O'Briant 13 it was said: "The standard of conduct imposed by law upon those who have assumed the duties and obligations of directors in a corporation is very high, and rightly so."

In Evans v. Brandon,14 the stockholders of the corporation sued to recover for heavy losses which they alleged to be due to the mismanagement of the defendant directors. All that the court held in that case was that any such suit as this can be brought only by the corporation or by a shareholder in a suit for and on behalf of the corporation in what is designated as "a shareholder's bill." In Bounds v. Stephenson,15 the defendant directors had hired attorneys and had fixed their own salaries at a very high figure. In that case the court held that there was not enough evidence to show mismanagement or fraud so as to make the directors liable.

In Jewell v. Sal-O-Dent Laboratories Inc.,16 it was said: "The allegations of the petition seem to exonerate the directors, as such, from any wrongdoing. No attack is made upon them.

They are not charged with usurpation, fraud, or gross negligence, and, as stated in 14a C.J., p. 84, sec. 1843 [19 C.J.S.Corporations, § 743], the rule is that, in the absence of usurpation, fraud, or gross negligence on the part of the directors, a court of equity will not interfere at the suit of a minority of stockholders, merely to overrule and control the discretion of the directors on questions of corporate management, policy, or business." 

In First State Bank v. Metropolitan Casualty Ins. Company 17 the court said: "Banks occupy an important position in our business affairs. The officers and directors control the operation of 

13. Tex.Civ.App., 3 S.W.2d 842, writ of error refused.

the bank. The directors are trustees, and their acts with respect to the property of the bank are controlled by the principles of law governing other trustees. 

The law exacts of those who manage the affairs of a bank obedience to certain fundamental principles or rules. They owe a high duty to the general public and stockholders. The directors and officers owe to the bank scrupulous good faith in the performance of the duties which they have assumed, and they should discharge those duties with prudence and good faith, and with ordinary care and diligence." (Italics supplied.)

Therefore, in Texas the directors are liable if guilty of bad faith or negligence, but the courts have not defined the measure of diligence the directors must exercise. The expressions by the courts of other states are not uniform. Some say that they are not liable for honest mistakes of judgment, although so gross as to appear absurd and ridiculous, if fairly within the scope of the discretion confided to them.18

It would probably be pointless to state any measure of diligence required as a certainty. The quantum of care to be exercised must necessarily vary with the type of the corporation involved. What might properly be regarded as very slight negligence in the case of a small manufacturing company might well be regarded as very gross negligence in the case of a bank. 

The only proper rule is that the directors are liable on the ground of negligence when, and only when, they have failed to exercise ordinary care and diligence; and ordinary care and diligence is such care and diligence as ordinarily careful and prudent men generally exercise under similar circumstances. The various circumstances of the case under consideration should enter into the test to a very large measure.19 This is stated very well in Bouli-

 § 683. Liability for Misconduct of Other Officers or Employees 

There is no Texas case directly in point which determines the liability of the directors for misconduct of the other officers or employees of the corporation, but the courts of Texas will no doubt follow the important decisions of other jurisdictions. In order for the directors of a corporation, as well as for other officers, to be liable for the fraudulent or wrongful acts of other officers, it is necessary that they themselves participate in such action, or else they must be charged with negligence in allowing the action to take place. They must be blameable themselves in failing to discharge some duty which the law imposes on them, and it is only upon proof of such facts that they can be held liable to the corporation. One agent of a corporation does not become a particeps criminis merely because he approves a wrongful act committed by another agent of the same principal.23 With this rule in mind it is difficult to explain the holding of the Supreme Court of the United States in Briggs v. Spaulding,24 for it would seem that the directors in that case were very negligent. In that case it was said the directors of a corporation "are not insurers of the fidelity of the agents whom they have appointed, who are not their agents but the agents of the corporation; and they cannot be held responsible for losses resulting from the wrongful acts or omissions of other directors or agents, unless the loss is a consequence of their own neglect of duty, either for failure to supermining his liability instead of applying a general rule to all directors in

 § 684. Actions against Officers and Agents-By the Corporation 

The directors, officers, and managers of corporations are held bound by the restrictions which are imposed by the charter and by-laws of the corporation. They are expected to know these documents, and if they do an act in excess of their powers or in excess of the powers of the corporation, therein expressed, they are liable for the attending damages to the company.30 

There is some doubt as to whether the directors and officers are liable to the corporation when they have exceeded the authority of the corporation, if they acted under an honest mistake of judgment. Some states hold them liable, even though they acted with due care and in good faith, when they enter into ultra vires transactions.31 This rule seems harsh, in view of the recognized difficulty oftentimes of determining what is ultra vires. 

Other states hold that if they acted in good faith, and there was no lack of due care and diligence, they are not liable for damages caused by ultra vires acts on their part.32 Which of these lines of authority Texas will follow is shrouded in doubt.33 It will be very interesting to watch the outcome.

By Third Persons on Corporate Contracts 

The liability of officers and agents of a corporation on contracts entered into by them is the same as in the case of any other person assuming to act as agent for another.36 The questions that arise in this connection are not at all peculiar to the law of corporations, but depend entirely upon established principles of the law of agency. An agent of a corporation may enter into a contract without disclosing the fact that he is acting for the corporation. His liability in such a case is precisely the same as if he acted for an undisclosed natural principal. One of the familiar rules of agency is that where the agent acts for an undisclosed principal the third party must elect to hold either the principal or the agent liable. He cannot recover against both. But in 

Texas he is not put to his election until after all the evidence is when the directors are guilty of ultra vires acts which result in injury to the stockholders. No mention was made of the effect that good faith of the directors would have on the

Therefore, the third party may sue both the agent and the undisclosed principal, and after both sides have closed their testimony, elect the one against whom he wishes judgment.37 There are several exceptions to the general rule that the third party can hold the undisclosed principal liable. 

Two of these exceptions are that only those whose names appear on (1) sealed instruments and (2) negotiable paper can be held liable in suits on such instruments.38 For a comprehensive discussion of the law on this subject, therefore, reference should be had to works on the law of agency. 

When the officer of a corporation enters into a contract on behalf of the corporation in such a way as to bind the corporation, and the other party is aware of the true facts, the officer is not personally liable.39 In such cases it is the understanding of the parties that the corporation is the contracting party, and the officer, if he was acting within the scope of his authority, or if the transaction is ratified by the corporation, is merely acting as the agent40 of the corporation, and the usual rules of agency apply. That is, it is the principal alone who is liable on the contract, unless the agent misled the contracting party into believing that he was a principal.41 If the agent exceeded his authority so

On Warranty of Authority 

If an officer enters into a contract for and in the name of the corporation, but in excess of his authority, and the contract is not ratified by the corporation, and the other party did not know that the agent had no authority to bind the company, he is personally liable on the well established rule of agency. The agents' liability is predicated on "implied warranty of authority," and the measure of damages is the injury resulting from the agent's want of authority and not that resulting from the breach of the contract itself.46 This same principle applies to a contract made by an officer of a purported corporation, when in fact there is no corporation; i. e., where the promoters of the purported corporation did not so far comply with the laws of the state where it was supposed to be incorporated as to form either a de jure or a de facto corporation. If the unauthorized contract is subsequently ratified by the corporation, and it is intra vires of the powers of the corporation, the agent is not liable.47 If the trans-

But by the weight of authority where a person enters into a contract with the officers of a corporation, intending to contract with the corporation, and the contract is not binding on the corporation because it is ultra vires, the person so contracting is charged with notice of the want of power on the part of the corporation, and for that reason he cannot hold the officers personally responsible.52 One of the exceptions to the rule that every agent warrants his authority is where the agent shows the evidence of his authority to the third party. Since the law charges the third party with notice of the charter of the corporation with which he deals and the courts presume that everyone knows the law, where one enters into an ultra vires contract, he is charged with knowledge that the agent has no authority to bind the corporation. For the above reason, the agent is not liable to the third party on "warranty of authority" since he is charged with notice of the authority of the agent.53

Section 332 of Rest. of Agency provides: "An agent making a contract for a disclosed principal whose contracts are voidable because of lack of full capacity to contract, or for a principal who, although having capacity to contract generally, is incompetent to enter into the particular transaction, is not thereby liable to the other party. He does not become liable by reason of the failure of the principal to perform, unless he contracts or represents that the principal has capacity or unless he has reason to know of the principal's lack of capacity and of the other party's ignorance thereof." In Comment (a) to the above section it is said: "An agent does not warrant that his principal has full contractual capacity any more than he warrants that his principal is solvent. A review of the Texas cases will show that they follow the weight of authority as discussed in the preceding paragraph. 

In Ray v. Foster 54 an officer of a lumber company took in land on a debt owed to the corporation. It was claimed that the authority to take land in payment of a debt was not specifically given to this corporation, and that it was therefore ultra vires, and that the officer was consequently liable on the contract. The court held that he was not liable if he had acted in good faith in the transaction, without passing on the question whether the act really was ultra vires. 66 # The Court of Civil Appeals in Staacke v. Routledge 55 held the principal stockholders and officers liable for injury to a third person while carrying on an ultra vires transaction. This decision was reversed by the Supreme Court on the ground that the act was not ultra vires. In handing down its decision the Supreme Court by way of dictum said: 56 if it be granted that the acts of the Rambler Automobile Company complained of by defendant in error are ultra vires, still they were not in violation of an express statute; they were not mala in se or mala prohibita, or against public policy. The doing of such an ultra vires act would not make the plaintiffs in error, as stockholders or officers of the company, liable personally for the acts of the corporation." And in First National Bank v. Commercial National Bank 57 it was held that where an agent, acting as an officer of the corporation, performs an act which he believes in good faith to be within the authority of the corporation but which is actually ultra vires, the agent may not be held personally liable in the absence of a showing that the person with whom the agent dealt was misled by misrepresentations

From these cases it seems certain that Texas follows the cases which hold that the third party may not hold an officer personally responsible for an ultra vires contract made by him on behalf in the corporation 59 for the reason that the third party has notice of the charter of the corporation with which he deals, and, therefore, the case falls within the exception to the general rule of "warranty of authority" to the effect that the agent is not liable where he discloses his authority to the third party. 

The above rule is based on two fictions: (1) That everyone knows the law, and (2) that one is charged with knowledge of the provisions of the charter of every corporation with which one deals, and for that reason should not be extended any further. It could be argued with some reason that in the case where the agent does not warrant his authority because the principal does not have legal capacity to make the contract, that it is obligatory on the part of the agent to determine that question of law before he purports to have authority to find the principal.

If the agent acts for a foreign corporation, and the company has not complied with the local law which permits it to do business in the state, the agent is liable if because of non-compliance with the statute the corporation is not liable. The reason for this rule is that the agent has easier access than the third party to information as to whether the foreign corporation has complied with conditions precedent to its right to do business in the state where the transaction took place.63 These rules apply in the absence of a statute making the agent liable. 

The cases cited for the above rule of law involved strict statutes which virtually prohibited the foreign corporation from doing business in the local state before the statute was complied with. In most of these cases the acts of the foreign corporation in the local state were "null and void." Under the Texas statute the acts of the foreign corporation are not void. The penalty imposed on the foreign corporation is that it cannot sue in a Texas court on obligations due it arising out of the transaction of business in Texas, but it is liable to the other party on obligations created by it even though it has not complied with the Texas statutes applicable to foreign corporations transacting business in Texas.64 For this reason the above rule should have

By Third Persons for Torts 

It is well settled that a man is liable personally for all torts committed by him even though he is an agent of another when the tort was committed. The mere fact that he is working for a corporation does not relieve him from such liability, and he is personally liable whether the tort is committed within or without the scope of his agency. If the tort is committed by the agent while acting within the scope of his authority, the corporation itself is also liable; the injured party may sue and recover against either, or recover against them both as joint tort-feasors.67

In the case of Bates v. Van Pelt,68 the employees of an irrigation company, acting under orders from the president, wrongfully filled up ditches on the land of the plaintiff, and the court held the president liable therefor even though the corporation might also have been held liable. 

It is well settled that the managing agents of a corporation, whether they are directors or trustees, who mingle money collected for another with the funds of the corporation in violation of the instructions of the owner, or who knowingly permit their subordinates to do so, and the fund is thereby lost, are personally liable therefor.

In McCollom v. Dollar,69 the defendant was a director of a corporation which appropriated money from cotton shipments belonging to the plaintiff. He knew of and took part in the transactions, and was held to be personally liable for the loss. 

This holding was reversed by the Commission of Appeals on the ground that knowledge on the part of the director was not established. In Dollar v. Lockney Supply Co.70 the director of a corporation which had misappropriated funds from cotton shipments was held to be liable personally therefor, where he took an active part in the transaction. The court in this case said, "We think it clearly held in this state that the directors of a corporation are personally liable for false representations made by them to an injured party, whether they know they are false or not." It should be noted that in all these cases where the plaintiff was permitted to recover a personal judgment against the directors, the tort was directly and specifically against the plaintiff and the damages were suffered by the plaintiff individually and not by all the creditors of the company. For instance, in Cameron v. First National Bank 72 the plaintiff bank was allowed to recover against the directors for misrepresenting the condition of the corporation where the plaintiff relied on the statement in giving credit to the corporation, and in McCollum v. 

Dollar 73 there was a conversion of plaintiff's property. In these cases the injury was primarily inflicted upon the plaintiff individually and no legal wrong was suffered by the corporation itself. A director who takes no part in and who knows nothing of the false report of the condition of the company is not liable.74

§ 688. 

By Creditors 

The creditors of an insolvent corporation, according to the weight of authority, may, in order to procure satisfaction of their claims, enforce the liability of directors and other officers of the corporation for losses resulting from their mismanagement of the corporate affairs. Most of the courts have based the right of action in such cases upon the ground that the assets of a corporation are a trust fund for the benefit of creditors, and that the officers are trustees for their benefit.75 The trustfund doctrine, however, has been virtually exploded and it is perhaps safe to say that no court would now hold specifically that any trust relation exists between the officers and the creditors of a corporation.76 The true basis of the right of creditors to proceed against the officers of a corporation is their right to reach equitable assets of the corporation and apply them to the satisfaction of their claims. The officers of a corporation, as has been seen, are liable to the corporation for losses caused by their fraud, negligence, or willful breach of duty, and this liability may be enforced by or for the benefit of the creditors when the corporation becomes insolvent. As the injury is done to the corporation the trustee in bankruptcy or the receiver of an insolvent corporation could sue and collect the damages suffered by the company. In these cases the creditors are permitted to liquidate the equitable assets of the corporation." Mere creditors of a corporation have no interest in a proceeding charging its directors with wasting assets until their claims are established either at law or in equity, and the other assets of the company, for the satisfaction of claims, have been exhausted.78 

Whatever may be the grounds upon which the right of action is based by the different courts, it is well settled that where the

Herring-Showers Lumber Co.89 a creditor sued the corporation and two of its directors, Waggoner and Greene. In September, 1920 the corporation, Burk-Waggoner Oil Company, was hopelessly insolvent, having assets of approximately $100,000 and liabilities of approximately $300,000. At a meeting of the board of directors on September 27, 1920, to avoid receivership, the directors Greene and Waggoner entered into a parol agreement with the corporation to take over all the assets of the corporation and assume all its liabilities. The property, some of which was real estate, was later conveyed by the corporation to Greene. The Supreme Court held that Waggoner was not liable on the parol contract by which he and Greene assumed the obligations of the company, because some of the assets were real estate, and therefore, the contract came within the statute of frauds. However, the court said: (* We believe the petition sufficient as against a general demurrer to have authorized a recovery in this case against

Such being the status of the corporation's affairs, it is obvious that all of its assets, personal and real, became (italics supplied) a trust fund for the payment of the debts of the corporation, upon which the defendant in error, as well as other creditors, has an equitable lien. "We think the board of directors, as directors and trustees, had the right to sell the property to Greene or Greene and Waggoner, in order to have the debts of the corporation paid; but the property passed, under the facts of this case, charged with an equitable lien in favor of the creditors of the corporation, dischargeable only upon the payment of the creditors in full or pro rata from the funds received from the corporate property, in the absence, of course, of some element of estoppel on the part of the creditors. From these quotations it is evident that the court did not mean to say that a creditor can bring an individual suit and recover the entire amount of his claim from one director where the directors have abused their authority, but that in such a case a creditor's bill may be brought by one creditor for the benefit of all. Of course, if Waggoner personally converted the property of the corporation to his own use, he would be held liable to the extent of the property converted (this point was not actually decided by the case), but even in that case the proceeds of the judgment should be paid to all of the creditors on a pro rata basis. It is definitely settled by the Supreme Court of Texas that a stockholder has no right to recover individually against the directors where they have been guilty of negligence or any other wrong that causes damage to the corporation. This was early settled in Texas by the case of Evans v. Brandon.⁹⁰ In that case it was held that primarily the corporation should sue the directors for damage that their misconduct caused the corporation even though the market price of the stock was diminished, but, if the corporation refused to sue, the stockholder could bring a shareholder's bill, making the corporation a party defendant, and in such cases the damages are payable to the corporation. The reason given by Judge Gould for this rule is that "On principle and authority, it is clear that the liability of directors for a breach of duty that injures the corporate property as a whole, is primarily to the corporation whose agents they are." This case was followed by the Commission of Appeals in the recent case of Stinnett v. Paramount-Famous Lasky Corporation.91 It seems evident from the above quotations from the case of Waggoner v. Herring

The corporation was further indebted to Campbell and Sons in the sum of $5,000. Campbell and Sons sold the cotton and applied the proceeds upon the indebtedness of the corporation. Suit is by Dollar, and the other farmers who delivered the cotton, against the directors of the corporation. In this case the corporation committed a specific tort in converting the plaintiff's property. There was no mismanagement by the directors resulting in waste of the corporate assets. The corporation converted to its own use and benefit property belonging to the plaintiffs. The proceeds of the sale were not an asset of the corporation. Certainly the liability of the directors in such a situation is something entirely different and apart from the case where the directors have negligently mismanaged the affairs of the corporation causing loss to it and indirectly to (all) its creditors.

It therefore seems evident that this case cannot be cited for the proposition that the directors are liable directly to creditors of the corporation as trustees of the corporate assets for the benefit of the creditors, although admittedly there is some language in the opinion which is not entirely clear and might be variously so construed.

It is so obvious that Cameron v. First National Bank 96 does not support the statement, little comment is necessary. In that case the directors made false statement of the financial condition of the corporation to the plaintiff, and in reliance upon the statement the plaintiff extended credit to the corporation. The directors were held liable. This case falls within the well settled rule that an agent acting within the scope of his authority and thereby perpetrating fraud upon another is personally liable therefor notwithstanding that his principal is also liable. The court said: "The general rule that mere negligent mismanagement of the business of a corporation by which the corporation and its creditors suffer loss will not relieve the directors of lia-

bility from representations sanctioned by them for the purpose of inducing, and by which another is induced, to loan money to the corporation. It seems to us that the distinction between the two cases is obvious." Thus it seems that the court itself repudiates the very doctrine which the writer of the North Carolina 

Law Review comment cited as supporting.

Neither of these cases refers to directors as trustees of the corporate assets for the benefit of creditors. 

It may, therefore, be concluded that in Texas the directors and officers of a corporation will never be personally liable to the creditors in an immediate action, except for direct torts to the creditor. But in the case of direct torts the courts have imposed strict liability. 

It has been held that a depositor in a bank may maintain an action in tort against the directors or other officers for loss of his deposit by reason of their fraud or negligence in the management of the bank, on the ground of fraud or deceit in holding out the bank as solvent and thereby inducing the public to allow deposits to remain in the bank. In Seale v. Baker," the defendants, as directors of a bank, published statements to the effect that the bank was in sound financial condition when in fact it was not, which fact the defendants reasonably should have known. The defendants were held liable even though they did not know that they had made misrepresentations to the plaintiff, who deposited money upon his faith in such misrepresentations. The court said: "If the representations are false, but relied and acted on by a customer to his damage, to hold in such a case the directors who made such false representations are not liable because of their ignorance of the falsity of the representations would be to award a premium for negligence in the performance of important and almost sacred duties voluntarily assumed, and to license fraud and deception of the most flagrant and pernicious character."98

§ 689. Statutory Liability of Directors and Officers 

For the better protection of the creditors of corporations, the Texas legislature has enacted statutes making the directors and other officers personally liable for corporate debts if they shall neglect to perform certain duties imposed on them, or if they shall do certain acts which are prohibited. 

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1347, provides that, "If the directors of any corporation shall knowingly declare and pay any dividend when the corporation is insolvent, or any dividend the payment of which would render it insolvent, they shall be jointly and severally liable for all the debts of the corporation then existing, and for all the debts of the corporation which thereafter, during the time such directors respectively remain in office, shall be contracted. The amount for which they shall be so liable shall not exceed the amount of such dividend. If any director is absent at the time of declaring the dividend or shall object thereto at the time such dividend is declared and shall file his objections in writing with the secretary or other officer of the corporation having charge of the books, he shall be exempt from said liability." 1

Article 7091 provides: "Each director and officer of any corporation whose right to do business within this state shall be so forfeited (for failure to pay franchise tax) shall, as to any and all debts of such corporation which may be created or incurred, with his knowledge, approval and consent, within this state, after such forfeiture by any such directors or officers, and before the revival of the right of such corporation to do business, be deemed and held liable thereon in the same manner and to the same extent as if such directors and officers of such corporation were partners." 

Article 533 3 provides: "No president, director, manager, cashier, or other officer or agent of any bank or banking institution organized and doing business under the provisions of this article shall receive or assent to the reception of deposits, or create or assent to the creation of any debts by such bank after he shall have knowledge of the fact that it is insolvent or in failing circumstances. Every person violating the provisions of this article shall be individually responsible for such deposits so received and all debts so contracted. Any director who may have paid more than his share of the liabilities mentioned in this article may have the proper remedy at law against such other persons as shall not have paid their full share of such liabilities. In case of the insolvency of one or more of such officers, agents or managers, the same shall be paid for the time being by those who are solvent, in equal proportion."

Construction of the Statutes 

An attempt to formulate a general rule to govern the construction to be placed on all types of these statutes would be a hazardous undertaking. Consideration must be given to the result that the Legislature wished to attain. If the statute makes the director liable for the resulting damage to the corporation, stockholders or creditors, it is remedial as to them. 

On the other hand, if it exacts a sum for violation of a duty, without regard to the loss suffered, it is in the nature of a penalty. It is said that such statutes are penal in character. The use of the word "penal" may be confusing. The statutes are not penal in the same sense that a criminal statute is penal. The burden imposed upon the director or officer by these statutes is onerous. It is not apportioned to the amount of the interest which the director or officer may have in the corporation, thus differing from the statutory liability of stockholders in banks. 

It is not predicated upon the amount of benefit which the direc- 

5. Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 536. 

6. Baker v. Smith, 102 A. 721, 41 R. 

I. 17. 

Huntington v. Attrill, 13 S.Ct. 224, 146

See, Dean v. Shingle, 246 P. 1049, 198 Cal. 652, 46 A.L.R. 1156. 36

tor or officer received from doing the act which violated the statute. 

Since the penalty imposed by these statutes is onerous, they are strictly construed. The liability cannot be extended beyond the strict terms of the statute, and a clear case must be established to render an officer liable." 

Before the plaintiff can recover under Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 7091 against the officers after the company's right to do business has been forfeited for non-payment of the franchise tax, the plaintiff's petition must set forth all the essential facts prescribed by the statute for the defendant's liability. But in proving that the company had failed to pay its franchise tax the deposition of the Secretary of State is not admissible. Copies of the records are the best evidence. But in the above case the court held that copies of the records attached to the deposition of the Secretary of State were admissible to show that the company's right to do business had been forfeited for failure to pay the franchise tax.⁹ 

One of the directors or trustees, who is also a creditor of the corporation, cannot maintain an action under the statutes against his co-trustees or co-directors for breach of duty, and his assignee stands in the same position. To allow such an action would enable him to profit by his own wrong or negligence,10 except where the director or trustee is innocent and free from fault or culpability. Liability may be enforced by a creditor who is a stockholder, where the directors refuse to institute the suit. 

The suit should be in the form of a stockholder's bill.11

An action against a director by a creditor of the corporation under these statutes is within the statute of limitations regulating "actions for debt where the indebtedness is not evidenced by a contract in writing." 12 The statute begins to run from the time the cause of action accrues in favor of the creditor, and not from the time of default on the part of the directors.13 

It has been repeatedly held that these statutes are of such a penal character that there is no vested right in a cause of action arising under them until it has been reduced to judgment. 

The statutes may be repealed before action has been commenced or at any time before judgment, and an action previously commenced cannot be further prosecuted.¹4 Since Texas courts treat the cause of action as an action on a debt, as regards the statutes of limitation,15 it is very probable that they will hold that the purpose of our statutes is to protect the creditors and not to punish the guilty parties. 

Where a statute imposes a certain duty upon a director or an officer, and prescribes a penalty for its non-performance, the test prescribed in the statute is the only test, both of liability and of the standard of conduct required.16

Enforcement in Foreign Jurisdiction 

It becomes important in certain situations to determine whether these statutes are really penal or not. The courts of one state or country do not execute the penal laws of another. But in applying this rule there is a danger of being misled by the different shades of meaning allowed the word "penal" in our language.¹7 

Many courts have held that this rule applies to statutes of a state imposing personal liability upon the directors for corporate debts as a penalty for failing to do some act required of them by law, or for doing acts prohibited; that such statutes are penal statutes, within this rule, and that they will not be enforced in the courts of other states.18

The more recent cases, following Huntington v. Attrill, 19 hold that the above rule applies only to penal laws in the strict sense -laws imposing a punishment for offenses against the stateand that debts are not penal laws in this sense.20 In determin-

These authorities will be followed in Texas. In Southwestern 

Portland Cement-Latta-Happer case 43 the court held that an officer who buys property expecting to sell it to the corporation must disclose all facts concerning the price he paid; and if guilty of a breach of his fiduciary duties to his own corporation, a court of equity will give proper relief to the company. In that case Justice Higgins said: "Of course, the president of a corporation occupies a fiduciary capacity (relation), and, where he personally acquires property with the view of disposing of it to the company and does do so, he becomes liable to the company for any profit which he may make out of the transaction, unless he makes a full disclosure and the entire contract is open, fair, and honest." In that case it was shown that the officer did not buy the property which he later sold to the company with the idea of selling it to his own corporation. In view of that fact, and especially as the company paid less for the property than the officer had been offered for it, Justice Higgins was justified in appending to his clear statement of the law the "unless" clause. If facts had shown that the corporation was in the market for the land when the officer bought it, the court, no doubt, would have decreed that the officer was a trustee of the land for the corporation and would have forced him to convey the property to the corporation for what "the trustee" paid for it regardless of how much it had increased in value since he purchased it.

Just when a director of a corporation can purchase property that would be advantageous to the corporation, and be permitted to hold individually, is an unsettled question. One writer contends that a director cannot purchase such property where "the purchase is appropriate to the corporation." 4 Minn.Law Rev. 513-520.

Such a test is of little assistance in determining specific cases. Some courts have held that if the corporation is in the market for the property, a director cannot purchase the property for himself, but must hold it as a trustee for the corporation. The leading American cases on this question are cited. Farwell v. Pyle-National Electric Headlight Co., 289 Ill. 

157, 124 N.E. 449; Coleman v. Hanger, 210 Ky. 309, 275 S.W. 784; Harmony 

Way Bridge Co. v. Leathers, 353 Ill. 

378, 187 N.E. 432; Young v. Columbia Oil Co., 110 W.Va. 364, 158 S.E. 

678; Zeckendorf v. Steinfeld, 12 Ariz. 

245, 10 P. 784; Tierney v. United 

Pocahontas Coal Co., 85 W.Va. 545, 102 S.E. 249; Lagarde v. Anniston 

Lime & Stone Co., 126 Ala. 496, 28 

So. 199; Thilco Timber Co. v. Sawyer, 236 Mich. 401, 210 N.W. 204; Carper v. Frost Oil Co., 72 Colo. 345, 211 P. 

370. See, 39 Columbia Law Rev. 219, 4 Minn.Law Rev. 513, 44 Yale Law Jr. 

527, 84 U. of Pa.L.Rev. 1008, 2 U. of 

Chicago Law Rev. 323; Irving Trust 

Co. v. Deutsch, 73 F.2d 121. These cases do not give an absolute test for determining the problem. The final test must be what reasonable business men will determine is the duty of the director in view of all the facts of the specific case before the court. 

If the directors have never discussed the purchase of a new location for the principal office of the corporation, any director is free to purchase any real property in the city where the principal place of business is located. However, if the directors decided to move the present location of the principal office of the company, most reasonable business men would conclude that a director is not free to purchase a suitable new location without first submitting the offer to the corporation. Between these two extreme cases many troublesome ones will arise. But, as stated above, the final test which must be applied by the triers of the facts in each case must be, would reasonable business men, conversant with all the facts. 48

Ch. § 694 

director or officer has breached his duty to the corporation in this regard, equity will intervene to impress a trust for the benefit of the corporation upon the profits arising from the competitive business, or upon the competitive business itself.48 If the courts could be induced to look upon the corporation as a real legal person created by real men and women through state sanction, and not as a nebulous something, conflicts in the authorities on this question would be easily resolved. The law as to when a partner has reached his duty to the firm in the conduct of a competing business is fairly well settled. A corporation is a distinct legal person formed under state authority by real human beings to whom is granted the right to carry on a business with lund, 29 S.W.2d 165, 225 Mo.App. 262; 

Dodge Stationery Co. v. Dodge, 78 P. 

879, 145 Cal. 380; 9 Miss.L.Jr. 427;

Hopper v. Western Tablet & Station ery Co., C.C.A.Mich., 66 F.2d 172. 

Compare, Citizens Trust & Deposit Co. v. Tompkins, 54 A. 617, 97 Md. 182.

The general rule is stated in 64 A.L. 

R. 784 as follows: "Generally it is held that directors or officers of a corporation are not by reason of the fiduciary relationship they bear toward the corporation and the stockholders thereof precluded from entering into and engaging in a business enterprise independent from, though similar to, that conducted by the corporation itself, provided that in doing so they act in good faith and do not interfere with the business engaged in by the corporation." Very often it is difficult to apply this general rule to a fact situation. The truth this statement is illustrated in a recent Arkansas case in which two of the Supreme Court justices dissented. Witmer V. Arkansas 

Dailies, Inc., Ark., 151 S.W.2d 971.

In applying this test the triers of the facts should ask this question:

Would the average business man consider it honest and fair to the corporation for the director to purchase the property individually in view of all the facts known to the director at the time he purchased the property?

This question has not been decided by the Supreme Court of Texas.

limited personal liability. It is even less a fiction in law than the United States Army or a partnership. 

A stockholder in a corporation can invest his money in the stock of competing corporations. He should not, however, become the manager of a competing corporation. He should not be made a director of two or more competing companies lest information acquired in conducting the affairs of one corporation be used to the detriment of the other.49 The law should not sanction or condone piracy by officers and directors of a corporation any more than it does in the case of partners. 

It is generally held to be a breach of trust where the director or officer of the corporation obtains for his own benefit a lease of property which is under an existing lease to the corporation.50 But the acquisition of a lease by a corporate officer will not always be taken to be for the benefit of the corporation. 

Thus, a director and general manager of a corporation holding property under a lease providing that it shall become void if a paying marble quarry is not established on the land within a specified time, who knows that the lessor is about to forfeit the lease for failure of the lessee to establish the quarry, is not obligated to inform other persons interested in the corporation of that fact. He may individually lease the land after the lease to the corporation has been forfeited, where he used ordinary care in an endeavor to develop and establish the quarry for the benefit of the corporation and thus prevent a forfeiture of its lease, failing to do so through no fault of his own, but because the corporation could not finance it.51 If the president estab-

Purchase of Property at Public Sale 

The general rule is that a director or officer of a corporation has no right to purchase the corporate property at a judicial or public sale, and if he does so, the sale is voidable.68 Nor can he do indirectly what he could not do directly. He cannot evade the law by causing the corporate property to be purchased ostensibly for another but in reality for himself.69 The duty of the directors and officers of a corporation is to further the interests and business of the association and to conserve its property. The justice of applying this rule in certain situations is quite clear. An illustration of such a situation is where the officer as part of a conspiracy, instigated the sale in order to purchase the corporate property for his own benefit." Or where, in dereliction of his duty, the officer allowed the taxes to become delinquent in order that he might buy the property at the tax sale.72 Or where the officer, in violation of his instructions to purchase for the corporation, buys the property at the forced sale for himself.73

It is quite generally stated that, in order to have the sale disaffirmed, actual fraud need not be shown.74 Proof of a breach of official duty by the officer is all that is required.75 Thus, the appearance of a director as a bidder at the sale might have the effect of dampening the bidding, and in that respect there would be a breach of duty.76

The director may be forced to purchase the property at the sale in order to protect his interest. It is well settled that a director may lend money to the corporation and may take security. In such case he has the right to purchase at a judicial or other public 57

If the corporation is insolvent at the time of the forced sale or is rendered insolvent by such sale, the right of a corporate officer to purchase the property is even more limited, generally, than if the corporation were solvent.83 In Tobin Canning Co. v. 

Fraser, plaintiff, a director of the defendant corporation, sued on a note executed by the defendant corporation. Defendant, by way of counterclaim, sought to recover of plaintiff profits he had made in a purchase of corporate property. Two judgments had been taken against the corporation in a justice court. The corporation was virtually insolvent. Practically all its property was sold on execution to satisfy the above two judgments. If it was not insolvent at the time, this sale to the director made it insolvent. Plaintiff was not a party to the judgments under which the property was sold. He purchased the property at the execution sale at a price much less than it was reasonably worth. The court held that plaintiff was a trustee for the corporation of the value of the property, less what he had paid for it. The court, in speaking of the director's relation to the corporation, uses this language: "The assets of an insolvent corporation is a fund subject to the claims of creditors, and upon which they have an equitable lien for the payment of their demands. The property is chargeable in the hands of the directors as a trust, for the preservation of which they are bound to good faith and fair dealings in the management and disposition thereof. They are the agents and trustees of the corporation, and when they deal with its important interests they are charged with the utmost fairness, and will not be permitted to reap benefits to the injury of the corporation and its creditors. 

The law will not permit the directors to participate in acts relative to the corporate property that will result in their personal and private advantage, to the injury of the corporation, when

§ 698. - Transactions between a Corporation and Its Officers and Directors

Officers and directors are not absolutely precluded from dealing with the corporation. Contracts and other transactions between them are not void but are voidable at the option of the corporation under certain circumstances.88 In order for a transaction between an officer or director on the one hand and the corporation on the other to be sustained, it must have been authorized by directors other than the one who is interested in the transaction; that is, he must not have been counted to make a quorum, and he must not have voted on the transaction.89 But

equitable principles, and it has been frequently laid down in the broadest terms that, such is the duty of each of them to give to the company his disinterested efforts in promoting its interests, that a purchase from or sale to it by one of them may be avoided at its option, whether the transaction be fair or not and although the corporation were represented by other directors who would be competent to act for it in the same kind of a transaction with one not connected with the company. It is said that each director is under obligation in such transactions to give to his associates the benefit of his unbiased aid and counsel, and that he cannot divest himself of this duty nor be released from it by his cotrustees. For this reason, many of the authorities treat such transactions as being controlled by the principle that a trustee cannot purchase from, sell to, or deal with himself in the management of trust property, rather than that which governs transactions occurring directly between the trustee and cestui que trust. Carried to its logical results, this view would seem to avoid, at the mere option of the corporation or any one of its stockholders, any contract which a director might make with the company, for the reason given is that the danger of abuse and of concealment of fraud or unfairness is so great that a court of equity will not inquire into the fairness of the transaction but will allow the beneficiary the option of avoiding it whether fair or not. Aberdeen, etc., Railway Co. v. Blaikie, 2 

Eq. 1286; Imperial Merc. Ass'n v. Coleman, 40 L.J.Ch. 262, A.C. 

L.R. 6 Ch. 565; Cumberland Coal & Iron Co. v. Sherman, 30 

Barb., N.Y., 553. Actual adjudications have not always carried the doctrine to this extent, and in this country, at least, many of the decisions are wholly inconsistent with such an extension of it. "The right of directors to make fair contracts generally with the corporation is comprehensively stated by many authorities, and such contracts have been upheld in numerous cases, some of them involving purchases of corporate property. [Citing cases.] "It is doubtless right to allow a beneficiary the option of avoiding a trade affecting his interests which has been effected by a trustee representing both parties to it, for the reason that the 63

§ Ch. 14 

trustee ought not to be allowed to act for and bind two parties having conflicting interests. It may be perfectly just to apply this principle to transactions in negotiating which a director or directors of a corporation were personally interested, and, at the same time, represented the corporation, either alone or conjointly with codirectors; and this is probably the true spirit of the rule as it has been enforced in most of the cases. But we think it is not true that one who holds the position of director is incapable, under all circumstances, of divesting himself of his representative character in a particular transaction and dealing with the corporation through others competent to represent it, as other trustees may deal directly with the beneficiaries. "The corporation is a separate entity for which its board of directors acts. The persons having the beneficial interest in the property are the stockholders, but their rights are centered in the corporation and are managed and controlled through the board of directors as the active representative of the company, and it is through it and not the stockholders that business dealings are carried on. When a personal interest of one of them springs up adverse to that of the corporation, it disqualifies him to act concerning it as one of the representatives or agents. But the others do not lose their representative capacity and still have power to bind the company. The disqualified director can not deal with them as a stranger, because the position of confidence which he has held has enabled him to gather an intimate knowledge of the affairs of the corporation and to exercise influence upon those associated with him in their management. But the company is represented by those who alone can act for it, and if they are disinterested, he can, we think, deal with them as any other trustee can deal with the cestui que trust, if he makes a full disclosure of all facts known to him about the subject, takes no advantage of his position, deals honestly and openly, and concludes a contract fair and beneficial to the company. 

Such a transaction is always to be subjected to the closest examination, and a contract between those so situated which is prejudicial to the corporation should be held to be a fraud upon it; but it by no means follows from this, we think, 64

Ch. § 698 

that they can make no contract at all which is binding on the company and stockholders. The true interests of all may be best promoted in this way."

The court goes on to say that were this not the rule, one stockholder might prevent the corporation from making the best possible deal under the circumstances. The reason this is true is because the director, from his knowledge of the affairs of the corporation, might be willing to make a better trade from the standpoint of the corporation than it could otherwise obtain. 

The court further stated that when such transactions are attacked, the burden of sustaining them is upon the interested director. The corporation cannot sue for damages where the director acting in good faith, paid a fair price, since the corporation has suffered no damage,93 even though a full disclosure of all material facts was not made to the disinterested directors. 

The case of Tenison v. Patton 94 settled the law of Texas with reference to contracts between a director and his corporation. 

In this case the State National Bank of Dallas owned a tract of land that it wished to dispose of. Mr. O'Connor offered the 

Company $11,000, for the land provided that Mr. Tenison, a director, would handle the sale of the land for O'Connor, who agreed to give Mr. Tenison one-half of the profits resulting from the resale of the land. Mr. Tenison explained his connection with the transaction to his co-directors in detail, and was not counted to constitute a quorum when the resolution providing for the sale of the land to O'Connor was passed. Mr. Tenison did not take part in the director's meeting nor did he vote on the resolution. The testimony showed that Mr. Tenison made a full disclosure of all the facts to his co-directors and that the sale was fair and honest and the price obtained was reasonable even though Tenison and O'Connor thought that they could make a 25% profit out of the resale of the land by subdividing it. Supreme Court of Texas upheld the contract of sale to O'Connor on the ground that a director of a corporation may deal with the corporation if he does not represent the corporation in any way in making the contract with his own company. Judge Williams in the opinion stated that a director occupies a fiduciary relation to the corporation but said that in his dealings with the corporation it is in the nature of a trustee dealing with the cestui que trust rather than in the nature of a trustee buying or selling to himself individually. However, the court held that it is only where the director does not represent both parties that the contract is valid.

Judge Williams in the opinion states clearly that if the interested director "either alone or conjointly with co-directors" attempts to represent the corporation, the contract is voidable at the mere option of the corporation without showing non-disclosure, fraud, or that the director made a hard bargain with the corporation. 

He also said that "It is not true that one who holds the position of director is incapable, under all circumstances, of divesting himself of his representative character in a particular transaction and dealing with the corporation through others competent to represent it, as other directors may deal directly with the beneficiaries." In other words, Judge Williams made it evident that the only way that a director can contract with his corporation is to strip himself absolutely of his director relationship and not in any way attempt to represent the corporation in the transaction. It is evident from the above quotations that the court meant to hold that, if the director takes an active part in representing the corporation when the resolution concerning the contract is passed by the Board of Directors, the contract is voidable at the mere instance of the corporation even though the director is not counted to constitute a quorum and a majority of the disinterested directors vote in favor of the resolution. So far, no Texas court has held that the contract is valid where the director takes an active part in the meeting of the directors at which the resolution was adopted other than to disclose all the facts connected with the transaction, even though he is not counted to constitute a quorum and though his vote is not necessary to carry the resolution. 66

In Texas Auto Co. v. Arbetter,95 the sole question was whether a vendor offers a marketable title to the purchaser, where one link in the chain of title was a conveyance by a corporation where the deed was executed in pursuance of a resolution passed by two directors, one of them being the vendee. Here the interested director was counted to constitute a quorum and voted in favor of the resolution. The court held that the transaction was voidable without showing fraud, nondisclosure, or a hard bargain. 

It is true that in Brooks v. Zorn96 there is a dictum to the effect that a majority of the disinterested directors may ratify a voidable conveyance to one of the directors even though the interested director is present at the meeting when ratification was attempted, but the case was not decided on this point, and one judge stated that a majority of the directors were interested and for this reason the court was not called upon to consider the above question. In Leary v. Interstate National Bank" there were six directors of the corporation and only five of these directors were present when the resolution was passed. Two of the directors present at the meeting were interested personally in the contract that was authorized by the resolution. The Court assumed that the transaction was void as the Court said the two interested directors could not be counted to determine whether a quorum was present. 

Under the present Texas law they could be counted to determine whether a quorum was present, but the contract entered into at such a meeting with one of the directors would be voidable at the mere option of the corporation.98 The contract is voidable at the instance of the corporation, or a shareholder suing on behalf of the corporation, but it cannot be attacked by one who has no interest in the corporation.99

Ratification

Even though the transaction was not authorized by a majority of disinterested directors, it is binding upon the corporation if it is subsequently ratified by them, or by ratification on the part of the stockholders.11 But if there was fraud in the transaction, it can be ratified only by a unanimous vote of the stockholders.12 

Ratification can be by acquiescence,13 either on the part of the board of directors or stockholders.

It is said that courts will scrutinize such contracts and, upon the discovery of the slightest appearance of fraud or unfairness, will set them aside. The most frequent transactions which fall within this class are those where an officer, or one of the directors of a corporation enters into a contract with the corporation for his own benefit, or where two corporations having the same or a majority of the directors, or controlling officers in common, deal with each other through such directors, or managing officers. To this group or class we think the transaction here under consideration is more nearly referable. That this contract was not void absolutely we think is perfectly clear. * It frequently occurs in this country that two or more corporations have the same directors and managing officers in common. Are they for that reason to be deprived of the privilege of making advantageous agreements between themselves? Such a rule would seriously interfere with another well-established policy of the law-to allow freedom of commerce and trade. 

We think relief should not be withheld in cases like the one under consideration, unless it be shown that a trust relation has been violated in the making of the contract, and that fraud, or at least unfairness, has been practiced toward the party sought to be bound thereby.15

In the cases which hold that a voidable transaction between a director and his own corporation induced by fraud can be ratified only by a unanimous vote of the stockholders, the courts have seldom explained the meaning of the term "fraud." It is believed by the writer that the courts do not mean by that term what it usually connotes to judges and lawyers when they say that it takes a unanimous vote of the stockholders to ratify "fraud." In other words, do the courts mean to hold that a transaction between a director and his own corporation based on innocent misrepresentation can be ratified by a majority vote of the stockholders, but that the same transaction induced by a conscious false representation can be ratified only by a unanimous vote of the stockholders? That distinction should not be made by the courts, and it is not sustained by the cases in which the above statement is made. 

The most satisfactory discussion of this point is found in the case of Russell v. Henry C. Patterson Company.22 In that case the court said: "Of course, this assumes that the act is not fraudulent or detrimental to the interests of the corporation. 

The stockholders could not bind the corporation by ratifying a contract made by the directors with the company which would fraudulently dispose of or waste the assets of the corporation. 

To hold otherwise, would be to permit a minority stockholder to control the majority stockholders and their benefit. This cannot be done. The majority stockholders may not as against the stockholder and a minority stockholder dissipate

As we have already seen in our discussion of the power of the directors of the corporation, the statutes of practically all English jurisdictions provide that the business of the corporation shall be conducted by a board of directors.24 It is difficult for the writer to understand why the courts in the teeth of these statutes say that a voidable transaction between a director and his own corporation, in the absence of fraud, can be ratified by a majority vote of the stockholders. As we have already seen, the stockholders have no right to conduct the business of the corporation. This is a matter that falls within the sound discretion of the directors.25 What would the courts hold in the following hypothetical cases? Let us suppose that at the meeting of the directors the plaintiff offered to make a certain contract with his own corporation. Let us further suppose that at the meeting the interested director was guilty of innocent misrepresentation, nondisclosure, or that he drove a hard bargain with his own corporation. At the next meeting of the directors before there had been any performance of the contract the plaintiff told the directors that at the last meeting when he made a contract with the corporation he was guilty of innocent misrepresentation; that he now knows the actual facts about the matter, and explained them in detail to the directors. At this meeting the director was not counted to constitute a quorum and did not vote on the contract. However, all the other directors voted in favor of ratifying the voidable transaction. Soon thereafter a stockholders' meeting was called, and the stockholders by a majority vote resolved to disaffirm the above contract. 

Again suppose at the second meeting of the directors they voted to disaffirm the voidable contract. Soon thereafter a stockholdexercisable by a minority stockholder unless the contract is ultra vires, fraudulent or oppressive."

Should the courts not say that the statute gives the directors the right to control the business of the corporation and that the affirmance or disaffirmance of a voidable contract is an ordinary business transaction, and, therefore, hold that the affirmance or disaffirmance of the contract comes within the sound discretion of the directors rather than the stockholders? However, the courts have fallen in the habit of saying that whether the voidable transaction will be affirmed or disaffirmed comes within the jurisdiction of the stockholders. 

In other words, this is one of the few instances in which the courts say that the stockholders have the right to conduct the business of the corporation. The courts have given too little attention to this matter.

The reason usually given in the cases for the rule that a majority of the stockholders can ratify a voidable transaction is that in the last analysis the stockholders of a corporation are the owners of the property of the company. Throughout this text it is made plain that the law of private corporations will always be in a state of confusion if the fictitious character of the corporation is stressed. Even though it is admitted that a corporation is as much a reality as a partnership, and that its property really belongs to its stockholders, still that is scarcely a justification for saying that the statute which vests the management of the business of the corporation "in a board of directors" should be disregarded where the question is whether a voidable transaction should be ratified or disaffirmed.26

702. Purchase of Stock by Directors and Officers 

The relation of officers and directors to individual stockholders with respect to purchase of stock by the former from the latter has never been discussed in any Texas case. The prevailing view is that in such case there is no fiduciary relationship. 

An officer or director can deal with a stockholder as stranger and is under no duty to disclose information concerning the value of the stock, even though he has knowledge the stockholder does not have regarding its value, and has obtained it by virtue of his position as officer or director.34 However, some courts, recog-

Kasch38 the same principle was involved as where the officer or director purchases the stock from the shareholder. In the Conrads-Kasch case one of the principal shareholders induced the stockholders to sell all the property of the company to him. Most of the shareholders were farmers and many of them thought they were selling their stock to the defendant Kasch. Kasch was president, a director and general business manager of the corporation from its formation until its dissolution. He did not disclose the real value of the assets, and for that reason the court held that the sale was voidable. In that case Justice Baugh said: "Undoubtedly, we think he became a trustee for the corporation and for the other stockholders. See Tenison v. Patton, 95 Tex. 284, 67 S.W. 92, 95.

As such it was his duty not only to make full and fair disclosure of all material facts as to assets, values, etc., but to pay a fair and adequate price for all such assets acquired by him; and it was his affirmative duty to show as much when his dealings were called in question."

When the question is finally submitted to the Supreme Court if it does not blindly follow the "weight of authority" it will affirm Judge Baugh's decision in the Conrads-Kasch case and hold that an officer of a corporation does not deal at arm's length with a shareholder in purchasing the latter's stock. In the case of Trinity-Universal Ins. Co. v. Maxwell,39 a stockholder was seeking the rescission of his contract with the company on the ground of fraud. § 703. Limitations of actions against directors or officers 

The limitations of actions against officers begin to run from the time when those who are entitled to complain know, or are chargeable with knowledge of the facts.41 Knowledge of the directors who are adversely interested will not be imputed to the corporation, its stockholders or creditors.42 Nor is a stockholder charged with such knowledge merely because of entries in the corporate records which he had a right to examine.43

731. Officers and Agents-Distinction 

Generally at the time when a corporation comes into legal existence, there are no officers other than the board of directors named in the charter as required by the corporation laws of the state.¹ Some state statutes enumerate all the officers whose duty it is to govern and manage the affairs of the corporation, but the Texas statutes designate only three officers specifically; namely, the president, the secretary and the treasurer. In Texas it is customary to name only the directors in the charter, the other officers being designated in the by-

In order properly to understand the principles governing officers and agents in their connection with a corporation, it is imperative that the distinguishing features of corporate officers, agents, and servants be noticed. It is conceivable that a person might be a stockholder, a director, an officer and yet an employee of a corporation all at the same time. Prior to 1923 in Texas this was the holding of the courts for purposes of compensation under the Workmen's Compensation Law, and this notwithstanding the statute provided: "The president, vicepresident, vice-presidents, secretary or other officers thereof provided in its charter or by-laws and the directors of any corporation which is a subscriber to this act shall not be deemed or held to be an employee within the meaning of that term as defined in the preceding section hereof." 5 The courts construed the statute as excluding officers and directors only when their injury occurred in the course of their duties as such officers or directors, and not otherwise. Vernon's Ann. Civ.St. art. 1323 provides that "an annual election shall be held for directors or trustees, at such time and place as the by-laws of the corporation may require." In other words, this statute provides in plain and unambiguous language that the directors should be elected annually at such time during the calendar year and at such place in Texas as the by-laws require. And the amendment to article 1323 passed in 1927 provides that the corporations specified above "may elect directors for three years." The general incorporation statutes form a part of the charter of corporations formed under the general law. 

Therefore, as to the corporations named above, to which reference is made in the 1927 amendment, they "may elect their directors for three years" without a provision to that effect in their by-laws. As to all other corporations formed under the general incorporation statutes, the directors should be elected "annually". A majority of the board of directors is authorized by statute to fill vacancies in their own board.20 By a vote of its stockholders cast as its by-laws may direct, the corporation has the power to increase or diminish the number of its directors or trustees, such number cannot be less than three; 21 and it is unnecessary to amend the charter of a corporation in order legally to increase the number of the directors.22 From one 

Texas case the principle can be deduced that the members of the board of directors, to be a legally elected board, must be elected within the boundaries of Texas.23 But the failure to elect directors on the day appointed by the by-laws will not dissolve the corporation, nor prevent the corporation from proceeding with board and to transact all business of the corporation. 734. De Facto Officers and Directors 46 

"The doctrine de facto is of ancient origin and owes its practically universal acceptance by the courts to the justice and necessities of society. Text-writers trace its origin back as far as 1431 to a case recorded in the Year Books under the name of The Abbe de Fontaine."47 The doctrine originated in the field of public law and a great amount of the de facto law is concerned with public officers. At least one court has expressed a doubt as to whether "there is in law such thing as a de facto officer with respect to any other than a public office."48 However, practically every jurisdiction in the United States has in some manner applied the de facto doctrine to the law of private corporation, and to that application this section is principally devoted.49 

As stated by Justice Werner in Matter of Ringler & Co.,50 "The de facto doctrine is one of those legal makeshifts by which unlawful or irregular corporate and public acts are legalized for certain purposes on the score of necessity. It 'was introduced into the law,' said Chief Judge Butler in the leading case of State v. Carroll (38 Conn. 449, 9 Am.Rep. 409), 'as a matter of policy and
