The reason of the rule upon which this policy is founded is stated to be that 'third persons, from the nature of the case, cannot always investigate the right of one assuming to hold an important office, even so far as to see that he has color of title to it by virtue of some appointment or election. If they see him publicly exercising its authority, if they ascertain that this is generally acquiesced in, they are entitled to treat him as such officer, and, if they employ him as such, should not be subjected to the danger of having his acts collaterally called in question."51 

As is generally stated, "Under the de facto doctrine, persons holding office under color of an election (or appointment) and having charge of corporate affairs are capable of binding the corporation in all matters properly devolving upon directors (or officers); and the fact that their election was irregular and that they have been removed from the office will not affect the validity and binding effect of their acts while in office."52

Ordinarily statutes, charter or by-laws provide that officers shall continue in office a specified time and until their successors are elected and qualified. Thus it seems that officers holding over after the expiration of the term until successors are elected and qualify would be de jure officers, and there is authority to that effect.60 Certainly they are at least de facto officers.61 And even where officers of the corporation were formally removed yet continued in the office transacting the business of the corporation during the pendency of litigation over the removal it has been held that the officers are de facto officers and not mere usurpers.62 Though a person does not sufficiently meet the requirements to make him a de jure officer he may, nevertheless, be a de facto officer according to the great weight of authority.63

In general de facto officers may do whatever de jure officers can do, at least so far as third persons are concerned.71 Some authorities hold that de facto officers may make appointments and fill vacancies in other offices to the same extent as de jure officers and that such appointees are not merely de facto but are de jure officers.72

§ 735. Term of Office or Employment 

Tenure of office is generally controlled by statutes or by the corporate by-laws;85 the person seeking election or the officer after election is presumed to know the provisions of the statute or by-laws and is bound by their terms. There should be an annual election of directors or trustees in Texas.86 By force of the provisions of Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1323 the term of office for a director is fixed, and the statutory term cannot be changed by the by-laws,87 or by the stockholders of the corporation.88 

The directors and other officers cannot combine to effectuate a scheme whereby they will perpetuate their term of office at high salaries, because such a combination is illegal and an abuse of trust; if an attempt to combine for such a purpose is made in Texas, a stockholder may institute mandamus proceedings to compel the proper officer to call a stockholders' meeting to elect new directors.89

The tenure of office, other than that of directors and trustees, is not fixed by statute, and it may, therefore, be regulated by the charter or by-laws. If it is not regulated by statute, charter or by-laws, the term of office or employment, with certain qualifications, is dependent on the period specified in the contract.⁹0 

The following statement has been made: "The fact that the directors are elected annually does not require that the term of an officer appointed by them shall be one year." 91 The results of the cases cited in support of this proposition are predicated on their own facts. In Germania Spar & Bau Verein v. Flynn,92 the governing statute provided that the directors were to be elected annually, but that the term of office for other officers might be set out in the charter or by-laws. ing for their election annually, "Each new board is responsible to the stockholders for the manner in which the business is conducted, and should, in the nature of things, be free to select its own agents. If one board of directors may contract with a manager for employment extending over a term of five years, they can materially handicap the freedom and power of their successors in the management of the business of the corporation. 

The successful operation of concerns of this character must depend largely upon the efficiency of the manager. It is too obvious for argument that the financial welfare of the corporation is best served by allowing each incoming board of directors all the power they may lawfully claim. 

It is manifest that in providing for a change in the directorate once every year it was intended to reserve to the stockholders the power also to control all those important agents upon whose efficiency the business success of the corporation depended. The stockholders could do little at their annual meetings toward removing an inefficient management of the affairs of the concern if so important an official as the manager could not be changed when a change was needed. "It is unimportant that the same members were repeatedly elected as directors. The validity of their action is to be determined by legal rules, and not by particular conditions that may exist. The fact that a new board is composed of the same individuals as the old board did not enlarge the legal authority of the old board."

While the holdings of the Texas cases are not as definite as might be desired, the writer feels that if the directors of Texas corporations do not have authority to employ managers or attorneys for longer than one year, very often the business of the company will be seriously hampered. If the position of the employee is of sufficient importance to secure a contract for a fixed term, the business success of the corporation usually, in a large measure, depends upon the efficiency of such employee. On the other hand, if the new board is bound by service contracts for a longer period than one year, such board will not be able to change entirely the policies of the corporation without keeping a close and continued supervision over the long term employee. 

This hypothesis is strengthened by the fact that the court in the Blewett case pointed out that the statement in 14A C.J. p. 

72, 19 C. J. S. Corporations, § 732 et seq., is not supported by the cases referred to in the notes. On the other hand, very often it will be difficult for the directors to induce a competent attorney or manager or other officer holding an important position to enter the employment of the corporation unless a long term contract is made with such employee. In many cases the success of the corporation depends upon the continuation of the services of the executive officers of the company. When the Supreme Court of Texas finally decides the question, it must weigh these conflicting interests.

If the argument that the directors cannot make a contract that extends beyond their term of office were carried to its logical conclusion, the directors of a manufacturing company could not make a sale or purchase contract longer than one year; a building corporation could not enter into a construction contract extending over a period of more than one year, and no Texas corporation could lease a building for its main office for a long term. If such contracts are binding on the corporation and extend over a long period of years, the authority of subsequently elected directors is curtailed more than if an officer is employed for a long term since the directors can to a certain extent con-

Under many circumstances it is necessary for the directors to enter into long term contracts if the business of the company is not to be hindered. The right of the directors to make contracts extending beyond their term of office, other than employment contracts, has not been questioned in Texas or in any other jurisdiction so far as the author has been able to discover, in the absence of a statute.8 In one case the court held that the cor- 

8. 1 Wash.L.Rev. 274. In this comment it is said: "It would seem that a statute rendering nugatory a contract of employment between a corporation and a stranger for a fixed and definite term is harsh and not consonant with business practices. 

Law is unceasingly harmonizing itself with customs and rules extant in the marts of trade and adopting them as its own after they have been firmly established. Under present conditions, the person who offers his personal services to a corporation is penalized and placed at a disadvantage suffered by no other one dealing with a corporate body. All others who enter into a contract with a board of trustees receive a valid instrument even though it extends over a period of time. 

Where a manager is employed for a long term, the directors do not surrender their statutory power to control the business of the corporation. 

If they realize that the manager is not acting honestly, they have a legal right to discharge him. If they have no legal grounds for discharging him but realize that he is not the proper person to make a success of the business, they can appoint an assistant manager and decrease the powers of the manager. If they make a long time construction contract with an independent contractor, their hands are tied unless the contractor gives the corporation legal grounds for rescinding the contract, where the contract is upheld by the courts. If in the long term employment contract the directors directly or indirectly surrender their power of control, the courts should disregard the contract on the ground that it is illegal as being contra to the Texas statute vesting authority to conduct the business in the directors. "The interests of the stockholders should weigh no more heavily in connection with the employee to his prejudice than with the countless others dealing with the corporation. 

The evils of allowing the trustees to contract for supplies, equipment and kindred commodities have never been so great that they have been placed under the attention of the legislators of this state. The privilege, allowed in other jurisdictions but denied in this, has not been disastrous to the well-being of foreign corporations. Neither has it been irksome to the stockholders nor the cause of diminishing profits."

The opinion in the Denton Milling Company-Blewett¹6 case is based mainly on the case of Llewellyn v. Aberdeen Brewing Co.¹7 which was based on the construction of a Washington statute, and the case of Beers v. New York Life Insurance Co.18 which is no longer followed even in New York.19 Even if the Texas courts follow the Denton case, they should not hold that all long term contracts of employment are void. If the contract unreasonably hampers subsequent boards of directors in the control of the business of the company, the contract should be stricken down.20 Where the services are necessary or beneficial to the success of the corporation and cannot be secured unless a long term is agreed upon, the contract of employment should be sustained.21 It will not be very difficult for the court to determine when the board of directors is attempting to hamper the business and control the acts of future boards of directors by long term contracts. Judge Swan labored diligently in the case of 

In re Paramount Publix Corp.22 to sustain a long term contract even in the face of a statute which gave the directors power to remove all employees "at pleasure" of the directors. As long term employment contracts will not interfere with the control of the directors over the business of the company any more than many other long term contracts, it is difficult to determine why the Texas courts even in the absence of a statute should hold that the directors have no power to enter into such contracts of employment. This point has not as yet been decided by the 

Supreme Court of Texas. The only question involved in the case of Missouri K. & T. R. v. Faulkner23 was the authority of the vice-

When a director disqualifies himself by bad habits or otherwise, by the weight of authority the stockholders can remove him. 

The policy of this procedure would depend largely on the relationship of the director to the stockholders. This relationship is a singular one, and should not be controlled by the strict formulae of either trustees or agents. Certainly the courts through the exercise of their equitable powers should relieve the situation if the director were clearly disqualified.64 This point regarding directors has never arisen in Texas, but it has been held by Texas courts that equity can remove trustees under a declaration of trust on a proper showing of fraud or unfitness, even though there was no reservation of this right to the shareholders.65

In It is difficult to see why a court of equity does not have inherent power to remove a director for cause when all other remedies fail. On the contrary, it would seem that equity does have inherent jurisdiction to remove in such a situation, and that the courts should exercise that jurisdiction rather than slavishly following the weight of authority. Thus it seems that Morawetz's statement of the law is preferable." The most recent statement of the law is found in the case of Markovitz v. Markovitz.72 that case the court said: "Prior to the enactment of the Business

Corporation Law, the power to remove a director from office for reasonable and just cause before the expiration of the term for which he was elected, could be exercised only within the corporate structure by the body authorized to appoint or elect directors, generally the shareholders. Courts of equity in this state had no jurisdiction to remove an officer of a private corporation, or to restrain him from carrying on the functions of his office."73 

Whether the Texas courts would exercise jurisdiction in equity to remove a director for cause is not decided, for the point has not arisen. But to avoid any possibility of the courts refusing to exercise such jurisdiction, the Legislature of Texas should provide by statute for such authority. In the Markovitz-Markovitz case74 one of the directors could not work satisfactorily with his codirectors and deliberately acted in such an objectionable manner as to cause serious injury to the corporation. There was a statute in Pennsylvania which gave the court the power to remove a director. But suppose this case arises in Texas and the objection-

It seems evident from article 1324 that the old directors hold office until their successors are elected and qualify. These articles form the basis of the understanding between the shareholders of corporations organized under the Texas statutes to the effect that the directors when elected will represent all of the shareholders for one year. To permit a majority of the shareholders to remove the directors without cause would be a breach of the above understanding and would transfer control of the business of the corporation from the duly elected directors to a majority of the stockholders. For this reason, as we have already seen, a majority of the stockholders cannot at common law remove a director without cause.79 

But if the charter or by-laws when the directors were elected provide that a director may be removed by a majority vote of the stockholders without cause such provision would become a part of the understanding of the stockholders and would be valid and effective.⁰⁰ All general incorporation statutes provide that the charter may be amended by a certain vote of the stockholders. 81

§ 739. Compensation of Directors, Officers and Agents 

It is generally held that a director is not entitled to compensation while he or she is serving in the capacity of director. However, the charter may provide for the payment of a salary to the directors for serving as such; 88 it follows that the board of directors may not vote salaries to themselves for services rendered as directors merely8⁹ unless they are given such authority by the charter or by-laws of the corporation or the stockholders by resolution authorize the directors to fix their own salaries as such directors. The reason for the rule that directors or director-officers are not entitled to compensation for ordinary services rendered the corporation is that it is their own business that they are managing as well as the business of all the stockholders for whom they are trustees. This is true if a corporation is looked upon as a collection of individuals to whom a franchise has been given to

They are generally financially interested in the success of the corporation they represent, and their service as directors secures its reward in the benefit which it confers upon the stock which they own. In other words, the custom is to pay the ordinary employees of corporations for the services they render; but it is the custom of directors of corporations to serve gratuitously, without compensation or the expectation of it. The presumption of law follows the custom. From the employment of an ordinary servant, the law implies a contract to pay him. From the service of a director, the implication is that he serves gratuitously.

But such officers, who have rendered their services under an agreement, either express or implied, with the corporation, its owners or representatives, that they shall receive reasonable, but indefinite, compensation therefor, may recover as much as their services are worth; and it is not beyond the powers of the board of directors to fix and pay reasonable salaries to them after they have discharged the duties of their offices." § 740. -Amount of Compensation 

A contract for compensation for services rendered to a corporation may be entered into between the corporation and an officer; and, if the contract is valid, the courts will uphold it and its provisions relating to the amount of the compensation, unless the amount is clearly unreasonable, or unless the amount agreed upon is in excess of the amount fixed by the charter, statutes, or by-laws. But it has been held that the salary of the president of a corporation cannot be held excessive if no showing is made on the trial of the duties exacted of him,8 because the court refuses to substitute its judgment for that of the board of directors unless the salary fixed is clearly excessive. The question of the reasonableness of the salary of a corporate officer depends on what the services of a competent officer are reasonably worth, and not on what he could make in another business." The court is much more likely to grant relief to a director or stockholder who is a member of the minority and who has not acquiesced in the salary, than to a member of the majority who voted for the salary or a member of the minority who has acquiesced in it for a long period of time.10 If the direc-

The natural tendency of a bonus, the amount of which is contingent upon profits, is to build up that quality known as esprit de corps. It tends to produce profits beyond what may otherwise be expected. Hence, where the amount of the bonus is not unreasonably large, it tends to increase the profits of the employer as well as the compensation of the employed.

It tends to make employees less wasteful of materials and more watchful of the interests of the employer, because employees thereby conserve their Own interests. In affirming the rule as stated by Judge Swan in his dissenting opinion in the Rogers-Hill case, the Supreme Court of the United States stated that, as a general rule, the discretion of the directors in fixing the salary of the officers of the company is controlling, but stated the exception to the general rule in the following language: "But the rule cannot be used to justify payments of sums as salaries so large as in substance and effect to amount to spoliation or waste of corporate property." In the 

Rogers-Hill case, under the bonus plan approved by the directors, the salary and bonus of President Hill of the American Tobacco Company, together with the privilege given to him of buying the stock of the company at much less than its market price, amounted to more than a million dollars a year. The court held that the excess of a reasonable salary amounted to a confiscation of some of the profits of the company that should have been paid to the stockholders as dividends.15 Other recent cases which follow the rule of the Rogers-Hill case are cited in the note.16 This question has not been directly decided by stockholder, if he avers excessive salary, must show facts establishing unjustifiable oppression in such respect. 

The evidence fails to show that salary voted defendant by the board of directors was so unreasonable or excessive, under the circumstances, as in itself to be deemed fraudulent, and, therefore, authorizing restoration in whole or in part. 

We may not readjust the salary without a yardstick applicable to the particular circumstances and not even then upon mere difference of opinion from that of the board of directors, but only upon concrete proof that the salary evidences wrongdoing or inexcusable oppression to the point of being fraudulent. Power to Fix Compensation 

The directors are authorized to fix the salary of subordinate officers and agents.27 The directors usually exercise their power of fixing compensation by resolution.28 A Texas court has held that an informal agreement among three of the five members of a board of directors, made when the board was not in session as such, to grant bonuses to employees for services rendered the corporation, did not create in the proposed beneficiaries any right of action against the corporation to compel it to pay the bonus. Compensation for Past Services 

As to past services, the agreement for compensation must have existed prior to the performance of the services in order for the officer to have a right of action against the corporation for such services, and this is true regardless of whether an express contract is necessary, or whether recovery may be had on an implied promise. The voting of compensation to an officer or director for services already performed without prior agreement, express or implied, for remuneration, is without consideration and the money so paid may be recovered by the corporation, because such a contract would be void for want of consideration, and ultra vires.33 This rule does not require, however, that the amount of compensation shall be definitely fixed before the rendition of the services. § 761. Nature of the Suit 

Suits by individual stockholders are usually referred to as derivative or representative suits or merely as shareholder's bills. 

This does not accurately describe all situations where litigation is instituted by a single shareholder. However, all suits instituted by a shareholder may be placed in one of four classes. First, is the purely personal cause of action for the violation of a private right of the individual stockholder. In this category fall suits by the shareholder to recover damages for breach of a contract made with the corporation and suits to enforce his own personal rights; such as, to inspect the corporate books, or recover declared dividends and suits for the conversion of his stock, or to enjoin executory ultra vires transactions.¹ Second, are cases where the suit is to recover a claim for the corporation 

1. Bangs v. Sullivan, 73 S.W. 74, 33 Tex.Civ.App. 30, writ refused. 145 

3 HILDEBRAND TEX.CORP.-10

§ 

Ch. 16

which the directors have refused to collect. This is the suit usually designated as a "shareholder's bill." Third, are suits where the shareholder brings a suit on his own behalf for his individual injury though the main injury is suffered by the corporation; yet, due to a contract or otherwise, he suffers individually certain damages not common to the other shareholders. The fourth class consists of suits where the corporation is forbidden the use of our courts and the stockholders bring a suit to protect their property rights as beneficial owners.

§ 763. Asserting Corporate Rights 

As was explained in treating of the nature of a corporation, the corporate body exists in law as a legal entity, separate and distinct from the members who compose it. But, as is stated several times in this text, a corporation should always be defined as a collection of real human beings who are stockholders in the corporation and have collective rights in the assets of the company. The corporation and its members are not the same person for the purpose of suing to redress injuries to the corporation. A corporation is a collection of individuals, it is true; but the individuals in their collective capacity are represented by the corporation, the collective person. An infringement of their collective rights is an injury to the corporation, for which an action, if brought at all, should be brought by the corporation. 

For such injuries, as a general rule, the individual members cannot sue. This applies not only to injuries inflicted by strangers, but also to injuries resulting from the wrongs of the officers or

Morris, 72 S.W.2d 687. One exception arises when stock is issued for the purpose of buying realty, or personal property in which case a shareholder is not entitled to his proportionate share. Meredith V.

It is well settled that a stockholder cannot maintain an action at law for injury to the corporation, either by its officers or by a stranger.16 The property of a corporation belongs to the corporation as a distinct legal entity, or to the stockholders only in their collective capacity. For any injury thereto the corporation should sue. Neither a single stockholder, for instance, nor even all of the stockholders, could maintain a suit for money due the corporation; such a suit as a general rule must be brought by the corporation.¹

Nor can a stockholder maintain an action at law against the directors or other officers of a corporation for their negligence or misfeasance in conducting its affairs, whereby the capital is

A recovery by the corporation inures to their benefit in proportion to their respective holdings and affords them compensation for the indirect or consequential loss sustained by them. "The foregoing general rule announced by the text writers and decisions is predicated upon the proposition that the rights of the stockholders are merged in the rights of the corporation, and, if the stockholders sustained any loss or injury, it would inure to the corporation and to the individual stockholders in proportion to their respective holdings in the company." 

The rule which restrains the stockholder from suing to redress wrongs against the corporation does not operate to restrain him from suing to redress wrongs which are not only wrongs against the corporation, but also violations of duties arising from "contracts or otherwise" and owing directly to the stockholders. Thus, if a stockholder pledges his stock as collateral with directors of the corporation, and they enter into a conspiracy to depreciate the price of the stock by using their power as directors for the purpose of buying it for less than its value, a wrong is committed, not only against the corporation, but also against the pledgor, to whom the corporation is directly liable.20 

On the other hand, where a director pledged his stock to the plaintiff to secure a note, the court held he was under a personal duty to the pledgee not to depreciate the value of the pledged stock. Therefore, where the director deliberately or negligently wrecked the company, the pledgee could sue the director at law and recover his damages without resorting to a shareholder's bill.21

In a New York case, the plaintiff corporation was the principal stockholder in a subsidiary corporation, the general manager of which was a defaulter. Plaintiff alleged that defendant, who was one of its directors, knew of this misuse of moneys and acquiesced in it and approved of it, and for his own profit intentionally withheld and concealed the truth. It was also alleged that, had defendant given this information, plaintiff corporation could have prevented the misapplication and the loss. 

Defendant was held liable.22 The claim of defendant that he was not liable to plaintiff by reason of the fact that he was liable to the subsidiary company was held untenable. The majority of the court adopted the view that the wrong to plaintiff did not cease to be remediable because it was also a wrong to somebody else. In this case one judge filed a strong dissenting opinion in which he contended that the facts did not present a case where an exception to the general rule should be made. He contended the corporation was the real party that was injured, and that if it had brought a suit for damages and recovered, the plaintiff would have suffered no individual damages, and the creditors of the corporation would have been protected. Even 

Justice Cardozo, who wrote the opinion for the majority, was hard pressed by the arguments of the attorneys for the defendants. In the opinion he said: "The argument is made, however, that since the duties overlap a double liability is threatened. Toay the defendant is called upon to make good the diminished value of the plaintiff's shares. Tomorrow he may be called upon at the suit of the subsidiary company to replenish its wasted treasury. We think the argument confuses the cause of action with the damages. If the defendant is solvent, and has so made himself a party to the conspiracy that he is liable as a tort feasor to the subsidiary corporation, the existence of such a cause of action will be reflected, like the ownership of any other assets, in the value of the shares. The diminution in value will be one thing if the subsidiary corporation is without a remedy against any one. It will be another thing if there is a remedy against a solvent wrongdoer. 

22. General Rubber Co. v. Benedict, 617. See criticism of this case in 

109 N.E. 96, 215 N.Y. 18, L.R.A.1915F, 28 Harv.L.Rev. 409. 152

"The existence of a cause of action does not depend, however, upon the extent of the recovery. If the subsidiary company has no remedy that will enable it to make good the loss, the reduction in the value of the shares may be equal to the fund converted. If it has a plain and certain remedy either against the defendant or against some other solvent party to the wrong, the reduction in the value of the shares may be less than the converted fund, or, it may be, almost nominal. We can imagine a case where a director has borrowed money illegally, and may therefore, be required to repay it. The corporation in such circumstances has a cause of action to compel the money to be restored, yet the value of the shares in the hands of the stockholders may not be reduced at all. Whatever difficulty there is in determining the measure of the loss is inherent in the very nature of these problems of appraisal. To determine the value of the shares, every asset of the subsidiary company must be reckoned, and the defendant's liability to that company, if it exists, must be included like any other." 

It would have been very difficult to prove how much the stockholder was damaged. If the subsidiary corporation were insolvent or its assets including its claim against the guilty director were less than its obligations, the plaintiff really suffered no personal damages. Surely the plaintiff should recover only where the corporation is solvent. If the subsidiary corporation could recover and collect its damages against the wrongdoers, the plaintiff suffered no personal damages. So it is only where the subsidiary had no cause of action or when its judgment against the wrongdoers could not be collected that the plaintiff could recover in a personal action the amount that his shares had depreciated.23 But, as the defendant was a director in the holding company, if the plaintiff had showed he was guilty of negligence or assisted the actual wrongdoer in looting the subsidiary company, the plaintiff in the Benedict case should have recovered his personal damages-the amount the plaintiff corporation personally lost, subject to the limitations discussed in the previ-

In another important case the New York Court of Appeals held that where the director, who misappropriated the funds of the corporation, was in a fiduciary relation to the stockholder, the latter could recover in an action at law his personal damages even though a shareholder had recovered in a shareholder's bill for the corporation. In Matter of Auditore29 the director who misappropriated the funds of the corporation was administrator of the estate of deceased stockholder and as such gave a bond signed by the American Surety Company as surety. 

The director was unable to pay the judgment obtained against him in the shareholder's suit. The Court held that he was under a legal obligation to protect the assets that came to him as administrator, and therefore, held him and the surety on his administrator's bond for the damages that the estate suffered in the depreciation of the value of the stock belonging to the estate by reason of his misappropriation of the funds of the corporation. In the majority opinion the Court said: "For the misappropriations of the corporate funds by Frank, he has been held liable to the corporation in a suit brought in its behalf by a stockholder. The judgment has not been paid. The estate of Joseph 

Auditore owned fifty per cent of the stock. This was held in trust for the estate by Frank Auditore as administrator. As such he owed to the estate an active duty to use diligence and care to preserve its value and prevent its loss. By wrongfully taking judgment. The Special Term ren dered personal judgment against the directors, in favor of the holders of the remaining 35 shares instead of in favor of the corporation. On appeal the claim was made that judgment should have been given to the corporation, since this was a representative action. The court, however, said: 'If the full demand of the plaintiff were accorded by the judgment, it would result in the payment to the bank of the full sum of $109,702.72, with the resulting benefit of a distribution to all stockholders, in proportion to their stock holdings. In the interest of an equitable result, I can see no sound reason why the court may not, by its judgment, select the parties entitled to benefit by the damages recovered, and withhold beneficial results from those culpably negligent. 

That is what has been accomplished. by the judgment rendered.' (See 

Vogt v. Vogt, 119 App.Div. 518, 104 

N.Y.S. 164, reargument denied, 120 

App.Div. 896, 105 N.Y.S. 1148.)"

For the damage done he and his surety should be held liable. The damage is the reduced value of the stock due to Frank's misappropriations while administrator. The judgment recovered by the corporation is no bar to this proceeding. The remedies are not inconsistent; they are applied to different duties and relationships. 

The money taken or used by Frank is not a dividend of the corporation received by him as administrator, nor do we have to ignore the corporation or the corporate form. The action by the corporation stands. If its judgment had been paid, no harm would have been done the assets of the estate. It has not been paid and the stock has become valueless. The loss of value is due to the act of the one chosen to sustain its worth. The trustee is liable for the loss in value which he has occasioned. Of course if the liabilities of the corporation exceeded its assets there could be no damage done. The value depends upon the financial condition of the corporation as of the time of Frank's appointment as administrator and his misappropriations.”

A strong dissenting opinion was filed in this case in which 

Justice Lehman said: "He has been a faithless administrator only because he has stolen the assets of the corporation. He stole no assets of the estate, and the estate has not been injured by the waste of corporate assets, except indirectly. For loss indirectly suffered by the shareholder through wrong to the corporation, the shareholder has never been accorded an individual right of action. In Ritchie v. McMullen, C.C.A.Ohio, 79 F. 522, and the cases there cited, there was a direct wrong to a shareholder beyond the waste of assets which caused the shareholders direct damage which would not be repaired even by complete restitution to the corporation. In General Rubber Co. v. 

Benedict, 164 App.Div. 332, 149 N.Y.S. 880, the shareholders' cause of action was for a breach of a direct duty which was entirely independent of a waste by the wrongdoer of the corporate assets and might be proven even if the defendant was guilty of no wrong to the corporation. Here the defendant is being held 157

§ 

Ch. 16

liable as administrator for damages indirectly caused to the estate by his wrongful diversion of corporate funds perpetrated as a corporate officer. Distinctions which seem to me without substance between the acts of an administrator and a corporate officer are drawn to fasten upon the administrator's surety liability for damages resulting indirectly to the estate from a wrong to the corporation committed by an officer of the corporation, and which falls entirely without the purview of the bond when reasonably construed. "What I have said is intended to apply to the entire decree against the administrator and his surety. It applies, I think, with special force to that part of the decision of this court which holds Frank Auditore as administrator and his surety liable to the estate for damages caused by the theft of corporate assets even prior to his appointment as administrator. Concededly at that time no privity of any kind existed between Auditore and that estate. Theft or waste of corporate assets were at that time concededly a wrong only to the corporation, and the estate as shareholder had no cause of action against the wrongdoer. The theft gave rise only to a debt to the corporation, and not a debt to the stockholder. Only through his control of the corporation or by an action brought in its behalf could 

Frank Auditore have compelled restitution. His failure to bring such an action and to collect the damages may again have constituted a wrong to the corporation; it constituted no independent wrong to any stockholder as such, and I fail to see how a direct wrong to the corporation which constitutes no injury to its stockholders can become an injury to a particular stockholder merely because the man who wronged the corporation occupied a special fiduciary relation to the stockholder. To permit a recovery by the stockholder for wrong to it, there must be proof that independently of the wrong done to the corporation there was a wrong done to the stockholder. A wrong to the corporation may become morally greater when the wrongdoer stood in a fiduciary relationship to a stockholder, but when the only breach of a duty owed by the wrongdoer to the stockholder is a waste of corporate assets causing no direct damage to the shareholder, I fail to see any sound ground for transmuting the 158

injury done to the corporation into an injury to the stockholder in order to create a new liability against the surety on the administrator's bond."

In this case the Court held that the administrator and the American Surety Company were not only liable for the damage done by the administrator after he was appointed, but also for the damage done two or three months before he was appointed administrator. On this issue of the case, the reasoning of the dissenting judge is the stronger of the two opinions. 

As has been shown above, the shareholder should bring a shareholder's bill to right the wrongs done the corporation where the directors will not bring the suit in the name of the corporation. Before a stockholder can bring an individual suit, he must show some personal damage resulting from the breach of a duty to him individually due to "a contract or otherwise," in addition to the duty owed him as a shareholder, such as pledgor and pledgee, trustee and cestui que trust, or some other such relationship. As there was no such relationship in the Auditore's case before Frank Auditore was appointed administrator of his brother's estate, the administrator did not have an individual cause of action against himself for misappropriation of the corporate funds before he was appointed administrator. He may have been under a moral duty to bring a shareholder's bill against himself, but surely he would have had no standing in a court of law for his individual injury as a stockholder resulting from his own theft from the corporation. Therefore, the court went too far in holding the American Surety Company liable as surety on the administrator's bond for misappropriation of the funds of the corporation before Frank Auditore was appointed administrator of his brother's estate.30

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 7428 defines a conspiracy as follows: "Where any two or more persons, firms, corporations or associations of persons, shall agree to boycott or threaten to refuse to buy from or to sell to any person, firm, corporation or association of persons for buying from or selling to any other person, firm, corporation or association of persons." The statutes fix the damages that may be recovered by the party against whom the conspiracy was formed. It seems evident that under the above statute a conspiracy may be formed to prevent a plaintiff from entering into a business in the future. If so, the Stinnett case does not come within the exception to the general rule, since the plaintiffs clearly were suing for their personal damages resulting from the conspiracy that was in no way dependent upon their rights as stockholders of the Capitol Theater. If a stockholder of a mercantile corporation is negligently run down by the delivery boy while delivering goods to a customer of the store, the plaintiff stockholder would have a personal cause of action against the corporation for his damages. But this action would not come within the exception to the rule discussed above. The plaintiff is not suing for his personal damages as a stockholder. His right to recover is independent of any right that he has as a stockholder of the defendant corporation.

Moroney 35 the defendant Moroney was guardian of the estate of the plaintiffs who owned all the stock, except one share, of the Moroney Hardware Company, a corporation. The defendant Moroney wrongfully converted some of the money and personal property of the corporation to his own use. The court held that the wards suffered a personal injury since the guardian owed them the duty carefully to preserve the assets of the estate, and, as the corporation was entirely solvent, the amount converted by the guardian would be considered as a dividend paid to the defendant as guardian. In the opinion the court said: "But if the question depended upon a decision of the further question urged by defendant in error, we would not be willing to hold that even though the guardian withdrew these funds from the corporation intending to compensate himself for his services as president of the corporation, there being no pretense of an allowance and payment by the corporation for that purpose, and the undisputed fact being that such depletion of the assets of the corporation necessarily prejudiced the rights of his wards as stockholders, he would not be liable in this proceeding. We think he would. In its last analysis the situation is a very simple one. 

The guardian charged by law with the duty faithfully to administer the estate of his wards is liable in this proceeding for any direct loss they have sustained through his negligence or overt act of mismanagement. Without dispute, his conduct has resulted in a loss to the estate. The loss is sufficiently direct as

Thus it is evident that in many cases the Courts have permitted a stockholder to recover the amount of damages that he suffered personally although the injury was really suffered by the corporation. In most cases a recovery and satisfaction of the judgment by the corporation would prevent the accrual of any damages to the stockholder personally. However, the courts should be mindful of the fact that most corporations are seldom free of debts and should insist that unless the corporation is entirely solvent the recovery should inure to the benefit of the corporation so that its creditors will reap the benefit of the judgment.37 The claims of the creditors of the corporation should be given first consideration in all cases where the corporation has suffered a loss. This chose in action of the corporation is an asset which should inure to the benefit of the creditors of the company since it stands in lieu of the property of the corporation the corporation, the right of recovery therefor is in the corporation. 

Any money so recovered would become assets of the corporation, and should be applied first to the payment of its debts, and the excess only distributed to the stockholders."

§ 764. Jurisdiction of Equity 

It was at one time contended that a court of equity had no jurisdiction to remedy a wrong to the corporation at the instance of a stockholder. That it has such jurisdiction is now well settled. It was said by the Supreme Court of the United States in 

1855: "It is now no longer doubted, either in England or the 

United States, that courts of equity, in both, have a jurisdiction 

38. Cullum v. General Motors Ac ceptance Corp., Tex.Civ.App., 115 S.

In this case the court held the corporation was injured and, therefore, the plaintiff could not recover in an individual suit, though his stock depreciated in value due to the injury to the corporation. In this case Justice Stokes said: "The distinction between those cases in which the stockholder has the right to maintain such a cause of action and those in which he does not have such right is clearly drawn in the other case cited in the footnote in Corpus Juris, supra, under the text, viz., White v. First Nat. Bank, 252 

Pa. 205, 97 A. 403. In that case the bank's conduct was such as to destroy the corporation and put it in bankruptcy, which would not have resulted if the bank had not violated its contract with the corporation. White, the principal stockholder, brought the suit in his individual capacity against the bank for the damages which resulted to him in the reduction in value of his capital stock in the corporation. The court held he could not maintain the suit, inasmuch as he was not endeavoring to recover on behalf of the corporation, but seeking a personal judgment."

In Duquesne Gold Mining Co. v. 

Glaser, 103 P. 299, 46 Colo. 186, the court said: "When directors and officers of a corporation violate their duty to its stockholders and attempt to wreck its property, or wrongfully secure it for their personal profit, or if they neglect their duty, permit its property to be taken away without any effort to save it, or fraudulently refuse to protect its interests, the stockholders, as such, are not remediless. They may protect the interests of the corporation and incidentally their own, provided they first make due efforts to have the corporation, through its governing officers, take the necessary action. And if it appears that the officers refuse to act, or if the facts and circumstances are such that it is clear that it would be useless to ask them to do so, the stockholders themselves may, in their own name, protect the corporate interests. They may, in their own name, sue or defend in such behalf."

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a shareholder could bring a shareholder's bill after complying with 

Rule 23(b), Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, 28 U.S.C.A. fol lowing § 723c, to determine whether the Tennessee Valley Authority, a corporation organized under Act of Congress, had authority under the United States Constitution to sell power generated at a government dam to the Alabama Power Company and to acquire some of the properties belonging to the latter company. 

In several places in the opinion the court said that the contract was “illegal," rather than "ultra vires” if the Tennessee Valley

Authority had no authority under the Federal Constitution to make the agreement. Chief Justice Hughes said: "They challenged the contract both as injurious to the interests of the corporation and as an illegal transaction,―violating the fundamental law. In seeking to prevent the carrying out of the contract, the suit was directed not only against the Power Company but against the Authority and its directors upon the ground that the latter, under color of the statute, were acting beyond the powers which the Congress could validly confer. In such a case it is not necessary for stockholders—when their corporation refuses to take suitable measures for its protection-to show that the managing board or trustees have acted with fraudulent intent or under legal duress. To entitle the complainants to equitable relief, in the absence of an adequate legal remedy, it is enough for them to show the breach of trust or duty involved in the injurious and illegal action. Nor is it necessary to show that the transaction was ultra vires of the corporation. The illegality may be found in the lack of lawful authority on the part of those with whom the corporation is attempting to deal. Thus, the breach of duty may consist in yielding, without appropriate resistance, to governmental demands which are without warrant of law or are in violation of constitutional restrictions. The right of stockholders to seek equitable relief has been recognized when the managing board or & W. P. Ry. Co., 33 S.E. 866, 108 Ga. 151.

The fact that the directors in the exercise of their judgment, either because they were disinclined to undertake a burdensome litigation or for other reasons which they regarded as substantial, resolved to comply with the legislative or administrative demands, has not been deemed an adequate ground for denying to the stockholders an opportunity to contest the validity of the governmental requirements to which the directors were submitting.

The opportunity to resort to equity, in the absence of an adequate legal remedy, in order to prevent illegal transactions by those in control of corporate properties, should not be curtailed because of reluctance to decide constitutional questions." 

It would seem evident that the main question was the power or authority of the Tennessee Valley Authority to make the contract, rather than whether the contract of sale was against public policy or the Constitution of the United States. Therefore, it could be argued that in the Federal Courts a shareholder may bring a shareholder's bill to enjoin the performance of an executory ultra vires contract. But, as is shown in the preceding paragraph, a shareholder, by the better holding, has a personal 170

right to compel the corporation to confine its operations within the express' or implied powers stated in its charter.47

the corporation and not to the plaintiff stockholder. Of necessity, therefore, if a right of action exists, it exists in favor of the corporation, and of necessity the action must be brought in the right of the corporation, on its behalf, and for its benefit. A stockholder's action, in such cases, is brought for and on behalf of the corporation, and a stockholder is permitted to sue in the right of the corporation merely to set the judicial machinery of the court of equity in motion when the corporation refuses to enforce its own rights to the detriment of its stockholders. 

In these cases, the stockholder is not enforcing any personal right of his own. The real plaintiff is the corporation. The position of the stockholder who institutes such a suit, is after all, the same as that of the directors when they institute an action in the name of the corporation. The stockholder is permitted to sue merely because the directors disregard their duty by refusing to sue. The relief asked is on behalf of the corporation, not the individual shareholder, and, if it be granted the complaining shareholder derives only an incidental benefit from it. The mere fact that, in such a suit, the stockholder cannot use the name of the corporation as the plaintiff, but appears himself as the nominal plaintiff, makes no difference.50 The Court of Appeals of New 

York has said of such representative or derivative suits: "The plaintiffs do not bring this action because their rights have been directly violated or because the cause of action is theirs, or because they are entitled to the relief sought; they are permitted to sue in this manner simply in order to set in motion the judicial machinery of the court. * The cause of action belongs to the corporate body and not to the plaintiffs and other stockholders individually, nor to the body of stockholders collectively."5. * # fendants as stockholders and officers of the Goddu Company in the management of its business. The mere fact that some of the guilty may benefit is no reason for not giving redress to the innocent. The law cannot always apportion the punishment among the guilty, and cases are frequent where one person has been made to bear the brunt of a loss caused by him not alone but in conjunction with others.54 As said by Jessel, M. R., in a leading English case: "If the argument were once allowed to prevail, it would only be necessary to corrupt one single shareholder to prevent a company from ever setting the contract aside."55

Under our statutes,56 a stockholder can in a proper case make application for a receiver. The old cases were quite strict and stated that equity had no power to appoint a receiver for a corporation at the suit of a stockholder for fraud, mismanagement, or collusion on the part of the corporate authorities, or ultra vires acts of its directors, but would limit the redress granted to the specific wrongs charged, and enjoin them. The reason for this rule is that equity appoints receivers only as incidental to other relief.57 The recent decisions, however, are more liberal. And while stockholders cannot obtain a receiver for mismanagement only, yet where a ruinous business policy is adapted or where assets of the corporation are being dissipated, courts will appoint a receiver even where the stockholder brings a shareholder's suit to recover the loss the corporation has suffered by the misconduct

§ 765. Demand on the Corporation 

To entitle a stockholder to maintain a suit in equity to redress a corporate injury for an act done or to prevent a corporate injury from an act threatened, on behalf of himself and other stockholders, it must be shown that every reasonable effort to obtain redress or protection through the regularly constituted agents and controlling power of the corporation has proved unavailing. 

In other words, the dissenting stockholders must first seek to correct the abuses complained of within the corporation itself, before resorting to suit. Equity will permit a shareholder to bring a shareholder's bill only where he has exhausted all means of relief within the corporation.59 It must be made to appear from the bill

34 S.W. 828, 833, Justice Pleasants said: "While it is true that a stockholder in a corporation may maintain a suit in equity founded on a right of action existing in the corporation itself, and in which suit the corporation itself is the appropriate plaintiff, there must exist, to authorize such suit, some action or threatened action of the directors or trustees of the corporation which is beyond their authority, or such fraudulent transaction, completed or contemplated, by the managers, in connection with some other party, or among themselves, or with other shareholders, as will result in serious injury to the corporation or to the other shareholders, or where the board of directors, or a majority of them, are acting in their own interest, in a manner destructive of the interests of the corporation or the rights of the other shareholders, or where a majority of the stockholders themselves are oppressively and illegally pursuing a course, in the name of the corporation, which is in violation of the rights of the other shareholders, and which can only be restrained by the aid of a court of equity. In addition to the grievances which call for and permit the exercise of the equitable powers of the court, the shareholder, before he is permitted to maintain a suit in his own name, and conduct a litigation which usually belongs to the corporation, must show to the satisfaction of the court that he has exhausted all the means within his reach to obtain, within the corpora-

A similar holding was made where the directors fraudulently voted increases of salary to themselves which were in fact dividends instead of a salary, as each employee including directors was paid nine percent of the amount of stock each owned. Such actions cannot be confirmed and ratified by a majority of the shareholders since fraudulent acts can be ratified only by unanimous consent of the shareholders.

A sharp distinction has to be drawn, therefore, between acts legal, but voidable, on the one hand, and fraudulent acts or acts in breach of trust amounting to fraud on the other hand. As to the latter, the rule applies that even majority stockholders may not for selfish purposes act in hostility to the interests of the corporation with the intention of defrauding the nonassenting stockholders.73 Many cases, including several Texas cases, state that before a shareholder can bring a shareholder's bill, he must request the stockholders to sue in the name of the corporation after his request has been denied by the directors. This rule of the shareholder's bill was first stated in the case of Foss v. Harbottle.74 By the charter of the company in that case the directors were made the governing body, subject to the superior control of the proprietors assembled in general meetings who also had power to originate proceedings for the corporation "as well as to control the directors in any acts which they may have originated.” 

Of course, under the peculiar set-up of that corporation, if the stockholders had power to initiate proceedings for the company and control over the directors, it was inevitable that the court would hold that the shareholder must appeal both to the directors and to the stockholders before instituting a shareholder's bill.

In America, especially in Texas, the stockholders of a corporation have no control over the directors. This rule is followed in 

England except where the charter gives the stockholders some control over the directors. They have no power to institute.proceedings for the corporation.75 As the stockholders in Texas have no authority to control the directors nor institute a suit in the name of the corporation, the Supreme Court of Texas no doubt will follow the above authorities, especially the case of Continental Securities Co. v. Belmont,76 wherein it was held that it is not necessary to request the stockholders to institute the suit except in voidable transactions that can be ratified by the stockholders. 

We have already in another chapter of this text seen that in four cases a majority of the stockholders, acting honestly, may ratify a voidable contract. If a director makes a contract with his own corporation, the contract is voidable at the mere instant of the corporation (1) if he is counted to constitute a quorum of the directors, or (2) if he votes in favor of the resolution authorizing the contract. If the contract is (1) induced by fraud, or (2) by misrepresentation, or (3) is a hard bargain for the company, or (4) the director was guilty of non disclosure, the corporation may set the contract aside on proof of either of the above facts. 

However, in all of the above cases a majority of the stockholders can ratify the voidable transaction except the contract induced by fraud. In the latter case, it takes a unanimous vote of the stockholders to prevent the corporation from rescinding the contract.”

The original equity rule which is now 

Rule 23(b) was first published in the Volume of the United States Supreme Court Reports in which the noted case Hawes v. 

Oakland is reported.78 The opinion in that case was written before the equity rule was promulgated and published by the Supreme Court of the United States. For this reason it may be contended that the Hawes-Oakland case meant to set forth the general law in the absence of a specific rule by the Supreme Court. 

However, the Court must have formulated what is now Rule 23 (b), which was originally Equity Rule 94 and thereafter Equity Rule 27, before the opinion in the Hawes-Oakland case was written. For this reason, it cannot be contended seriously that the 

Hawes-Oakland case was meant to decide that in the absence of any rule of the Supreme Court a shareholder must request the stockholders to institute a suit in the name of the corporation after the directors have refused to bring the suit. 

But it must be frankly admitted that the Texas Courts even in recent cases say that if the directors refuse to bring the suit, the plaintiff must in all cases, except where he is excused from doing so under the rules discussed in this chapter, seek relief from the stockholders before he institutes a shareholder's bill. For instance in Rex Refining Co. v. Morris,79 the court said: "The gravamen of plaintiffs' charge is that the conduct of Wier and Newkirk, managing directors, completed and contemplated, was illegal and beyond their authority as officers of the corporation, and in furtherance of a conspiracy to obtain control of the corporation for the sinister purpose of rendering valueless the stock of the corporation and appropriating its assets to their own use and benefit, but the petition is void of any allegation assigning a reason why the wrongful conduct of the two directors was not

This should have been alleged, and its absence, in our opinion, rendered the petition insufficient for the appointment of the receiver. "The case of New Birmingham, etc., v. Blevins, 12 Tex.Civ.App. 

410, 34 S.W. 828, presented a similar situation. The Galveston court held that shareholders could not successfully sue to protect their corporate rights from the fraudulent action of officers, in the absence of a showing that the shareholders had made an earnest effort to obtain redress at the hands of the other stockholders." 

In Barthold v. Thomas,80 the court said: "In a suit brought for and on behalf of the corporation, the petition must allege and the evidence must show that the plaintiff has made a good-faith effort to obtain action by the corporation, or must allege and prove such a state of facts as makes it clear that an appeal to the directors or stockholders would have been useless. Where the wrongdoers are in complete control and management of the corporation, this fact dispenses with the necessity of an appeal to them or to the corporation; but the facts necessary to excuse the failure to make application to the corporation for redress must be both alleged and proved by the plaintiff."

The quotations from both of the above cases were dicta, as the cases were decided on other grounds. This is true of most of the cases in which the courts state that the shareholders must be requested to bring the suit after the directors have refused to do so. 

It is, therefore, desirable for the Texas Supreme Court to consider this question very carefully the next time it is presented to that court. In most cases it is practically impossible for a shareholder to assemble the stockholders of the corporation, and, as they cannot bring the suit in the name of the corporation, the plaintiff should not be required to request the stockholders to bring the suit except where they can ratify a voidable transaction. The court should not require the plaintiff to do a useless or foolish act. 

80. Tex.Com.App., 210 S.W. 506.

The same statement was repeated in 

Stinnett v. Paramount-Famous Lasky 

Corp., Tex.Com.App., 37 S.W.2d 145. 184

But, according to Subdivision (b) of Rule 42 of the Rules of Civil Procedure promulgated by the Supreme Court of Texas, Vernon's 

Tex.Rules Civ.Proc., and not changed by the Texas Legislature at its session in 1941, the plaintiff must seek relief from the shareholders "if necessary". As soon as the Court realizes how unsuited the federal rule is to the state courts the Court will change or omit most of subdivision (b) of the rule. 

When the directors or officers of a corporation cause a loss of corporate property by negligence or culpable lack of prudence or failure to exercise their functions; or fraudulently misappropriate the corporate property in any manner, whether for their own benefit or for the benefit of a third person; or obtain any undue advantage, benefit, or profit for themselves by contract, purchase, sale, or other dealings under color of their official functions; or violate the rules established by the charter or bylaws for their management of the corporate affairs; or in any other similar manner commit a breach of their fiduciary obligations towards the corporation, so that it sustains injury or loss, and a liability devolves upon themselves,-the corporation is the party to sue for relief. In such cases no equitable suit for relief can be maintained against the directors or officers by the stockholder in a representative capacity on behalf of all the others similarly situated, unless the corporation either actually or virtually refuses to prosecute the suit.81 It must clearly appear that the corporation has been or will be damaged, since one asserting a derivative cause of action must first establish the existence of a cause of action in the party whose rights are sought to be enforced.82

86. Rule 23(b) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, 28 U.S.C.A. fol lowing § 723c, was adopted in 1938. 

That rule provides: "In an action brought to enforce a secondary right on the part of one or more shareholders in an association, incorporated or unincorporated, because the association refuses to enforce rights which may properly be asserted by it, the complaint shall be verified by oath and shall aver (1) that the plaintiff was a shareholder at the time of the transaction of which he complains or that his share thereafter devolved on him by operation of law and (2) that the action is not a collusive one to confer on a court of the United States jurisdiction of any action of which it would not otherwise have jurisdiction. The complaint shall also set forth with particularity the efforts of the plaintiff to secure from the managing directors or trustees and, if necessary, from the shareholders such action as he desires, and the reasons for his failure to obtain such action or the reasons for not making such effort."

When this rule was originally formulated by the Supreme Court of the 

United States it was Equity Rule No. 94. 

The rule was first promulgated 

January 23, 1882. The original Equi ty Rule No. 94 provided: "Every bill brought by one or more stockholders in a corporation, against the corporation and other parties, founded on rights which may properly be asserted by the corporation, must be verified by oath, and must contain an allegation that the plaintiff was a shareholder at the time of the transaction of which he complains, or that his share had devolved on him since by operation of law; and that the suit is not a collusive one to confer on a court of the United States jurisdiction of a case of which it would not otherwise have cognizance. It must also set forth with particularity the efforts of the plaintiff to secure such action as he desires on the part of the managing directors or trustees, and, if necessary, of the shareholders, and the causes of his failure to obtain such action." 

Equity Rule No. 94 was amended 

February 1, 1913 and was thereafter known as Equity Rule No. 27. That rule provided: "Every bill brought by one or more stockholders in a corporation against the corporation and other parties, founded on rights which may properly be asserted by the corporation, must be verified by oath, and must contain an allegation that the plaintiff was a shareholder at the time of the transaction of which he complains, or that his share had devolved on him since by operation of law, and that the suit is not a collusive one to confer on a court of the United States jurisdiction of a case of which it would not otherwise have cognizance. § 767. Inability of the Corporation to Sue 

The privilege of suing or defending actions in the courts is conferred upon a corporation by its charter and the law of its creation. Under its reserved power, the state may at any time abolish a corporation's charter. Since the state by abolishing a corporate charter may destroy completely the right of a corporation as an entity to prosecute or defend an action in the courts, it logically follows that it possesses the lesser power of restricting a corporation's right to the use of our courts only so long as it discharges its obligation to the state by the payment of the required franchise taxes.3

5 The power reserved to "alter, reform or amend" corporate charters does not give the legislature the right to impair or destroy the previously vested rights of shareholders to their proportionate interest in the property of the corporation. A court of equity, in such cases, possesses full power and authority to take whatever action is necessary and proper to protect the interests of the stockholders in the corporate property and the creditors of the corporation."

It has been said that the same rule applies where a foreign corporation has failed to secure a permit to do business in this state and is thus precluded from bringing suit. It has been held that a stockholder in such a foreign corporation, may sue to cancel an assignment of an oil lease by the directors to third parties in fraud of the rights of the stockholders. The court in the case cited in the preceding note gave the following reasons for its decision: "It will be noted that the statutes regulating the transaction of business by foreign corporations in regard to obtaining a permit do not, as in some states, make void any transaction entered into by such corporations while illegally transacting business. The law does not attempt to forfeit the property acquired by such corporations while unlawfully doing business in the state. "If we should give the statute the construction placed upon it by defendants in error, it would tend to encourage many corporations to fail to comply with the terms of the statute. Boards of directors who desired to defraud stockholders * * * could successfully accomplish their unholy purpose by merely failing to comply with our laws in regard to obtaining a permit to do business. This would result in the entire corporate property being subject to spoliation by the managing officers of the corporation, and the stockholders would be utterly without a remedy. This would be true because the cause of action based upon the fraudulent conduct of the directors is in the corporation. If it is unable to, or will not, assert such cause of action, the only ones left to prosecute it are the stockholders. 

If they are not permitted to maintain the action then the directors could deal as they pleased with the corporate property with the perfect assurance that the courts of this state would be closed to the stockholders in any effort to set aside a fraudulent disposition of the corporate property. We decline to sanction a legal proposition leading to any such result.

It should be noticed that the statute provides that a corporation "desiring to transact or solicit business in Texas, or to establish a general or special office in this State," must obtain a permit. In the above cases the court held that if it did not obtain a permit to transact business in Texas, the corporation could not recover on any claim arising out of the transaction of business in Texas. The reader should notice specifically that the statute is not limited to the "transacting or soliciting business" in Texas, but if the company wishes merely to establish "a general or special office in Texas," it must take out a permit to do so. 

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1536 provides that, "No such corporation can maintain any suit or action, either legal or equitable, in any Court of this State upon any demand, whether arising out of contract or tort, unless at the time such contract was made, or tort committed, the corporation had filed its articles of incorporation under the provisions of this Chapter. If any corporation shall transact intrastate business in Texas without first having obtained a permit under the provisions of this Chapter such corporation shall forfeit to the State of Texas not less than One Hundred ($100.00) Dollars nor more than Five Thousand ($5,000.00) Dollars for each month or fraction thereof it shall transact such business without a permit as required hereunder, to be recovered in a suit to be brought by the Attorney General in Travis County, Texas, and the State shall have a lien on all properties of the corporation for said penalties and any corporation may be enjoined by the Attorney General when transacting such business without a permit as required hereunder."

The reader should remember that this statute provides that a foreign corporation that is transacting business in Texas without a permit cannot "maintain any suit or action, either le- 195

§ 

Ch. 16

gal or equitable, in any court of this State upon any demand, whether arising out of contract or tort, unless at the time such contract was made or tort committed," the foreign corporation had a permit to do business in Texas. 14 It is settled by an unbroken line of decisions in the English speaking world that a shareholder's bill is brought by a shareholder for and on behalf of the corporation. The corporation must always be made a party defendant in the suit, and the judgment where the plaintiff is successful runs in favor of the corporation, and the money obtained under execution must be paid to it. In other words, the court of equity, on account of necessity, permits a shareholder to bring a suit that is in fact the suit of the corporation.13 In the Pratt-Hewit Oil Corp. v. Hewit case,¹ the Supreme Court held that although the foreign corporation did not take out a permit to do business in Texas, a shareholder could bring a shareholder's bill for and on behalf of the corporation (1) where the directors were guilty of fraudulent conduct causing damage to the corporation, (2) where they were guilty of negligence, and (3) where they entered into ultra vires transaction, and that the stockholders had an individual cause of action where the defendant converted to his own use and benefit some or all of the property of the corporation. In other words, if the defendant steals 1,000 head of steers belonging to the defendant foreign corporation which is transacting business in Texas without a permit, a stockholder could either sue and recover his pro-rata share of the injury done the corporation or in a class suit could recover the entire damage done to the corporation for himself and all other stockholders even though thereby the creditors of the corporation lost 50% of their claims. This must be the result of the above holding since the court said that under the facts of the above case the stockholders had an "individual right" to recover the loss suffered by the corporation.

In the above case, the court said that neither a stockholder individually, the corporation, nor a shareholder in a sharehold-

Therefore, if instead of stealing the cattle of the above corporation, the defendant traded its directors 100 imported burros from Mexico for 3,000 head of fine high-grade, four year old cows, where the burros were worth $1 a head and the cows $50 a head, this trade could not be rescinded even though it was induced by a flagrant fraud, since the cause of action arose on behalf of the corporation out of the transaction of business in Texas. In both of the above cases, the injury was to the corporation, and the stockholders are only indirectly injured.

In Ballantine on Corporations, Section 185, page 609 it is said: "In like manner, if the property of a corporation is converted by a stranger, or if a trespass is committed thereon, or if an injury to its property is caused by the negligence of another, or if an injury is threatened, the injury is to the corporation, not to the stockholders individually, and it is for the corporation, and not for the stockholders as individuals, to take proper steps, by action or otherwise, to prevent or redress the injury. This is true when a corporation is injured by the fraud, excess of authority, or negligence of its own officers or agents. The injury is primarily to the corporation, and not to the individual stockholders, and it is for the corporation to seek redress." Professor Ballantine's statement is supported by every case decided in the English speaking world except the above Hewit case. The writer cannot understand why the court legislated and added so much to the above two articles of the Texas Revised Statutes.

If the legislature intended to make the exceptions that have been injected into the statutes by the above decision, our statutes should be amended at the next meeting of the legislature. 

It is settled in Texas that either party may recover on an ultra vires contract if wholly executed on the plaintiff's side.16 

Suppose that the foreign corporation that is transacting business in Texas without a permit is a mercantile corporation. It lent the defendant $1,000 and took his note as evidence of the obligation. Under ordinary circumstances this loan would be ultra vires, but under the doctrine of the Bond-Terrell case the corporation could recover if it is a local corporation. Under the above Hewit case, a shareholder could bring a shareholder's bill under one of the rules set forth in that case as the contract is ultra vires. Did the court mean to hold that even though the debt arose out of the transaction of business in Texas, a shareholder could recover for the corporation merely because the transaction was ultra vires? Suppose the directors authorize the attorney of the company to bring suit in the name of the corporation for all claims due the company. And suppose that the attorney actually brings the suit in the name of the company on one of the four claims specified in the opinion of the Hewit case wherein a shareholder is permitted to bring a personal suit or a shareholder's bill. And suppose further that in this suit recovery is denied the corporation, for the reason that it is a foreign corporation and has no permit to do business in Texas. 

Under the above decision would such judgment be res adjudicata as to another suit either by a shareholder for the corporation or by a class bill by one or more of the shareholders for them-
