It seems to the writer that the Hewit decision is based on a fiction, because in all of the four exceptional cases specified in the opinion the damage is actually to the corporation and not to the stockholders individually. All rules of law based on fiction must break down sooner or later. The holding in the Hewit case authorizes foreign corporations doing business in Texas without a permit to evade a plain unambiguous statute of the State of Texas. The legislature must have meant what it said. 

In other words, surely the legislature meant to prohibit all suits by foreign corporations doing business in Texas without a permit, whether the suit arose out of a breach of contract or the commission of a tort.17

The above statutes and all other statutes with reference to foreign corporations transacting business in Texas were not passed merely as revenue measures. For instance, one of the main articles of the statute provides that the foreign corporation must appoint an agent upon whom service may be had. Under the statute the agent may be served anytime within four years after the corporation withdraws from the State of Texas.18 In reaching its conclusions in the last cited case, the court seems to have been imbued with the thought that justice demanded the result reached by the court. 

It seems to the writer that the technique adopted by the court to reach the result of the opinion failed to consider both sides of the question. It may seem unjust to permit the directors or even a third party to loot the corporation, but is this not a matter that should be considered by the legislature rather than the

Suppose, for instance, that a mercantile corporation comes to Texas and transacts a loan business without a permit. According to the above opinion, a shareholder could always bring a shareholder's bill and recover for the corporation on every ultra vires loan made by the company in Texas. On the other hand, let us suppose that the foreign ranch corporation owes many obligations in the State of Texas; but, as it has not taken out a permit thereby appointing a service agent, it withdraws all of its property from the State before suits can be instituted against it. Under the above decision, corporations will be encouraged not to take out a permit, especially if they sell only for cash. For in many cases they withdraw from the State before citation is served on the proper agent, thereby either escaping all liability on their just obligations or causing the plaintiffs a great deal of trouble and expense in suing the corporation in a foreign jurisdiction. The ultimate result of the decision in the Hewit case is difficult to determine. Therefore, would it not have been much better for the court to follow the statute and suggest amendments to the legislature if thought to be desirable? Under the dictum of the Court in the Hewit case if a foreign bank lends money in Texas while it is without a permit even a shareholder in a shareholder's bill could not recover because the loan would be intra vires, but if the company is a foreign ranch company the shareholder could recover in a shareholder's bill since the loan would be ultra vires. Other inconsistencies of the Hewit opinion are pointed out, and how the questions suggested by the Court in the opinion should have been decided, are suggested more in detail in the chapter on Foreign Corporations herein. § 768. Acts within the Power of the Directors or the Majority 

Stockholders-Discretionary Powers 

The rule is well established that the courts will not interfere with the management of the affairs of a corporation in regard to matters involving merely the exercise of discretion at the in- 200

-- § 

stance of a minority of the stockholders.19 In Farwell v. Babcock cited in the preceding note the court said: "The court never substitutes its judgment on questions of policy for that of the governing body of the corporation, and does not seek to decide business questions, nor to set aside the acts of the majority, because the court may think that another course would have been wiser, or even that the course adopted was plainly unwise. The course of conduct by the directors must have been such as to plainly show an intention to sacrifice the interest of the corporation and the minority stockholders." 20

A minority stockholder may secure judicial aid under certain circumstances. These were aptly set out by the Supreme Court in Cates v. Sparkman.21 In that case the court said: "The breach of duty authorizing a suit by an individual stockholder for damage in the depreciation of his stock does not refer to mere mismanagement or neglect of the officers or directors in the control of the corporate affairs or the abuse of discretion lodged in them in the conduct of the company's business. On this ground the courts do not interfere. The breach of duty or conduct of officers and directors which would authorize in a proper case the court's interference in suits of this character

But if the acts or things are or may be that which the majority of the company have a right to do, or if they have been done irregularly, negligently, or imprudently, or are within the exercise of their discretion and judgment in the development or prosecution of the enterprise in which their interests are involved, these would not constitute such breach of duty, however unwise or inexpedient such acts might be, as would authorize the interference by the courts at the suit of a stockholder." 

A stockholder, or a minority of the stockholders, cannot maintain a suit to set aside a transaction entered into by the directors, if it is one which a majority of the stockholders may lawfully ratify, and thus render binding as against the minority. 

In Foss v. Harbottle,22 the complaint in a suit by stockholders was that the directors had purchased land from themselves for the corporation at an excessive price. Vice Chancellor Wigram held that the suit could not be maintained, since the transaction, though subject to rescission by the corporation, was not void. 

It might be ratified by a majority of the members.23 However, as we have seen, acts of the directors which are fraudulent or ultra vires, cannot be ratified by a majority.24

Even when it is clear that a corporation has a right to sue to redress or enjoin wrongs committed or threatened, the fact that it refuses to do so does not necessarily entitle a stockholder to sue on behalf of himself and the other stockholders. As a rule, 22. 2 Hare, 461.

These rules also apply to a shareholder's bill where the corporation is in the hands of a receiver. The receiver takes the place of the directors. Even if the directors are the wrongdoers, whether a suit should be brought against them is a matter that falls within the "unprejudiced exercise" of the receiver's judgment. A refusal to bring the suit constitutes no legal wrong to the stockholders of the corporation, if the refusal is based upon the honest judgment of the receiver. Therefore, the court must be convinced by the allegations in the plaintiff's petition that the receiver has abused his discretion before a shareholder will be permitted to sue for the receiver. In a recent New York case, the highest court of that state held that the plaintiff showed that the receiver abused his discretion by alleging "that the receiver is a clerk in the office of the attorneys for the defendants and that his primary interest is to prevent the corporation from redressing the wrongs committed by the clients of his employer." 33

§ 770. Who may Sue as Stockholders 

The right to sue or defend on behalf of the corporation is confined to persons who are stockholders at the time when the action is brought.39 But where the owner makes an executory contract to sell his stock and title has not passed he can bring a shareholder's suit.40 Even though the shareholder owns stock when the suit is instituted, if he sells it voluntarily or if it is sold under execution, he cannot prosecute the suit to judgment.¹¹

I am unable to see any real or substantial distinction by virtue of which a stockholder transferring his certificates would transfer all of his indivisible interest in bonds or real estate on hand; but would not transfer his interest in a right of action to recover bonds or real estate which had been fraudulently withdrawn from the possession of the corporation, and which it was entitled to recover; and if the subsequent holder, by acquiring the certificates, does acquire such latter interest, it seems to follow that he may, if necessary, in behalf of the corporation, assert and prosecute an action to protect and enforce the same." Rule 42, subdivision (b), is published on page 458 of 136 Texas Reports. By an amendment promulgated by the Supreme Court of Texas, after the above paragraph was written, which became effective December 31, 1941, subdivision (b) of Rule 42 was eliminated from the Texas Rules, as is shown in note 48 herein. 

For this reason if the shareholder brought a suit after Rule 42 went into effect and before Dec. 31, 1941, he must have alleged that he was a shareholder when the transaction of which he complains occurred "or that his shares thereafter devolved upon him by operation of law." If he institutes a shareholder's bill after Dec. 31, 1941, such an allegation will be unnecessary if the Texas Supreme Court follows the weight of authority and what seems to be the better rule. This question has not been determined by the Texas Supreme Court. 

Some writers contend that subdivision (b) of Federal Rule 23, which requires the shareholder to allege that he "was a shareholder at the time of the transaction of which he complains," is substantive and not procedural, and, therefore, the federal courts must apply the law of the state by virtue of the Erie Railroad Co.-Tompkins holding. For instance, Prof. Moore in section 23.05 of his treatise on Federal Practice under the New 

Federal Rules in his 1941 Cumulative Supplement says: "Analy sis seems to demonstrate that this provision of the Rule is more than one of procedure." If the Supreme Court of the United

The preferable view for the state courts to adopt is that where the subsequent transferee files a suit in good faith, and his transferor could have filed such a suit, the court should entertain it. It is settled law that a person cannot maintain suit for the corporation after he ceases to be a stockholder.49 The necessary consequence, if the above view is not adopted, is that if there is only one man in the corporate body who is not disqualified to bring the suit and he sells his stock, no one can compel restitution for fraudulent acts. 

By the weight of authority the owner of the equitable title to stock of a corporation can bring a shareholder's bill. In 54 

Harvard Law Review, page 1064, it is said: "Since the theory of a stockholder's suit is the protection of the equitable owners from the inactivity of the management in remedying damage to the corporation, there seems to be little reason for denying any beneficial owner of shares the right to maintain such a suit, and there is considerable authority recognizing such a right.” 50 If

There is some conflict in the authorities as to when the nonparticipating preferred shareholders are so injured that they can bring a shareholder's bill to right the wrong suffered by the corporation.53 These points have not arisen in Texas, but they are discussed in a recent number of the Harvard Law Review referred to in the notes.54

§ 772. Motive of Stockholder 

Many courts have held that the motive of a stockholder in bringing a shareholder's bill is immaterial.67 Under the holding of these cases, even though it is shown that the shareholder brought the suit merely for the purpose of wrecking the corporation, he would still have a right to bring the suit, and proof of the above facts would be no defense. This was the old idea, but the modern cases hold that an evil motive quite often destroys the so-called "inalienable right." Under the modern cases spite fences may be enjoined,68 and a competitor may be enjoined from carrying on a lawful business if his sole motive is to wreak vengeance upon his enemy.69 As every legal right ceases sooner or later, the better holding, although not the weight of authority at this time, is that the stockholder has no right to bring a shareholder's bill if his purpose in doing so is for the sole purpose of destroying the company.70 By the weight of authority, the fact

 § 773. Parties to Suits 

All the shareholders in a corporation are interested in the result of a shareholder's suit, as all of such suits are instituted to redress an injury to the corporation. Therefore, the suit must be brought on behalf of the plaintiff and all other stockholders who wish to come in as co-plaintiffs, except the shareholders who are implicated in the wrong; and, therefore, are made defendants in the suit.75 But failure to allege that the suit is brought on behalf of all stockholders who wish to join in the action is a defect of parties and is waived unless the defendants. in their answer call the court's attention to the defect."6

By the weight of authority the equitable owner of stock, such as the cestui que trusts where the stock has been conveyed to a trustee, may bring a shareholder's bill.77 

A representative suit in equity by a stockholder can only be maintained on the ground that the rights of the corporation are involved, and the suit should be so conducted that any decree on the merits will be binding upon the corporation. It is therefore necessary to make the corporation a party defendant.

Of course, the directors of a corporation have authority to employ and pay an attorney for representing the corporation in all of its business or legal affairs.87 But if the directors are the defendants in a shareholder's bill wherein the plaintiff is attempting to recover for the corporation damages caused by the fault of the directors, they cannot pay their attorney out of the funds of the corporation for defending them in such suit. The reason for this holding is that in such litigation the attorney is not representing the corporation but the directors individually. If the directors are successful in the suit and they proved themselves absolutely innocent, it seems rather harsh to put this expense on them personally. But, this is a risk they ran when they accepted the position of a director of the corporation.88 As suits by a shareholder to enjoin executory ultra vires transactions are not brought for and on behalf of the corporation and are brought to vindicate individual rights of the shareholder he cannot recover his expenses, such as attorney's fees, from the corporation.89

In 46 Yale L.Jr. 424, it is said: "Prior to the institution of suit, all stockholders share the same privilege to bring an action on behalf of the corporation; but, when the machinery of suit on behalf of the corporation has been set in motion by one stockholder, the privileges of the others to do likewise may be viewed as suspended. The equitable purposes, for which the stockholder's privilege to sue is recognized, have been temporarily satisfied. Since bringing a suit by one stockholder merely suspends and does not extinguish the privileges of other stockholders to sue, if the suit is discontinued by the plaintiff stockholder, the rights of other stockholders to commence action on behalf of the corporation are revived. Considering the institution of an action by one stockholder as a temporary bar to another suit can, it appears, work no injustice to the would-be plaintiffstockholder. He can always intervene and be joined as a party plaintiff in the original action, thus gaining an equal voice with the original plaintiff in its conduct."

In determining whether the federal court has jurisdiction, the value of the claim sought to be enforced for the corporation is the amount in controversy and not the value of plaintiff's shares.¹ 

As every shareholder's suit is brought in the court of equity, a shareholder cannot in a shareholder's suit ask for vindication of the rights of the corporation where a statute limits the enforcement of such rights to an action at law where the plaintiff would have the right of trial by jury. For this reason the United States 

Supreme Court held that threefold damages could not be recovered for the corporation in a shareholder's suit for violation of the Federal Anti-Trust Law. Since in Texas, law and equity are blended and either party may demand a jury whether equitable or common law relief is sought, the federal rule does not apply if the suit is brought in a Texas state court.3 Under the recent rules bring the action on behalf of the resisting corporation should also entitle him to enforce the judgment on behalf of the resisting corporation. The corporation, its directors and majority stockholders having failed to sue, has no rights with regard to the cause of action except to accept the benefits. The more reasonable thing to say is that the suit, begun by the minority stockholder in equity, is not completed until the coffers of the corporation have been swelled by the money realized on the judgment. As Chancellor Walworth said in speaking of the right of a minority stockholder to institute such a suit: 'But as this court never permits a wrong to go unredressed merely for the sake of form, if it appeared that the directors of the corporation refused to prosecute by collusion with those who had made themselves answerable by their negligence or fraud, or if the corporation was still under the control of those who must be made defendants in the suit, the stockholders who are the real parties in interest, would be permitted to file a bill in their own names, making the corporation a party defendant.' So here, since it appears that the directors refuse to issue execution on a judgment rendered against themselves, the stockholders, who are the actively interested parties, should be permitted to issue the execution."

In the case of Erie Railway Company v. Tompkins the Supreme Court of the United States held that where the question before the court involved a rule of substantive law the federal courts would follow the applicable law of the state rather than what was heretofore designated as the general federal substantive law. In other words, the above case overruled several previous federal cases which held that the federal courts were not compelled to follow the general law of the state if the case involved a substantive rule of law rather than procedural law. 

The question of interest now before the courts is, therefore, whether Rule 23 (b), Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, 28 U.S.C.

A. following § 723c, involves substantive rules of law or merely rules of practice and procedure. For instance, one part of the rule provides that the petition must allege that "the plaintiff was a stockholder at the time of the transaction of which he complained." Does that part of the rule embody a rule of substantive law or one of procedure? In view of the holding of the Tompkins' case the federal rule will not be sustained if it embodies rules of substantive law. This question is discussed in the 25 Virginia

As the rule in its present form was recently promulgated by the Supreme Court of the United States and as that court must finally decide the question, it is probable that the court will hold that the rule is one of procedure rather than substantive law. A federal district court has recently decided that the determination of diversity of citizenship as grounds for the jurisdiction of the federal courts is a question of procedure and not of substantive law. In this case a New York stockholder brought a shareholder's bill against a New Jersey corporation and its directors, some of whom were citizens of New York in a federal court in the state of New York. There was no federal question involved in the case, and, as the plaintiff and some of the defendant directors were citizens of New York, the defendant corporation moved to dismiss the bill for the reason that there was no proper diversity of citizenship. However, the plaintiff contended that under the New York substantive law in a shareholder's bill the defendant corporation is primarily interested in the result of the litigation and is considered the real plaintiff in a shareholder's suit. Thus the plaintiff contended that there was the necessary diversity of citizenship to give the federal court jurisdiction of the case under the rule of the Erie-Tompkins case. The court held that even assuming the applicability of the Tompkin's case, the question involved was one of procedure and not of substantive law, and, therefore, the New York rule was not decisive, and that under the federal rule the court had no jurisdiction of the shareholder's bill.8 This decision seems correct, as whether there is

§ 791. In General 

In the early history of corporations the courts held that a corporation could not do acts unauthorized by its charter; and, therefore, held that a corporation could not commit a tort. It was argued that corporations were organized for lawful purposes, and not to do unlawful acts. This conclusion followed logically from the fictional theory of the corporation. The torts of the agents or servants of the corporation were considered the personal wrongs of the employees and not the torts of the corporation.¹ However, this view has never been entertained in Texas.

If from early times the courts had looked at the corporation realistically, and considered it in its true light as a collection of human beings, no judge or lawyer would ever have doubted its liability for the torts of its agents in furtherance of the master's business any more than the liability of a partnership for its torts. 

The courts of Texas, following the present majority rule, hold that it is no defense in tort that the corporation is not authorized 

1. Chestnut Hill & Spring House 

Turnpike Co. v. Rutter, Pa., 4 

Serg. & R. 6, 8 Am.Dec. 675. 

Orr v. Bank of U. S., 1 Ohio 37, 13 

Am.Dec. 588; 24 Harv.L.Rev. 233

§

in its charter to do wrong.

Our own Judge Batts, while on the 

Circuit Court of Appeals, in the case of Clinchfield Fuel Co. v. 

Henderson Iron Works² admirably stated the reason for holding a corporation liable for its wrongs. "Of course, no corporation can lawfully authorize the doing of an unlawful act, or of a tortious or negligent act. Neither can an individual acquire a right to commit a tort; but the absence of the right to do that which is wrong will not absolve him from the consequences of the wrong." 

Professor Warren expressed the correct idea in saying, "A command to the corporation to use only lawful means in attaining its objects is not equivalent to imposing a legal incapacity to use unlawful means."3 The Texas courts hold that a corporation is liable for the torts of its servants, agents, and officers if committed in the scope of their authority to the same extent as the individual master. This is true even though the act is done in disobedience to express orders. Corporations have also been held

§ 792. Involving Wrongful Intent or Malice 

It has been contended that, in the nature of things, a corporation cannot be liable for a tort involving intent or malice as an essential element. It was argued that such malicious intent could not be attributed to the stockholders, who themselves are not really implicated in the acts of their officers and agents, nor to the fictitious ideal entity.13 However, this idea has long since been abandoned, and Texas is in line with the present view. "Whatever controversy may at one time have existed, it must be held that a corporation may become civilly responsible for libel." This was held by the Supreme Court in a case where the corporation compiled a list of discharged employees, stating therein their faults, and placed it in the hands of an employment agency of the corporation.14 Some courts make a distinction be-

§ 793. Exemplary Damages 

In Texas exemplary damages are awarded to punish the offender.31 With this in mind, the Supreme Court32 has formulated the following rule as a guide in holding a corporation liable for exemplary damages: 

"It is now the well settled law of this state, that, to make a corporation liable for exemplary damages, the 'fraud, malice, gross negligence, or oppression' which must authorize and justify the same, must have been committed by the corporation itself, or some superior officer representing it in its corporate capacity; or, if committed by a subordinate servant or agent, the act must have been either previously authorized, or subsequently ratified or approved by the company or such superior officer, after knowledge of the facts." 33

Before three recent cases discussed in a subsequent section the corporation was not liable in exemplary damages when the tort was committed by a subordinate servant, unless the tort was authorized or ratified by an officer or agent vested with authority to conduct the business of the corporation between meetings

Nor will the retention of the guilty servant in the employment of the corporation of itself render the corporation liable in exemplary damages for the tort on the ground of ratification.38 

However, where a conductor assaulted a passenger and the corporation furnished counsel to defend him in the criminal prosecution, paid his fine, and retained the conductor in its employ, the corporation was held to have ratified the act of the conductor.39 

In three recent cases 40 the Texas Supreme Court seemingly has modified the rule of exemplary damages in suits against corporations. Until recent cases were decided, the law in Texas was that a corporation is not liable in exemplary damages for torts committed by a non-executive servant in the scope of the master's business, unless the head officer or officers in actual charge of the business of the corporation in Texas authorized or ratified the tort. In its recent decisions the Supreme Court of 

Texas held that a corporation is liable in exemplary damages if the tort was wilful and malicious and committed by a vice-principal of the corporation. The court designated four different classes of employees as vice-principals: (a) corporate officers; (b) those who have authority to employ, direct, and discharge servants of the master; (c) those engaged in the performance of non-delegable or absolute duties of the master; 41 and (d)

those to whom a master has confided the management of the whole or a department or division of his business. In the opinion the court said: "The Texas rule, reduced to its simplest terms, and applied to a case of gross neglect, means that the default for which punitive damages may be recovered must be that of the corporation, that the grossly negligent act must be the very act of the corporation itself; or, if the act is that of a mere servant or employee as such, then it must have been previously authorized or subsequently must be approved by the corporation." 

"If in an action for actual damages for negligence the vice principal is to be regarded as the alter ego of the corporation, and his acts corporate acts, how can it be said that his grossly negligent acts are not also those of the corporation? If he represents the corporation when negligent, whom does he represent when grossly negligent? There can be but one logical answer, and this is, he still represents the corporation; provided, of course, the work in hand is within the duties delegated to him." "The insistence that a corporation can be held liable in exemplary damages only for the torts of a "superior officer representing it in its corporate capacity" is, we think, without merit. Language in support of this view is to be found in Western 

Union Tel. Co. v. Brown, 58 Tex. 170, 44 Am.Rep. 610; St. Lou 

S. W. Ry. Co. v. McArthur, 31 Tex.Civ.App. 205, 72 S.W. 76.

We are of the opinion, however, that the courts in these cases intended to follow the rule announced in the Hays and Cowser Cases, supra, and that the language employed with reference to a corporate officer was an inaccurate statement of the rule from the Cowser Case, wherein this court said that punitive damages are recoverable against a corporation "for the willful act, omission or gross negligence of one representing it in its corporate capacity, as a corporate officer, but not of a mere ordinary servant or agent." (Italics ours.) It is plain, we think, that the words "as a corporate officer" were not intended to mean that the tortious act must be committed by a corporate officer; but 244

that what was meant was that the act complained of must be the act of the corporation, or of "one representing it in its corporate capacity,” citing as an example, "a corporate officer." "The rule deducible, it seems to us, from the Texas authorities, is that exemplary damages are not recoverable against a corporation where the grossly negligent act involves only a breach of duty by a mere servant or employee as such, unless the act was previously authorized or was subsequently approved by the corporation. But where committed by an agent who represents it in such manner and under such circumstances that under the general rules of law his acts are regarded as the acts of the corporation itself, as distinguished from the acts of a mere servant, then an action for punitive damages does lie, regardless of the question as to whether or not the agent was a corporate officer."

From the above quotations, and other parts of the opinions, it seems evident that the court held that a corporation in Texas is liable in exemplary damages for every wilful and malicious tort committed by an agent or servant in the scope of the master's business. In several places in the opinions, the court said that a corporation is liable in exemplary damages, where the agent who committed the tort was the "alter ego" of the corporation. 

It is very evident from the opinion that in all of these cases the court meant that the corporation was bound by the act of the agent, and not that the agent was the same person as the corporation; in other words, the court could not have meant that the servant was the alter ego of the corporation. For instance, in one of the above quotations the court said, "that the grossly negligent act must be the very act of the corporation itself." 

In another part of the opinion the court said, "that the act must be the act of the corporation, instead of the act of the servant.” 

Again the court said, "what was meant was that the act complained of must be the act of the corporation, or of one representing it in its corporate capacity." In another place the court said the corporation is liable in exemplary damages where "his (servants) acts are regarded as the acts of the corporation it- 245

self, as distinguished from the acts of a mere servant." If the servant or agent is acting in the course of the master's business, his acts are always regarded as the acts of the corporation itself. 

In the very nature of the corporation it can act only vicariously. 

From these and other parts of the opinion the court attempts to make a distinction between the acts of the corporation and the acts of a servant or agent acting for the corporation in the scope of the master's business. In this latter case the act of the servant or mere agent is as much the act of the corporation where the servant is acting in the scope of his authority as if the directors themselves acted for the corporation in the same transaction. 

Therefore, the logical conclusion from these opinions is that in Texas a corporation is liable in exemplary damages whenever an agent or servant of the corporation commits a malicious tort in the scope of the master's business. This conclusion is inevitable as is clearly shown from the above quotation wherein the court says: "If he (vice-principal) represents the corporation when negligent, whom does he represent when grossly negligent? 

There can be but one logical answer, and that is, he still represents the corporation; provided the work in hand is within the duties delegated to him." In other words, whenever a representative of a corporation acts within the scope of his authority he binds the corporation and, according to the court's argument, since his acts are binding on the corporation the latter is liable not only in actual damages but also in exemplary damages. 

In many places in the opinion the court said that a corporation is liable in exemplary damages only for the acts of a vice-principal and classified four different employees as vice-principals. 

The court's designation of vice-principals is not in accord with previous Texas cases. One of those divisions is those engaged in the performance of the absolute duties of the master, such as using ordinary care in the selection of competent fellow servants, a reasonably safe place in which to work, and the promulgation of reasonable rules with reference to the manner of doing the work. In the second case above cited the court held that if the master fails to perform one of these absolute duties, and the plaintiff is injured thereby, he can recover actual and exemplary 246

damages even though the wrong was committed by a menial servant. In the third of the cases cited above the court held that the manager of the Southwestern Gas & Electric Company was a vice-principal, even though the evidence was very meager on the point, and did not set forth the duties of the manager. 

If the court in future cases holds that the corporation is liable in exemplary damages where the tort is committed by one of the four classes of vice-principals, it will be extremely difficult to apply the court's tests to specific cases. Take, for instance, the fourth designation of vice-principals, "those to whom a master has confided the management of the whole or a department or division of his business." The question that will cause much doubt and difficulty will be the meaning of "department or division". Inquiry will be made as to how large must each division of the business be. For instance, is the young lady in a department store who sells nothing but thread from a counter four feet long and two feet wide in charge of "a division" of the business of the corporation, especially if she is given authority to order the thread and determine the quantity and quality of the goods purchased? Is the section foreman who keeps in repair six miles of the right of way of the railroad in charge of "a division" of the master's business?

Again, did the court mean to say that a corporation is liable in exemplary damages for a wilful or wanton tort committed by any "corporate officer"? If so, will the mercantile corporation be liable in exemplary damages for the wilful tort of the treasurer of the corporation, who is paid a very small salary for taking care of the stock certificate book, and who commits a wilful tort in issuing a new certificate to a stockholder upon the surrender of an old one? Suppose in these last two cases the directors and head officers repudiate liability as soon as they have notice of the commission of the tort and condemn the acts of the guilty servant. Did the Supreme Court mean to hold that a corporation is liable in exemplary damages for the wilful tort of any corporate officer, or only those who are designated as officers in the charter of the corporation? These and many other questions are left in doubt by the three opinions cited above. 247

§ 

Ch. 17

When a corporation is chartered under the general incorporation statute of Texas, the only representatives that are named in the charter are the directors for the first year, but Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1325 provides that "the directors or trustees shall choose one of their number president and shall appoint a secretary and treasurer and such other officers as they may deem necessary for the corporation." One class of vice-principals named by the court in the Russell case is "corporate officers." Did the court mean to say that all "corporate officers" are vice-principals, or only those named in the charter and those specifically designated in article 1325? The court said "corporate officers", and a literal construction of those terms would certainly include all officers chosen by the directors or trustees in accordance with article 1325. Whether the court intended also to include the directors is not determined by the opinion. 

Just why the corporation should be liable in exemplary damages for the torts of a minor officer and not if the servant is what the court designates as a "mere servant", who has not been designated as an officer of the corporation by the directors, although the servant occupies a much higher position and performs much more important duties than the minor officer, is difficult to ascertain. Possibly the court did not mean that any "corporate officer" is a vice-principal. These inquiries show how difficult it will be to apply the rules discussed in the three opinions cited above in actual practice. As a matter of fact up to this time the courts have failed to draw a sharp line of demarcation between "officers of the corporation" and "employees" or "mere agents." 42

In Young v. Hahn 43 the Supreme Court of Texas, following previous decisions, defined who is a vice-principal, as follows, "that mere difference in the grade of employment, or the fact that one servant is the foreman or boss of another, does not take them out of the general rule of the common law upon the subject; and that the common master is not responsible for the 

42. 93 A.L.R. 336; 53 A.L.R. 599; 

S. H. Kress & Co. v. Rust, 120 

S.W.2d 425, 132 Tex. 89. 

43. 70 S.W. 950, 96 Tex. 99, reversing, Civ.App., 69 S.W. 203. 248

negligent acts of the foreman or boss, unless the latter has been entrusted with the power to employ and discharge." In other words, it has long been settled in Texas that only the employee who has the right to employ and discharge servants is a viceprincipal. According to the first of the three opinions cited above, there are now in Texas four classes of vice-principals. 

Why the court designated a servant who performs one of the absolute duties of the master as a vice-principal, however menial his services, is difficult to determine. In Texas a railroad corporation is under a non-delegable duty to protect its passengers from assaults. If the conductor of a passenger train fails to perform this duty for the corporation master, the company is liable in damages, regardless of whether the tort was committed by a menial servant or one of the highest officers of the corporation. 

It is, therefore, unnecessary to determine the position of the employee who fails to perform an absolute duty imposed upon the master. Why should a master in such a case be liable not only in actual damages, but also in exemplary damages if the wilful tort is committed by a menial servant? If the corporation is liable not only for actual, but also for exemplary damages, under the above circumstances where it fails to perform a nondelegable duty, although the failure was due to the act of a menial servant, why should not the corporation also be liable in exemplary damages in every case where the tort is malicious and committed in the scope of the master's business? If exemplary damages are imposed for punishment, why not punish the master for the act of a mere servant by imposing exemplary damages where the wilful tort is committed in the scope of the master's business, regardless of the character of the work being done, as well as where the failure is to perform an absolute duty due a passenger or any other member of the public? The basic assumption of the court in the three recent cases is that "the acts of the vice-principal are the very acts of the corporation itself." Some vice-principals, even under the old Texas test, have merely the right to employ and discharge men working under them, but have nothing to say about the real operations of the corporation. Why did the court say that their acts 249

§ 

Ch. 17

"are the very acts of the corporation itself," if the court meant anything except that their acts are binding on the corporation? 

Many writers 44 contend that exemplary damages should never be awarded in civil actions. This, it seems to the writer, is the better view. The plaintiff should always be satisfied with actual damages; and if in committing the tort a crime was committed, the defendant should be indicted and tried in accordance with the criminal statutes. In this modern era the Texas courts should consider the reasons for imposing exemplary damages on individuals and corporations in civil actions, rather than showing absolute reverence for the "Code of Hammurabi and the Hebrew Laws." If the court is fully convinced that malicious torts will be minimized by the imposition of exemplary damages, there may still be some reason for assessing smart money damages.45

The opinions do not purport to overrule Dillingham v. Russell,46 but, as a matter of fact, this and other cases are directly overruled. A common carrier is under a duty to protect its passengers while in transit. The conductor of the defendant-road assaulted the plaintiff, and the court held that the plaintiff was entitled to actual damages, but not to exemplary damages. In this case the court directly decided that the usual rule of exemplary damages applies, even though the tort is committed in the performance of one of the master's non-delegable duties. However, in Texas at this time, according to the three recent cases, the master is liable in actual and exemplary damages under the above circumstances, even though the tort was committed by a person that the court designates as "a mere servant.” “ In 7

§ 794. Corporation's Right to Recover Exemplary Damages 

Under Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1320 every corporation is empowered "to maintain and defend judicial proceedings." Under this authority a corporation has a right to recover exemplary damages in wilful and malicious torts committed against it wherever an individual is permitted to recover such damages.6⁰ 60 

§ 795. Torts in Ultra Vires Transaction 

The Texas courts are in accord with the majority view in holding that the corporation is liable for the torts committed by its agents while in the scope of their employment, though they

The liability of the corporation in such a situation is the same as where the business or transaction is intra vires.61 This view is in perfect accord with the Texas theme that is implicit in many cases that "a corporation is liable for the torts committed by its servants or agents precisely as natural persons are." 62 

The liability of corporations for the acts of its agents while employed in an ultra vires business of the corporation is based on fairness and justice. The Texas courts have said, "The doctrine of ultra vires, when invoked for or against a corporation, should not be allowed to prevail when it would defeat the ends of justice or work a legal wrong.' ❞ 63 The directors of a corporation are invested only with the ordinary powers of the company.64 Fundamental changes must be authorized by a vote of the stockholders.65 Adding a new business not authorized by the charter would be a change of the original agreement and understanding of the stockholders. 

Therefore, in order to make the corporation liable for the torts committed in conducting the unauthorized business, it must be shown that the ultra vires undertaking was authorized or ratified by all of the stockholders. This may be shown in many ways. For instance, if the stockholders accept dividends knowing that part of them were paid from profits of the unauthorized business; or even if they receive such dividends over a long period of time without knowing the source of them, such silent acquiescence may be sufficient evidence of ratification.66 Some

§ 796. Liability by Reason of Ratification 

The Texas courts, still in keeping with the idea that a corporation is liable for the torts of its agents in the same manner as an individual master, hold that though the agent may not have been acting within the scope of his authority, yet the corporation will be held liable if it ratifies or adopts the tortious conduct of the agent where it receives a direct benefit from such act.69

 § 799. Responsibility for Crime 

Some early cases stated that at common law a private corporation is not indictable for crime.¹ The great weight of authority today, however, is that a corporation may be criminally liable not only for crimes involving general intent but even for crimes which require a specific intent, provided a suitable penalty that can be imposed on the corporation is provided in the penal code.2 1. 

There are three limitations upon this rule. In the first place there are certain crimes which, in the very nature of things, a fictitious person is incapable of committing, such as bigamy and perjury.³ In the second place the punishment provided for by the statute must be such as can be imposed upon a corporation. Therefore, if the only punishment provided for by the statute is imprisonment or death, it is evident that such statute would not apply to a corporation. In the third place the statute

venue statute, where the point in issue was one of venue. It was specifically held that when appellant sued the corporation on a claim for damages based on a malicious prosecution, he admitted that the corporation can be guilty of a crime, offense, or trespass, and this is now the universal ruling in the United States.31 

It, therefore, seems evident that in Texas the above decision by the Court of Criminal Appeals stands unchallenged in any criminal prosecution, and therefore in Texas, a private corporation will not be liable under a general criminal statute which does not specifically make corporations subject thereto. 

The Vernon's Annotated Penal Code does not provide that the word "person" includes "corporations". Article 1 of the statutes provides that "The design of enacting this Code is to define in plain language every offense against the laws of this State, * "9 and article 29 provides that, "With the exceptions stated in this chapter, all persons whether inhabitants of this State or the United States or aliens are amenable to punishment for offenses punishable under this Code." In other words, no act is criminal in Texas unless the statute clearly makes such act illegal. Even though article 29 provides that "all persons whether inhabitants of this State or the United States" are punishable for offenses defined in this Code, the Texas courts could very easily hold that corporations are amenable to the criminal laws of Texas since all courts hold that corporations are "persons" and many courts do not hesitate to hold that corporations are "inhabitants" of the state.32 But since the Texas Court of 

Criminal Appeals in the case of Judge Lynch International Book & Pub. Co. v. State 33 held that corporations are not amenable to punishment for acts made crimes by our Penal Code, should not the Legislature revise our criminal statutes so as to include the corporation? It may be argued that this is not necessary, as the criminals will not go unpunished, since the agents of the corporation who commit the crimes will be punished. This is 

31. Warwick v. First State Bank of 32. Galveston, H. & S. A. Ry. Co.

true in some cases, but in many cases, on account of the wording of the statute, no one will be punished. Suppose, for instance, the statute provides that "a contractor of a public building who compels his employees to labor more than eight hours any day" may be fined, or "the owner of a lot who lowers the curb without the consent of the city engineer may be fined", and a corporation is "the contractor" in the first case and "the owner" in the second illustration, can the officers or the agents of the corporation be fined? In these, and many other cases, an act which would be criminal if done by an individual principal, will not be punishable if done by the corporation under the present holding of our Court of Criminal Appeals. Therefore, this matter should be called to the attention of the Texas Legislature. 

The above suggestion may be untimely as the Court of Criminal Appeals may overrule the case of Judge Lynch International Book and Publishing Company v.  § 801. Liability of Agents for Torts 

The agent who commits a tort while engaged in performing an act in the scope or apparent scope of the business of a corporation is personally liable to the plaintiff for the proximate damages suffered. In that case either the agent or the corporation, or both, could be held liable for the tort.38 Thus, if the president assaults a person while acting for the corporation, the president would be liable for such tort.39 If the officer or director of a corporation knowingly directs or participates in the commission of a tort, he is personally liable.40 A common tort committed by officers or agents is the making of false representations in the sale of the stock of the company or its condition.41 

Where the officer commits the tort or directs an agent of the company to commit it, he is personally liable for the resulting damage.42 But if the director or officer is not directly or indirectly implicated in the wrong, he is not liable. The cases make a distinction between nonfeasance and misfeasance-holding the agent liable for misfeasance but not for nonfeasance.43 An officer is not liable for the tort of subordinate agents where he took no part in the commission of the tort, did not know of it, and did not consent to its commission.44 The Texas courts still at-

In a recent case the Supreme Court held that where the defendant is sued out of the county of his residence the burden is on the plaintiff to prove that the case comes within one of the exceptions set out in the Texas statute and that the defendant has the right to demand a separate trial on his plea of privilege. "The character of agency that establishes residence, within the meaning of the venue statute, is an agency for the prosecution of the charter purposes of the corporation.”18

§ 814. County Where Part of the Cause of Action Arose 

By statutory enactment20 suit may be brought in any county in which the cause of action, or a part thereof, arose. Subdivision 

23 of article 1995 provides: "Suits against a private corporation, association or joint stock company may be brought in any county in which the cause of action, or a part thereof, arose, or in which such corporation, association or company has an agency or representative, or in which its principal office is situated.". Subdivision 

27 of article 1995 provides: "Foreign corporations, private or public, joint stock companies or associations, not incorporated by the laws of this State, but doing business within the State, may be sued in any county where the cause of action or a part thereof accrued, or in any county where such company may have an agencyº¹ or representative, or in the county in which the principal office of such company may be situated; or, when the defendant corporation has no agent or representative in this State, then in the county where the plaintiffs, or either of them, reside."22 volving title to lands alienated by railway companies.

bess,23 where the plaintiff deposited money in the defendant bank at its office in Nacogdoches, Texas. The plaintiff resided in another county. He drew a check on the defendant in the county of his residence. When it was presented at the defendant's office in Nacogdoches the bank refused payment. The plaintiff sued in the county of his residence. In holding that the plea of privilege should be granted as no part of the cause of action arose outside of Nacogdoches County, Justice Critz said: "In the case at bar the record shows that the entire transaction by which appellee became an ordinary or general depositor in appellant occurred or arose in Nacogdoches county. After the deposit was made, appellee gave checks to a bank in Randall county. Appellant took no part in that transaction. The Randall county bank, which was selected by appellee and which had no authority to act for appellant, presented such checks to appellant for payment. These presentations were made in Nacogdoches county, and payment was there refused by appellant. It is thus evident that all transactions with which appellant had any connection occurred or arose exclusively in Nacogdoches county, and not, in whole or in part, in Randall county, where this suit was filed. "The provision of exception 23 of article 1995, which permits 'a private corporation, association or joint stock company' to be sued 'in any county in which the cause of action, or a part thereof, arose,' means that either some part of the transaction creating the primary right, or some part of the transaction relating to the breach of that right, must have occurred in the county where the suit is brought. "If we properly interpret the opinion of the Court of Civil Appeals, it, in effect, holds that the provisions of exception 23 of article 1995, which permit private corporations, etc., to be sued in any county 'in which the cause of action, or a part thereof, arose,' makes it permissible to maintain an action for damages against a private corporation in any county where the plaintiff suffers damages, notwithstanding the fact that the corporation has taken no part in any transaction producing such damages in the county where the suit is brought. In support of its holding, the Court of

Civil Appeals cites Phillio v. Blythe, 12 Tex. 124. We think the opinion in the Phillio Case, when read as a whole and construed in the light of the facts there decided, supports our ruling in the case at bar. We here quote the following excerpt from the opinion in the Phillio Case: 'It may be admitted that the terms 'cause of action' are sometimes used in a more limited sense, and that where the cause is founded on a contract, the contract itself is denominated the cause of action; but more frequently, and where the terms are used with more precision, the terms embrace a much wider scope, and include, not only the contract, but its performance, if executory, and also the breach of such contract.' "Under the record before us, if appellee has any right of action against appellant within the meaning of the part of exception 23, under consideration, it consists of two elements, both of which arose entirely in Nacogdoches county, viz.: His primary right which arose out of the transaction by which he became an ordinary or general depositor in appellant bank, and appellant's violation of that primary right by its refusal to pay the checks drawn against that deposit. Both the transaction creating the primary right and the transaction constituting the violation of that right occurred wholly in Nacogdoches county. It follows that within the meaning of that part of exception 23, under consideration, no part of appellee's cause of action arose in Randall county, or anywhere outside of Nacogdoches county." 24 As we have seen25 this provision is constitutional.26 And where the plaintiff under the

§ 815. Component Parts of a Cause of Action 

The legislature having authorized suits against corporations: in any county where the cause of action or a part thereof arises, it becomes important to determine the constituent parts of a cause of action. The construction of this part of the venue statute has given rise to much litigation.29 "In the abstract, a cause of action consists of the right claimed, or wrong suffered by the plaintiff, and of the duty or delict of the defendant.

When used with reference to the pleadings by which the cause of action is alleged, the phrase signifies the facts upon which the plaintiff's right to sue is based, and upon which the defendant's duty has arisen, coupled with the facts which constitute the latter's wrong. "It occurs to us it is in the latter sense in which our venue statute uses the term 'cause of action, or a part thereof arose.'

Ch. § 815 

"A cause of action upon which recovery is sought does not comprise every piece of evidence which is necessary to prove each fact, but every fact which is necessary to be proved. We believe under our statute on venue it is too narrow to confine it to the genesis of the right, but it embraces every fact necessary to be shown in order to recover. 'Arose,' we do not think, refers alone to the very beginning of the right, but to every fact which has arisen and inheres in the cause of action. 

It is the right to bring a suit, or that right which is based upon the ground or grounds on which an action may be maintained.” 30 

Or as succinctly stated by another court: "A cause of action, as that term is used in the venue statute, consists both of the right of plaintiff and the injury to such right. It embraces the entire state of facts that give use to an enforceable claim, and necessarily comprises every fact which a plaintiff must prove in order to obtain judgment." 31

Where it does not appear that any of the component parts of the cause of action arose in the county of the suit, obviously venue cannot be established in such county by virtue of this provision. If there is no other ground for the court's jurisdiction, the defendant's plea of privilege should be sustained and the suit transferred to the proper county.32 Obviously if the above

Waggoner v. Edwards, Tex. Civ.App., 68 S.W.2d 655.

In a recent case the Supreme Court of Texas held that under subdivision 5 of Article 1995 it is only necessary to show that defendant contracted in writing to perform the alleged obligation in the county where the suit was brought, Petroleum Producers Co. v. 

Steffens, 162 S.W.2d 698, Tex. 

In that case the Court said: "Subdivision 5 of Article 1995 was amended in the year 1935. As amended, same reads as follows: 

"If a person has contracted in writing to perform an obligation in a particular county, expressly naming such county, or a definite place therein, by such writing, suit upon or by reason of such obligation may be brought against him, either in such county or where the defendant has his domicile.' "It is quite clear from the language used in this subdivision that, aside from the fact that the pleadings in the suit disclose that the suit is 'upon or by reason of' an obligation of some sort-either written or unwritten, express or implied-there is but a single fact which need be shown in order to cast venue in the county where the suit is brought. This single fact is to the effect that the defendant has contracted in writing to perform the alleged obligation in said county-the county or some definite place therein being expressly named in the writing. 

Proof of the existence of a cause of action is not required now, and was not required before the subdivision was amended in 1935. Farmers Seed & Gin Co. v. Brooks, 125 Tex. 234, 81 

S.W.2d 675; Bradley v. Trinity State 

Bank, 118 Tex. 274, 14 S.W.2d 810. * * * "The terms of the lease instrument set out above-nothing to the contrary appearing in the instrument -imply an obligation on the part of the lessee to drill offset wells and development wells. Grubb v. McAfee, 109 Tex. 527, 212 S.W. 464; Texas Pacific Coal & Oil Co. v. Barker, 117 

Tex. 418, 6 S.W.2d 1031, 60 A.L.R. 

936; Freeport Surphur Co. v. American Sulphur Royalty Co. of Tex., 117 

Tex. 439, 6 S.W.2d 1039, 60 A.L.R. 

890. The place for performance of this implied obligation is expressly named in the lease instrument, towit, the parcel of land in Jones County in respect to which the parties to the lease were contracting."

§ 817. Performance by Plaintiff 

In order to state a cause of action, the plaintiff must not only allege that a contract was made but that he has complied with its terms. Since substantial performance or tender by plaintiff is an essential element, it is not surprising to note that venue may be had in a certain county because of the plaintiff's performance of his duties in such county where the contract provided for such performance.49 Subdivision 5 of article 199550 authorizes suit in a county where a person has contracted in writing to perform an obligation. This subdivision does not assist us in a case where no mention is made in the contract, as to where the defendant corporation is to perform.51 The courts 64

have also utilized subdivision 23 to obviate the necessity of determining whether all of the performance was to be had in one county,52 a requisite under subdivision 5. In many cases the contract is oral and subdivision 5 is inapplicable. 

Suit may be brought in the county of plaintiff's performance of his obligation under the contract even though the contract was made, and the breach of the defendant occurred, in another county.

The leading case, announcing this rule, is Savage v. H. C. 

Burks & Co.53 In this case the contract was oral. The plaintiff was employed by the defendant corporation, a cotton broker, to purchase cotton for it. As added compensation, plaintiff was to receive fifty percent of the profit realized from the resale of the cotton purchased by him. He bought 833 bales of cotton in D county, which the defendant resold at a profit. The plaintiff filed suit in D county for his share of the profits. In sustaining the venue of such suit the court said: "It is thus seen that there are two conditions precedent to the coming into existence of a valid claim in favor of appellant on this phase of his contract; one to be performed by appellant in D County, the other to be performed by appellee [corporation] with no restriction as to place of performance. 

When appellee refused to account to appellant for 50 per cent of the profits arising from the resale of the cotton, a cause of action accrued in appellant's favor against appellee *. Appellant could not establish his cause of action without first pleading and then proving, not only the profit made by appellee on the resale of the cotton, but also that he had purchased the said cotton in Dcounty *. It follows, therefore, that in the opinion of this court a part of the cause of action asserted by appellant in this suit arose in Dallas county and the judgment of the trial court granting the plea of privilege is erroneous."

§ 818. Breach by the Defendant 

As we have seen, 62 one of the essential elements of a cause of action is a breach of duty by the defendant. It follows that suit may be maintained for breach of an obligation under the contract in the county where the defendant-corporation's breach occurred.63 thereby conferring venue there. The opinion is in harmony with the holding of the Supreme Court in Stone 

Fort Nat. Bank v. Forbess, supra, that the venue of the suit was in Mc- Lennan County because of the express provision of the contract. Such is not the case here; there is nothing in this case showing that the Exchange participated in any transaction in Dallas County, or contracted to perform any obligation in Dallas

County; therefore, venue of the suit does not lie in Dallas County; likewise, venue of suits against the allied associations, brought into the suit solely on plaintiff's claim that they are necessary parties to the primary action against the Exchange (under Art. 1995, subds. 5 and 29a), does not lie in Dallas County."

By the terms of the contract, a corporation promised to purchase the city's bonds in J county, and it was further stipulated that for failure to do so the liquidated damages would be $1,000. 

As evidence of the corporation's good faith it attached to the contract its check for $1,000 payable in D county. The corporation failed to purchase the bonds and stopped payment of the check. 

The city brought suit in J county to recover the sum of $1,000 as liquidated damages. The corporation filed its plea of privilege to be sued in D county, asserting that it had the option of buying the bonds or paying liquidated damages, and that as the check was payable in D county, suit should be brought in that county. The court held that since the suit was not brought upon the check itself but for damages for breach of a contract which the corporation had promised to perform venue was proper in J county.66 If the suit had been brought on the check itself, venue would have been in D county." 67

1003, for a discussion of where a corporation may be sued for failure to 68. 297

§ Ch. 18 

mits a corporation to be sued in any county in which the cause of action, or any part thereof, arose. It is admitted that Stone 

Fort National Bank is a corporation whose domicile is in Nacogdoches County, Texas. The venue of this suit must therefore be changed to Nacogdoches County, unless it can be said that appellee alleged and proved a cause of action, or some part thereof, which arose in Randall County. "It is elementary that the making and acceptance of an ordinary or general deposit of money or its equivalent in a bank creates, as between the bank and the depositor, the simple relation of debtor and creditor. The title to the money passes to the bank, and the bank impliedly contracts with the depositor that it will repay such money on the written check or order of the depositor,—not at any place, but only at the bank. "In the case at bar the record shows that the entire transaction by which appellee became an ordinary or general depositor in appellant occurred or arose in Nacogdoches County. After the deposit was made, appellee gave checks to a bank in Randall County. Appellant took no part in that transaction. The Randall County bank, which was selected by appellee and which had no authority to act for appellant, presented such checks to appellant for payment. These presentations were made in Nacogdoches County, and payment was there refused by appellant. It is thus evident that all transactions with which appellant had any connection occurred or arose exclusively in Nacogdoches County, and not, in whole or in part, in Randall County, where this suit was filed. "The provision of exception 23 of Art. 1995, supra, which permits 'a private corporation, association or joint stock company' to be sued 'in any county in which the cause of action, or any part thereof arose,' means that either some part of the transaction creating the primary right, or some part of the transaction relating to the breach of that right, must have occurred in the county where the suit is brought." 69 

69. In support of his statement, Justice Critz cited the following cases:

Graves v. McCollum & Lewis, Tex.Civ. 

App., 193 S.W. 217. 

Guinn v. Texas Drug Co., Tex.Civ. 

App., 219 S.W. 507. 

Pittman & Harrison Co. v. Shook, Tex.Civ.App., 228 S.W. 993. 298

Ch. 8 818 

Where the suit is not brought to recover the purchase price of specific goods sold and delivered, or tendered for delivery, but the damages sought are for the failure of the defendant to perform a condition precedent-such as select the bales of cotton from samples tendered it-the breach occurred in the county where the defendant failed to perform this condition precedent, and suit could be maintained there but not in the county where plaintiff would have performed, since this breach by the defendant rendered final delivery or tender by the plaintiff unnecessary,70 Quite a number of cases have arisen involving sales contracts wherein the defendant corporation has delivered goods to a carrier pursuant to the terms of the contract. In the absence of a contrary stipulation in the contract, it is generally held that delivery to the carrier is delivery to the buyer, and the breach by the corporation, if any, occurred at the point where the carrier received the goods." This rule is not changed by a stipulation in the contract that the seller reserves title to the goods until the purchase price is paid, since this provision only gives the seller a lien for the purchase price and delivery of possession to the carrier passes title to the buyer. Where the contract of sale is otherwise absolute, a stipulation in the contract to the effect that retention by the buyer for five days after arriving at destination shall constitute an acceptance, does not change the above rule, since in the absence of such a provision the buyer would have the right of inspection upon arrival at the destination and if the property did not comply with the contract the buyer has the right to refuse to take the goods. The evidence of breach bears upon the issue of whether he performed the obligation, not where he contracted to perform it. Where the plaintiff corporation claimed jurisdiction over the defendant in the county where the suit was instituted on the ground that the obligation sued on was payable in that county rather than on the fact that the plaintiff was a corporation, one Court of Civil Appeals made this difference in those two situations as to the proof the plaintiff must make on the defendant's plea of privilege. "While it is true that where venue is sought to be fixed in the county of suit upon the ground that defendant is a corporation, the effect of the filing of a plea of privilege is to require plaintiff to prove the corporate existence of defendant. 

But a plaintiff, filing a suit as a corporation, is not required to prove its corporate existence, where it sues and seeks to maintain venue upon the ground that the note sued upon is payable in the county where the suit is filed. A plaintiff suing as a corporation need not prove on plea of privilege that it has changed its name by charter amendment, especially where the fact of incorporation is not the ground upon which it seeks to fix venue, since article 2007 only requires that a plaintiff desiring to fix venue need only 'file a controverting plea under oath, setting out specifically the fact or facts relied upon to confer venue of such cause on the court where the cause is pending.' "Manifestly, it is not material, and the venue statutes do not require a corporation bringing a suit on a note in the county where the note is payable, to prove the allegation that it has changed its name by charter amendment, because that is not a 'fact or facts relied upon to confer venue where the "" 90 cause is pending.'

§ 820. County Where Damage Suffered 

There have been a few decisions upholding venue in a given county upon the ground that the injury to the plaintiff occurred in that county.

The general rule is well established that where the goods sold have been and are loaded by the seller, f. o. b. the shipping point, the breach for inferior quality occurred at the point of shipment. However, where the seller is a corporation, may the buyer maintain suit in the county where the damages were suffered on the ground that part of the cause of action arose in that county? In Pittman & Harrison Co. v. Boatenhamer 10 the plaintiff ordered broom corn seed. The seed shipped proved to be a mixture of sorghum and broom corn seed which rendered the crop valueless. In allowing the buyer to maintain suit in the county where the seed were planted the court said: "True, when appellant [corporation] placed the seed in the post office at S, it accepted the order and consummated the contract, and it may be said that it at the same time breached its contract by sending seed not ordered. But this was not all of the cause of action. The contract, the breach, and the damages as well constituted the cause of action. "In this case, when the seed were ordered, appellant must have known that the order was of that kind which would pro-

By statute, suits against an insurance company may be brought in the county where the loss was suffered.16 Remote purchasers of certain commodities, such as food or drugs, have been permitted to maintain suit against the manufacturer in the county where the purchaser was injured, on the ground that part of the cause of action arose in that county.17 On the other hand, it was held by one Court of Civil Appeals that when the retailer, purchasing direct from the manufacturer, was injured when he imbibed formaldehyde from a bottle labeled "Aromatic Elixir", suit could not be maintained in the county of plaintiff's residence.18 

The court in that case said that no part of the cause of action arose in the county of suit, since the contract was breached where the manufacturer shipped the medicine improperly labelled.19 If the latter view is to be followed, the remote purchaser is in a more advantageous position as regards place of suit, than the person purchasing direct from the manufacturer. Whenever a promise based on consideration is broken the plaintiff can recover nominal damages even if he has benefited by the broken contract. 

Therefore, the court should not lose sight of this rule in determining what court has jurisdiction in cases of breach of contract under the above statute.20

In the Hutson case the court said: "The statute, Sec. 23 of

Art. 1995, R.C.S. [Vernon's Ann.Civ.St.], provides that a suit against a private corporation may be brought in any county in which such corporation has an agency or representative. The only rational interpretation that can be placed upon the language is that the suit may be brought in any county in which the corporation has an agency or representative at the time the suit is filed. When the agency is discontinued or the representative dispensed with before the suit is filed, the venue upon that ground is destroyed." In the above case the corporation was dissolved after the cause of action arose but before the suit was instituted. 

The trial court overruled the plea of privilege because Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1389 provides that the existence of the corporation is continued for three years after its dissolution for the purpose of winding up its affairs.26 But where it is doubtful if the corporation has an agency in the county where the suit is instituted when the case is filed, the court has jurisdiction if the plaintiff amends his petition before trial and proves that an agency exists in the county of suit even though the corporation has its principal place of business in another county.27 When the corporation had its domicile in Dallas county, it could be sued in Shelby county where it by letter stated it had a superintendent in charge of its construction work in the latter county.28 And the "agency" means an agency for the prosecution of the charter purposes of the corporation.29 For this reason the corporation does not establish an "agency" for jurisdictional purposes within the above statute by the appointment of an attorney in the county where the suit is instituted.30 The statute 31

regulating service of citation on corporations uses the word "local agent" and this term is held to mean one who serves his principal in a certain fixed locality.32 The office of these two statutes is separate and distinct. The first serves to fix the venue of suit, while the latter designates those persons who are authorized to receive notice of the pending suit on behalf of the corporation.

The courts have not always kept this distinction in mind. For example, in Houston Packing Co. v. Cuero Cotton Oil & Mfg. 

Co.33 in its original opinion the court stated that the local agent of the corporation had been served with citation and the court proceeded to set out facts going to show a permanent agency in the county where the suit was filed. The court then said that the venue could not be upheld even though the corporation had an agency or representative in the county.

1 ported by his own affidavit and the affidavit of at least three credible persons, residents of the county in which the suit is pending, for any following cause: "1. That there exists in the county where the suit is pending so great a prejudice against him that he cannot obtain a fair and impartial trial. "2. That there is a combination against him instigated by influential persons, by reason of which he cannot expect a fair and impartial trial. "3. For other sufficient cause to be determined by the court." 

In Ferguson Seed Farms v. McMillan 45 the court held that a corporation was entitled to a change of venue where prejudice existed against the president of the corporation. The court said: "It is true that the president of the corporation and the corporation are two distinct entities in law; but, in its transactions, a corporation must always act through and by its officers and agents. In matters involving local prejudice, such prejudice against the president or a part owner of the corporation would, in many instances, be just as potent to defeat a fair trial as prejudice against the corporation itself. The purpose of the act is to guarantee to every litigant a fair and impartial trial, be such litigant a corporate or natural person, and, if local prejudice exists in any county against the officers of a corporation to such an extent that the corporation cannot get a fair trial, the venue should be changed where application therefor properly supported and proved is seasonably filed." It is not clear from a reading of this case, whether the result was achieved by disregarding the corporate fiction and thereby holding that prejudice against the president amounts to prejudice against the corporation. It would seem that the result could be upheld upon the third ground mentioned in the statute, i. e., "for other sufficient cause." A change of venue is authorized when another "sufficient cause" is proven.46

 § 823. Service of Citation in General 

Article 2029 47 provides that, "In suits against any incorporated company or joint stock association, the citation may be served on the President, Vice-President, Secretary, Cashier, Assistant

Cashier, or Treasurer of such company or association, or upon the local agent of such company or association in the county where the suit is brought, or by leaving a copy of the same at the principal office of the company during office hours. If neither the 

President, Vice-President, Secretary, Assistant Secretary, Cashier, Assistant Cashier, or Treasurer reside in the county in which suit is brought, and such company or association has no agent in the county, then the citation may be served upon any agent representing such company, corporation, or association in the State."

Article 2031 48 provides: "In any suit against a foreign corporation, joint stock company or association, or acting corporation or association, pending or hereafter filed in this State, to which any foreign corporation is a party or is to be made a party, process may be served on the President, Vice-President, Secretary, Treasurer, General Manager, or upon any local travelling agent or travelling salesman of such corporation, joint stock company or association, or acting corporation or association in this State."

It should be noticed that article 2029 provides how domestic corporations are served and that article 2031 applies to foreign corporations, and that under article 2029 when the domestic corporation is cited by serving a "local agent" the citation must be served "upon the local agent of such company or association in the county where the suit is brought," but when a foreign corporation is served, the citation may be served upon "a local agent." In other words, it is not necessary in citing a foreign corporation to serve a "local agent" in the county where the
