A corporation is a legal personality although it is in reality a collection of human beings. Therefore, in suing a corporation it is not necessary to make any of the officers or agents of the company parties to the suit. For this reason it is not necessary to name the officers in the petition or citation.55 But the citation must be served on an agent specified in the statute or left at "the principal office of the company" as provided in the above statute. 

The president of the corporation may be served as the corporation's agent although it is agreed that the other officers will do all the work necessary to carry on the business of the company.56

The old statute did not provide for service on "the manager" of the corporation. Therefore, service on the manager before the statute was amended in 1933 was insufficient,57 as the court will not assume that "the manager" is "president, secretary" or some other officer named in the statute. Even under the statute as amended in 1933 "the manager" is not named as one of the

If the corporation has ceased to do business and has abandoned its former principal office service cannot be had by leaving a copy of the writ at the abandoned office.63 In the Bozeman case the court said: "Alternate provisions of the statute authorizing service of citation in a civil suit, on an incorporated company or joint stock association, by leaving a copy of the writ at the principal office of such company during office hours, contemplate that the company or association, its officers or agents, would, in the ordinary course of events, find the writ, or would legally be charged with failure to do so. So, when a citation has been served on defendant, by leaving a copy of the writ at a time or place authorized by statute, but the plaintiff knew the defendant would not thereby be advised thereof, or, when the writ was left at a place not within the legal contemplation of the law, and not known to defendant until the final disposition of the case, the purpose of the law is obviously defeated. Where the company has no principal office, has ceased to do business, and has abandoned the place where its principal affairs and business had theretofore been transacted, and its officers and agents perform no service for the company at the place where the writ was left, no legal presumption can arise that the defendant had notice of the suit. The Arlington Heights Sanitarium, while still a corporate entity, had ceased to exercise its corporate purposes, had closed its sanitarium and offices therein for the transaction of its affairs, and its officers and agents were no longer employed or engaged in the discharge of any duty for the corporation, at the time and place where the service was attempted.

Even if a corporation is considered, as was stated in many old cases, as a nebulous being that cannot be seen or felt, the corporation, in the very nature of things, can not be served personally. Therefore, if the return of the citation shows service only "on the corporation," the citation is insufficient.91 

However, where a corporation is sued and the sheriff's return stated that citation was delivered to "each of the within named defendants" but named only one individual defendant, a judgment by default can be set aside on a direct attack.92 

Article 202693 provides that the citation shall be served by the officer delivering to each defendant a true copy of the citation. It follows that where one person is the local agent for two corporate defendants, a copy for each of the defendants should be left with such agent. "It is reasonable to presume that the law contemplated that the agent should transmit the copy served upon him to his superiors, and therefore a writ for each would be necessary for the purpose. In this case the sheriff's return upon each citation showed that he had delivered a copy of "this writ." Under such returns the court presumed that the agent was served as the agent of each corporation.

Gage, 63 Tex. 572, it is said: "The petition averred that the appellant had an agent in the county of Uvalde, but it did not state who the local agent was; and the citation directed the sheriff to summon the Galveston, Harrisburg & San Antonio Railway

Company to appear at the time fixed by law for the term of the district court for Uvalde county. The citation, however, gave no specific direction upon whom or in what manner it was to be served. There is no doubt that the better practice requires that the fact that there is a local agent of the corporation in the county in which the suit is brought should be stated in the petition, and that the name of such agent should be given; and, further, that the citation should direct the sheriff or other officer to execute it by serving a copy of the citation on the named local agent. Sun Mutual Insurance Co. v. 

Geo. Seeligson & Co., 59 Tex. 3, 6;

Galveston & R. R. Railway Co. v. 

Shepherd, 21 Tex. 274, 277.'”

If the citation is to be served upon a defendant within the county where the suit is pending, it is required to state "the nature of the plaintiff's demand."98 On the other hand, where the service is to be effected without the county in which the suit is pending, a certified copy of the plaintiff's petition must accompany the citation.99 Thus, where the citation is served upon an agent of the defendant corporation within the county of suit, the citation need not be accompanied by a certified copy of the plaintiff's petition, even though the principal office of the corporation is located in another county.¹

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 2044, provides that, "Any mistake or informality in a return may be corrected by the officer at any time under the direction of the court." This statute applies to the return of the officer in citing a corporation as well as in the case of individual defendants. Immaterial errors in the citation, such as using the pronoun "he" for "it", does not invalidate the citation or writ of garnishment. But if the return shows that the citation was served on "an officer" or "an agent", the service is incomplete as the court will not assume that one of the officers named in the statute was served. As the corporation can act by and through its agents only if the return shows that the corporation was served or that its agent was personally served, the service is invalid and a judgment by default should not be granted.10 

And if the citation does not name the agent for service, the service is complete if the return or an amended return shows that a local agent of the corporation was served.11 The return is defective unless it shows that it was made by the sheriff or a duly authorized officer.12

841. When Dissolved

A corporation is dissolved, using the latter word in its proper sense, when it ceases to exist as a legal entity. The insolvency 336

of a corporation, even though coupled with complete cessation of business, with no intent to resume corporate activity, will not operate to bring about a technical dissolution.¹ In dealing with statutes and cases on dissolution, it is of primary importance to distinguish between dissolution and the loss of some right or rights of the corporation. The court in Canadian Country Club v. Johnson recognized such a distinction by saying: "The corporation was not dissolved; hence the property was not held in common by the stockholders, but was then in the corporation whose entity was not destroyed, but whose rights to sue and act were forfeited." 

$842. Methods of Dissolution 

The various methods by which a corporation may be dissolved in Texas are: by expiration of the time limited in the charter; by judicial decree; by voluntary surrender of the corporate franchise; by forfeiture without judicial ascertainment under some specific provision of law; by failure to organize within three years after filing the charter; and by a judicial ascertainment of insolvency.3

When the period limited in the charter has expired, the corporation is ipso facto dissolved without judicial action or without any other affirmative relief. According to a Texas Statute,⁹ a corporation under proper circumstances can be dissolved by a judgment of dissolution pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction, but the statute does not state which courts are courts of competent jurisdiction for this purpose. Therefore there is no question involved in the particular statute as to whether or not proceedings for dissolution may be brought in equity.10

But as we have just seen the Legislature by a specific provision of article 1538j exempted corporations from making such proof as to their non-par stock although only ten percent must be subscribed when the charter is approved by the Secretary of State according to article 1538d. 

However, assuming that non-par corporations should be exempted from article 1338, why did the Legislature not exempt them from article 1339? That article provides that, "In cases of the failure to pay the unpaid portion of capital stock, and to make proof thereof to the Secretary of State within two years from the date of the filing of the charter, the charter of such company shall become forfeited." If this article has no application to the non-par stock of a corporation, the company can continue to do business without ever having more than ten percent of such stock sold or paid for, since the non-par statute does not provide when the balance of the stock which was not subscribed for when the charter was approved by the Secretary of State must be "subscribed and paid for." amount so paid shall be less than $25,000.00." Did the Legislature intend such a result? The Texas Courts have not as yet decided this question. In other words, did the Legislature intend to permit a corporation with non-par stock to continue with only ten percent of the non-par stock subscribed and paid for, and such corporation not be subject to forfeiture of its charter under the provisions of Article 1339?

Another statutory provision that must be noticed in this connection is the one relating to the franchise tax. Article 7091 21 provides that "if the amount of such tax and penalty be not paid in full * * * such corporation shall for such default forfeit its right to do business in this State; which forfeiture shall be consummated without judicial ascertainment by the Secretary of the State entering upon the margin of the record kept in his office relating to such corporation, the words 'right to do business forfeited,' and the date of such forfeiture." The question arises whether, after all the steps required by this statute are complied with, the corporation is dissolved; that is, whether the corporation thereby loses its corporate entity. It will be noticed that the statute provides that "the right to do business shall be forfeited," and not that the corporate existence shall be forfeited. 

Of course, if the corporate charter is forfeited, the corporation loses all of its authority to act.22 Article 7095 23 makes it the duty of the Attorney General to bring suit to forfeit the corporation's charter after its right to do business has been forfeited by the Secretary of State for failure to pay the franchise tax.24 If the corporation whose right to do business had been

This appellant paid into the state treasury more than ten thousand dollars for the evident purpose of enabling it to prosecute this suit. In all probability no part of this delinquent tax would have been paid had the corporation known that its right to do business and privilege of suing in the courts could not be lawfully restored by such payment." 31 If the corporation was in good standing when the obligation arose it cannot sue to enforce its rights after its right to do business has been forfeited by the Secretary of State for the non-payment of the franchise tax unless it pays the tax and is re-instated.32

Suppose the corporation transacts business after the Attorney General has instituted a suit to forfeit the charter of the company for nonpayment of the franchise taxes. The status of transactions entered into by the corporation after the suit is instituted has not been determined by any Texas court. It would seem to the writer that if such a suit was subsequently dismissed by the Attorney General for any cause, the above rules would apply to transactions entered into by the corporation after the suit was instituted. The writer hesitates to hazard a guess as to what the law is where the corporation transacts business after the suit is instituted by the Attorney General and a negotiable instrument evidencing this transaction is sold to an innocent purchaser before the charter of the company is forfeited. If the obligation is not evidenced by a negotiable instrument, it seems clear that as the corporation can never pay the back franchise taxes after its charter has been forfeited, no recovery could be had on such obligations either by the obligee or his assignee. 

According to the opinion of one Court of Civil Appeals a corporation cannot sell its property while the tax is delinquent,36 but 

36. Davis V. Texas Co., Tex.Civ.

S.W. 304. 348

another Court of Civil Appeals held it could sell its assets even though its right to do business had been forfeited for failing to pay the franchise tax.37

Several of these questions have been settled by a recent decision by the Supreme Court. In the case of Ross Amigos Oil 

Co. v. State 38 the court held that the Secretary of State could not forfeit the charter of the corporation, and that all contracts made by the corporation before the State forfeited its charter by a suit for that purpose are valid; that the penalty, imposed on the corporation, is that it cannot sue on any obligation while the tax was delinquent, after its right had been forfeited; and that the purpose of the statute was for revenue only. For this reason, the state can collect the franchise tax, whether the corporation is active or not, up to the time judgment of forfeiture of its charter is entered. In this case Justice Sharp said: "When all the articles of this statute are considered together, and full effect given to the object sought to be attained therein, the conclusion is inescapable that this statute was enacted solely for the purpose of raising revenue. "The Oil Company could have made valid contracts, because the law does not expressly declare that contracts made by a corporation whose right to do business has been forfeited are void. 

Nor does the law declare that the business transacted during the time of such forfeiture is void. It is undisputed that the Oil 

Company continued to do business in Texas as a chartered corporation. The only right or privilege taken away from such corporation by the forfeiture of its right to do business by the Secretary of State was its right to sue and defend in the courts of the State. "The failure of a corporation to pay a franchise tax does not authorize the Secretary of State to declare a forfeiture of its charter. All that the law authorized him to do is to forfeit the

"The law undoubtedly levies a franchise tax against corporations such as this, regardless of whether or not they do busiand this liability (to pay the tax) continues so long as such corporation remains undissolved, or until its charter is forfeited by legal proceedings as required by law." Under this decision the holding of the court of civil appeals, cited above, which held that the corporation could not dispose of its assets while the tax is delinquent, is clearly erroneous. But when the corporation is sued after its permit to do business has been forfeited for failure to pay the franchise tax, the burden is still on the plaintiff to make out a cause of action, and the corporation will be permitted to interpose any negative defense. On this question in the case of Bryan v. Cleveland Sand & Gravel 

Company 39 Justice Combs said: "We overrule appellant's contention that the defendant company was denied the right to make any defense to his suit by reason of the fact that its right to do business had been forfeited for failure to pay the franchise tax. Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 7091 denies to a corporation, whose right to do business has been forfeited by the Secretary of State for failure to pay franchise tax, the right to any affirmative relief in the courts of Texas, either as a party plaintiff or by way of a cross-action in a suit wherein it has been made a defendant. We do not understand our courts to hold that such a corporation cannot interpose a defense purely negative in character against a suit brought against it, grounded upon matters which arose during the time it was lawfully engaged in business. That is to say, the plaintiff in such case is still under the duty of establishing his cause of action, and the corporate defendant may, as in the instant case, offer proof which negatives the plaintiff's case. Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 7091 provides: "Each director and officer of any corporation whose right to do business within this State shall be so forfeited shall, as to any and all debts of such corporation which may be created or incurred, with his knowledge, approval and consent, within this State, after such forfeiture by any such directors or officers, and before the revival of the right of such corporation to do business, be deemed and held liable thereon in the same manner and to the same extent as if such directors and officers of such corporation were partners." In order to make the directors liable under this statute the burden is on the plaintiff to show that the individual defendants were directors when the obligation was incurred. One case seemed to hold that the directors named in the charter would be presumed to hold such position for a calendar year from the time the charter was approved. But the next fiscal year of the corporation, according to its by-laws, may start a short time after the charter was granted. It would therefore seem that the presumption suggested by the court should not be indulged.40

§ 843. Death or Loss of Members 

The statement has been made that a non-stock corporation is dissolved by a withdrawal of all of its members, or by the withdrawal of such a number of the members that too few remain to fill vacancies and continue succession.50 In the early stages of private corporation law, it was held that death of all of the members of a corporation dissolved it; of course, this rule does not apply to the modern business corporations for the reason stated by the court in Boston Glass Manufactory v. Langdon: 51 

"The shares, being property, pass by assignment, bequest, or descent, and must ever remain the property of some persons, who, of necessity, must be members of the corporation as long as it may exist." 

In Accidental Oil Mills Co. v. Tomlinson,52 one Briant owned all but two of the shares of stock of a corporation. Shortly after his death, an employee sued the corporation on an employment contract. The contention was made that the suit should have been against Briant's executor rather than against the corporation. The court in ruling against this contention said: "Unquestionably, the corporation did not cease to exist upon the death of its principal stockholder and president. It continued as a legal entity." 53 The court also held in the last cited case that the executor of the stockholder who owned most of the stock of the corporation could not pay the debts of the corporation out of the other assets of the estate.

The early Texas cases followed a very strict rule in not allowing the appointment of a receiver even in the case of fraud and mismanagement. In the case of People's Investment Co. v. Crawford the court said:67 "Courts of equity, by virtue of their general equitable jurisdiction, will not appoint a receiver of a corporation, and assume control and management of its affairs, at the suit of a stockholder alleging fraud, mismanagement, and collusion on the part of the corporate authorities, or ultra vires acts of the directors or of the corporation itself, but in such cases will limit the redress granted to the specific wrongs charged, and will go no further than to enjoin or forbid the misconduct complained of."

They can only resort to equity when they have shown that they have exhausted other means of redress. This strict rule has been modified by the later cases. In the Berkshire Pet. Co. v. 

Moore case,68 Judge Fly stated: "In the older cases it was held that the general equitable powers of courts of equity would not justify the appointment of a receiver to assume the management of the affairs of a corporation at the suit of a stockholder alleging fraud or mismanagement. 

However, the trend of modern authority favors the inherent power of the court in a proper case to place the affairs of a corporation, at the suit of stockholders, in the hands of a receiver, when the officials are guilty of fraud or neglect."

The strict rule laid down in The People's Investment Co. case has also been criticized by the court in the Prairie Lea Production Co. v. Tiller case.69 There the court said: 

"This pronouncement of the rule in Texas seems to have been followed and approved in the cases cited. 

But such a rule of equity cannot, of necessity, be arbitrarily observed or enforced, regardless of the facts of the particular case. "Though the appointment of a receiver for a corporation is an extraordinary power and one that must be exercised with the 

67. People's Inv. Co. v. Crawford, Tex.Civ.App., 45 S.W. 738. 

Petroleum Co. 

68. Berkshire 16 

Moore, Tex.Civ.App., 268 S.W. 484. 

69. Tex.Civ.App., 286 S.W. 638. 357

§ 

utmost care, the tendency of the courts is to permit such appointment when the properties of the corporation are in danger of being lost or dissipated and cannot be preserved to the corporation and the minority stockholders in any other way." 

Where a corporation has forfeited its right to sue or be sued by failure to pay the franchise tax, the stockholders may bring a suit in equity to prevent a failure of justice, but not as trustees under the statute.70 When equity has thus rightfully gained jurisdiction, it may go ahead and wind up the affairs of the corporation." In the Canadian Country Club-Johnson case, the court, in applying these principles, on page 843, said: "The corporation was not dissolved; hence the property was not held in common by the stockholders, but was then in the corporation, whose entity was not destroyed, but whose rights to sue and act were forfeited. Being in that condition, clearly, the statutes recognize the right of any stockholder for the corporation to sue for the property and to place the property in court, for the reason under the law there was no managing officer or corporate body with right to do so as such. In that sense, the corporation is a party. The court, having taken charge, instead of the directors, can pay the debts and distribute the assets to those entitled thereto. The court having rightfully acquired jurisdiction to protect the property at the suit of a stockholder, and having found it to be insolvent, and in such condition as that it cannot perform its charter purposes, we see no reason why a court of equity, having thus rightfully acquired jurisdiction, may not wind up its affairs and adjust the rights of the various stockholders." 

The fact that the corporation cannot sue because it has not paid the franchise tax can be urged only in a plea in abatement.72

Abuse and Non-Use of Charter Powers 

The failure to exercise the powers conferred upon it by its charter, or an abandonment of its corporate enterprise, does not dissolve the corporation, but merely furnishes grounds for dissolution.73

The court in the case of State v. Dilbeck said:74 "Mere non-user of the corporate franchise (except failure to organize in six years) 75 does not, under any of these methods, ipso facto work a dissolution there must for mere non-user be a judicial decree forfeiting the charter rights. 

* * 66# a total non-use of those functions and abandonment of all vestige of corporate existence for a period sufficient to raise the presumption of voluntary surrender of the corporate rights to the state will work a forfeiture of those rights and support dissolution."

However, the failure on the part of the corporation actively to engage in business within the statutory three year period after the filing of its charter with the Secretary of State does not ipso facto dissolve the corporation. Ann.Civ.St.], and it is further true that, before its amended pleading was filed, showing compliance with that act, more than four years had elapsed since the maturity of the last note sued upon, but it appears that appellee had paid its franchise tax on June 24, 1911, within less than 12 months from the filing of the original suit and within less than four years from the date of the maturity of the first note. The amended petition did not allege the fact that appellee had obtained permission to do business in Texas, and revived its right to sue by complying with the law, until more than four years after the cause of action had accrued. It has been frequently held in this state that a suit will prevent the running of the statute of limitation, although the petition be bad on general demurrer, and is not amended until after the period of limitation has elapsed."

§ 846. Statutes Governing Insolvency of the Corporation 

The Texas courts in construing the Texas statutes89 concerning insolvent corporations have held that a corporation is not insolvent, within the meaning of the statutes, because of the fact that the corporate liabilities exceed the corporate assets.⁹⁰ 

Chief Justice Stayton in his opinion in the Lyons-Thomas Hardware Company case,91 in discussing the insolvency of a corporation, quoted with approval the following language: "It is not enough that its assets are insufficient to meet all its liabilities, if it be still prosecuting its line of business, with the prospect and expectation of continuing to do so,-in other words, if it be, in good faith, what is sometimes called a "going" business or establishment. Many successful corporate enterprises, it is believed, have passed through crises where their property and effects, if brought to present sale, would not have discharged all their liabilities in full. We feel safe in declaring that when a corporation's assets are insufficient for the payment of its debts, and it has ceased to do business, or has taken, or is in the act of taking, a step which will practically incapacitate it for conducting the cor-

In determining whether the corporation is insolvent a reasonable valuation will be put on its assets rather than the rule of the federal income tax regulations which require the taxpayer to inventory his assets at their cash value or market value, whichever is lower. Even though the corporation's liabilities exceed its assets if it is a going concern with reasonable prospects of success the company is not insolvent within the meaning of the statutes discussed in this section.92 Article 2293, subds. 3 and 4 provide: "Receivers may be appointed by any judge of a court of competent jurisdiction of this State.

Many successful corporate enterprises, it is believed, have passed through crises where their property and effects, if brought to present sale, would not have discharged all their liabilities in full. We feel safe in declaring that when a corporation's assets are insufficient for the payment of its debts, and it has ceased to do business, or has taken, or is in the act of taking, a step which will practically incapacitate it for conducting the corporate enterprise with reasonable prospect of success, or its embarrassments are such that early suspension and failure must ensue, then such corporation must be pronounced insolvent"."

While it is the duty of the Attorney General to bring suit to forfeit the charter of corporations organized under the Texas law when grounds for such forfeiture exist, the Attorney General must exercise his discretion in determining whether such grounds exist and whether the evidence is sufficient to convict the corporation, and mandamus will not lie to compel him to institute such suit.1 18 § 848. Reasons for which Judicial Forfeiture may be Granted as 

Result of Statute Frequently a statute will provide that for a violation of its provision, or for some other cause, the corporation's charter may be forfeited. Thus, article 138019 provides: "The Attorney General, when convinced that any corporation is insolvent, shall institute quo warranto or other appropriate proceedings to forfeit its charter or cancel its permit."20 

If the statute provides in mandatory terms for a forfeiture under certain circumstances, neither the court nor the attorney general may inquire whether the circumstances in fact justify a forfeiture or not. "For whenever the state declares, by its legislature, that a particular act of malfeasance, or non-feasance, done by a corporation, or its officers, shall be a forfeiture of its charter, the discretion is then exercised, and the will of the state, that the forfeiture shall be claimed, is then expressed."21 A statute, however, may, by its very terms, put the question of whether certain misconduct shall result in forfeiture within the discretion of the attorney general or the court. Thus, article 743022 reads: "The charter of any corporation chartered under the laws of this State, adjudged guilty of violating any provision of this sub-

Another ground on which judicial forfeiture may be based is nonuser, because, 66* * every legislative grant creating corporate existence is subject to the condition that the privileges and franchises conferred be used in the manner designated in the grant and in compliance with law, and that a failure therein for an unreasonable length of time, whether through neglect, design, or misfortune, is a breach of the implied agreement under which the right was granted, and authorizes the state to repossess itself of that right."28

§ 850. Effect of Subsequent Good Behavior

While there is no yardstick for measuring the degree of abuse of its powers by a corporation sufficient to justify a court in decreeing a forfeiture, the question of whether the abuse is willful or not is a material factor. "Willful abuse or improper neglect may work a forfeiture of the charter, when excess of power or mistake in the mode of exercising an acknowledged power would not have that effect." 32 § 851. Waiver of Forfeiture

It was stated in an early Texas case that, although a ground for forfeiture might exist, the state can waive its right to forfeit the charter. "Whether such proceeding (to forfeit the charter) shall be taken or not depends upon the will of the state, for it has the election to enforce the forfeiture or to waive it." 33 The rule is generally stated that the legislature is the proper body to waive a forfeiture, and this rule seems to find support in the following passage from State v. Morris: 34 "Whether a franchise shall be forfeited depends on the will of the same body that has power to confer it in the first instance; and if by that the harsher remedy is waived, and a milder one adopted, it is not for the courts to declare whether the legislature acted wisely or unwisely, but it is their duty to give effect to what seems to them the will of the legislature." 35 

The fact that provision is made for a recovery of a penalty by those injured by the misuse or nonuse of a franchise does not operate as a waiver by the state to have a forfeiture declared.36

The state can claim no exemption from the ordinary rules which govern contracts, and there is not to be one law for them and another for private persons."

That court held the trustees, under the Oklahoma statute, liable for all debts created by them in winding up the affairs of the dissolved corporation. Three of the judges of the Supreme Court of Oklahoma dissented. The Court did not discuss that part of the Oklahoma statute which is identical with the last sentence of the above Texas statute. That part of the statute provides that the trustees should be severally responsible to the creditors of such a corporation to the extent of its property and effects that shall have come into their hands.51

It seems very evident that the Texas Legislature by the above statute intended to give the trustees of a dissolved corporation authority to wind up the affairs of the company, and to limit the liability of such trustees to the extent of the property of the company that came into their hands. Why the Oklahoma court did not discuss the last sentence of the Oklahoma statute, which is identical with the Texas statute, no one can surmise. If the trustees become personally liable for all debts created by them in winding up the affairs of the dissolved corporation, the above statute is a trap for the unwary. As directors of the corporation they realize that they are not responsible for contractual obligations created by them in the conduct of the legitimate business of the corporation. They also realize that they are not liable on tort obligations created by other agents of the corporation unless they participate in the tort. Under the plain terms of the above statute they are exempt from personal liability in winding up the affairs of the corporation except to the extent of the property received by them as such trustees. It, therefore, seems fairly certain that the Supreme Court of Texas should not follow the above case decided by the Supreme Court of Oklahoma.

non's Ann.Civ.St. arts. 1388 and 1389, the directors as trustees of the dissolved corporation had such authority. The court said that under article 1388 the trustees have the right to "sell, convey and transfer all real and personal property belonging to such company" and that under that provision of the statutes, the "trustees" could sell the assets to the new company and compel the stockholders in the old company to take stock in the new corporation, although the new company is chartered for fifty years. Justice Young filed a dissenting opinion which seems stronger than that of the majority of the court. That part of the statute [Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1388] quoted above, is only a part of that article. Both articles 1388 and 1389 provide for the "winding up" of the affairs of the defunct corporation. The existence of the corporation is continued for three years for that purpose. 

Most assuredly such a statute would provide that in winding up the affairs of the dissolved corporation the trustees have authority to sell all the real estate and personal property belonging to the company. The whole purpose of both sections of the statute is "to settle the affairs" of the defunct corporation. In passing those articles the Texas Legislature must have known the lawyer's meaning of the phrase "to settle the affairs" of the corporation. By the specific terms of article 1388, the trustees of the dissolved corporation can sell only for cash and not for stock in a new corporation. That article provides, "Upon the dissolution of a corporation the directors of the corporation shall be trustees of the creditors and stockholders, with power to settle the affairs, collect the outstanding debts, and divide the moneys and property among the stockholders after paying the debts due and owing by such corporation at the time of its dissolution." In other words, the trustees are specifically directed to convert enough assets of the company into cash as is necessary to pay the debts of the company. After defining the duties of the trustees the statute provides, "and for this purpose they may sell" the assets of the company. 

383

§ Ch. 19 

Where the trustees merely renew the charter of the dissolved corporation and merely transfer the assets of the old company to the new corporation, they are not attempting "to settle" up the affairs of the old company, pay the debts and distribute the remaining cash and other property to the stockholders. statute authorizes the trustees "to settle the affairs" of the dissolved corporation and as a means to that end, authorizes the trustees "to sell" its property. Clearly it does not authorize the trustees "to sell" its property for the sole purpose of continuing the business of the old corporation.60 

The power to renew the charter falls within the powers of the stockholders, and not the directors. It would take a very plain unambiguous statute to confer such power on the directors. The above articles make no such attempt. The Supreme Court of the 

United States has held, under 12 U.S.C.A. § 55, which gives the comptroller of the currency authority to levy an assessment upon the shareholders of a national bank whose capital has become impaired, that the directors cannot decide to pay the assessment and continue the bank rather than have a receiver appointed to wind up the affairs of the bank; but that the stockholders must make that decision. As Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. arts. 1388 and 1389 do not give the directors authority to continue the business, no one except the shareholders could decide that question; for that would be a fundamental change, and not an ordinary business transaction that falls within the jurisdiction of the directors.61

It is obvious, we think, that, at the beginning, the officers of the dissolved corporation could have refused to act as trustees, there being nothing of a contractual obligation existing, or any law compelling them to accept. 

As the statute in question makes no provision for the resignation of trustees, or for the filling of vacancies caused by death or otherwise, by analogy, the rules of equity should, in our opinion, control. So in the situation presented, we think appellants had the right to appeal to the court, asking to be discharged and

If those who refuse to act and those who petition the court to permit them to resign are a majority of the trustees, they should ask the court to appoint a receiver to wind up the affairs of the corporation. On this point in the above cited case the court said: "Should the court have appointed a receiver, as contended by appellants, or new trustees to take the place of those resigning, as contended by appellees? The statute, in our opinion, answers the inquiry. The provision is that, upon dissolution, unless a receiver is appointed, the affairs of a dissolved corporation shall be wound up by its then existing officers; no other provision being made, the implication, we think, is inescapable that none other than one of the two methods provided by statute may be adopted. The reason for entrusting to the president and directors of a dissolved corporation the business of winding up its affairs, obviously, was because of their familiarity with and interests in its affairs. This could not be said of any stranger selected to fill a vacancy on the board."

 § 858. Effect of Dissolution upon Title and Right to the Corporate 

Property Under the old common law real estate belonging to the corporation when the company was dissolved reverted to the grantor or donor, and its personal property became vested in the sovereign as bona vacantia. When these rules of law arose, most of the corporations were religious, eleemosynary or municipal corporations. The present day business corporation was unknown at that time. If a person donated real estate to a religious corporation it was not unjust for the courts to hold that the land reverted to the grantor when the corporation ceased to function. 

However, such a rule would be very unjust if applied to business corporations today as the stockholders contributed the funds with which all of the property was purchased. For this reason the old common law rule is now obsolete as to all the property belonging to a business private corporation upon dissolution. 

Therefore, in Texas, upon the dissolution of a private business corporation, the shareholders become the owners in common of the corporation's property subject, however, to the claim of creditors." While the property remains within the control of the

Effect of the Rule that after Dissolution Those in Control 

Hold as Trustees

Although, as above shown, upon dissolution the corporation's property is engrafted with a trust and those in control become trustees, all of the usual incidents of a trust do not follow. Thus, the fact that those in control hold as trustees for the creditors does not stop the running of limitation against the creditors.85 "A trust which has devolved upon them (the directors) by the operation of the Statute is not such a trust as arrests the running of the statute of limitations, such as those trusts which are within the exclusive jurisdiction of equity, arising in cases of partnership, agency, and the like.'" 80 In an ordinary trust it takes the unanimous consent of the trustees to transact business.87 But it is held that under the Texas dissolution statutes a majority of the statutory trustees may transact the business.

§ 861. Effect of Dissolution Upon Obligations of the Corporation 

Upon the dissolution of a corporation, the rights, privileges, or franchises of a property nature survive its dissolution. The dissolution of a corporation results in corporate death, and the effect upon the corporation's obligations is analogous to the effect of the death of an individual upon his obligations. As said in 

Morris and Cummings v. State:91 "The same obligation to perform its contracts rests upon a corporation as upon a natural person." In discussing the common law a Texas court said: "At one period it was considered to be the common law that upon dissolution of a corporation its debts were extinguished. 

Suits pending against it abated. But courts of equity viewed the difficulty as one of procedure only, and gave remedy to creditors in pending suits, as well as generally, against the assets of defunct corporations. § 863. Judicial Construction of These Statutes 

Before 1919 there was no provision similar to that of Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1390. Before 1919 there was a conflict among the decisions as to the effect of the dissolution of a corporation upon the right to sue in the corporation's name. The 

United States Supreme Court interpreted the provisions of what are now articles 1388, 1389, and 1391 as sufficient to allow suit by or against the corporation in its corporate name after dissolution, and this regardless of whether suit was pending at the time the corporation was dissolved.98 Another view expressed by one of the Texas Courts of Civil Appeals was that the action was not abated, provided suit was pending at the time of dissolution,⁹⁹ but intimated that a suit was not authorized if instituted after the corporation defendant was dissolved. Most of the cases before 1919, however, without making a distinction between a dissolution of the corporation before or after the institution of the suit, held that upon dissolution the action to which

In a suit where the last board of directors as trustees under the above statutes sought to intervene after the three years had expired, the court justified its conclusion in these words:⁹ "As we construe our statutes, the Legislature has given to creditors and stockholders of a dissolved corporation the same broad measure of relief which equity would have afforded in the absence of legislation. Article 1388 without any time limitation, authorizes these trustees to defend and maintain suits and generally settle up the affairs of the dissolved corporation. 

This very article authorizes the substitution of these trustees as parties plaintiffs in the further prosecution of the case at bar. "Article 1389 is merely cumulative of Article 1388. It but provides that, as an aid to the trustees in performing their duties as prescribed in Article 1388, the corporation itself, for limited purposes only, may continue for three years, and even longer, under a receivership, if the court thinks it necessary. But, even if such continuance of the corporation itself for limited purposes. is not had at the option of the trustees, they still have the right, and are charged with the duty, of defending and maintaining suits in the protection of the assets of the corporation." 

The objection to this justification is that it would not apply to a situation where an assignment is made to a third party.

In the case of Waggoner v. The court also held that in a suit against a dissolved corporation the company is properly served if the citation is served on one of the agents named in article 1391, which article is copied in full above. 

All of our courts should have held even before the 1919 amendment that a suit against the corporation was not abated by its dissolution, as the statute specifically continued the existence of the corporation "with full power in the name of the corporation to maintain or defend judicial proceedings." If it was necessary to amend our statute and thereby add article 1390 in order to prevent a suit from abating against a dissolved corporation, it would seem equally necessary now again to amend the statute and provide that a suit by a corporation is not abated by its dissolution. § 864. Effect of Dissolution on Proceedings by or against Share holders "If a corporation, except a railway, charitable or religious corporation, be dissolved leaving debts unpaid, suit may be brought against any person or persons who were stockholders at the time of such dissolution, without joining the corporation in such suit; and if judgment be rendered and execution satisfied, any defendant may sue all who were stockholders at the time of dissolution for the recovery of the portion of such debt for which they were liable." 25

It will be noticed that recovery is limited to the "portion of such debt for which they were liable." This provision should be considered along with article 1395,26 which reads: "No stockholder shall be liable to pay debts of the corporation beyond the amount unpaid on his stock."

These articles apply only when the corporation has been dissolved; yet in the case of Peden Iron & Steel Co. v. Jenkins27 the 

Court of Civil Appeals referred to the stockholder's liability under article 1395, although in that case the company had not been dissolved but was placed in receivership. However, the only real question in that case was whether a ten acre oil lease was worth the par value of $120,000.00 of stock. The lower court held that the lease was worth that amount and the Court of Civil Appeals held that the lower court did not commit error in admitting evidence on that issue. Therefore, as a matter of fact, the above article of the statutes was not involved in the case.

§ 865. Care and Custody of Records upon Dissolution 

Very often after a corporation is dissolved many questions arise, the solution of which requires an examination of the books of the company. Too often, soon after the corporation is dissolved the records of the company become lost, and no one is charged with their custody and preservation. If the corporation is voluntarily dissolved, the directors would have authority to pay some one a reasonable fee from the assets of the corporation to care for the records of the company for a reasonable time, and to explain them to interested parties. For this and other reasons, the directors would have implied authority to pay a reasonable fee for taking care of the records of the company.

§ 891. Scope of Discussion 

The power of any government to impose taxes presents many interesting and intricate problems. It is beyond the scope of this work to undertake to discuss all of these problems. However, it was felt that a brief discussion of the Texas statutes imposing taxes on corporations and shareholders only should be included.

The framers of our constitution authorized the taxation of corporations.¹ The Legislature, pursuant to the Constitutional authorization, has exercised its authority by enacting a scheme of taxation. Several of these enactments have been held to be unconstitutional as applied to a given situation. The legislature 2.

§ 894. Franchise Tax 

The state by legislative enactment collects a sum from domestic and foreign corporations with a permit to transact business in this state annually in the form of a franchise tax. The franchise tax is not a property tax, but a tax enacted by the state for the privilege of doing business.13 The tax is to be paid on or before the first day of May for the succeeding year.14 When a corporation is chartered or granted a permit to do business at any other date, the amount due in advance is the proportionate part of its annual franchise tax that the time from such date to May first bears to the calendar year.15

Corporations authorized under Subdivision 88, Art. 1302, to carry on more than one business are required to pay the franchise tax provided for each purpose.16 It has been held by the Supreme 

Court that a foreign corporation applying for a permit to engage in a combination of the purposes enumerated in subdivision 88 is also required to pay a franchise tax for each purpose.17

Franchise Tax of Local and Foreign Corporations 

The statutes regulating the amount of the franchise tax to be paid by domestic and foreign corporations, appeared in the 1925 codification as articles 7084 and 7085, respectively.18 The Legislature in 1930, amended and combined these two statutes into a single article.19 The Franchise Tax Act of 1930 was held to be constitutional by the state 20 and federal 21 courts. Notwithstanding the fact that the act was constitutional the Legislature in 1931,22 in an attempt to render the tax more equitable, added clauses E and F to the Act of 1930. Article 7084 was again amended in 1941.23 It now provides: "(a) Except as herein provided, every domestic and foreign corporation heretofore or hereafter chartered or authorized to do business in Texas, or doing business in Texas, shall, on or before May 1st of each year, pay in advance to the Secretary of State a franchise tax for the year following, based upon that proportion of the outstanding capital stock, surplus and undivided profits,24 plus the amount of outstanding bonds, notes and de-

In filling out the blank report furnished corporations by the Secretary of State for the determination of the amount of the franchise tax due, it is the duty of the officer of the corporation who fills out the blank to state what part of the gross receipts of the corporation was due to the business of the corporation conducted outside of the State of Texas. If the officer of the corporation fails to do his duty in this matter and pays more tax than is actually due the state, the corporation has no claim on the state for the excess payment; and, therefore, even though the Legislature makes an appropriation in favor of the corporation for the amount of overpayment of the tax, the appropriation is unconstitutional.39 But if the statute imposes an illegal tax on

The purpose of the amendment of 1931 was to relieve some of the burdens imposed by the Act of 1930 on certain types of corporations as revealed in Gulf States Utilities Co. v. State.43 

Under subdivision (f) of the Act of 1931 and under that subdivision of the present law, if a corporation is engaged in Texas only in three businesses, permitted by subdivision 88,44 and two of the businesses are public utilities and one is not, how is it to determine the amount of its franchise taxes? If two-thirds of its gross receipts are received from its public utilities, it will pay a tax on one-third of its taxable capital as computed under Clause A, and a tax on two-thirds of its taxable capital as computed by Clause D. Since its receipts from the public utilities are received from two businesses, by Clause F it will be required to add one-fourth to the amount computed under Clause D.45

Corporations Exempt 

By statute¹⁹ the following corporations are not required to pay the annual franchise tax: "The franchise tax imposed by this chapter shall not apply to any insurance company, surety, guaranty or fidelity company, or any transportation company, or any sleeping, palace car and dining car company which is now required to pay an annual tax measured by their gross receipts, or to corporations having no capital stock and organized for the exclusive purpose of promoting the public interest of any city or town, or to corporations organized for the purpose of religious worship, or for providing places of burial not for private profit, or corporations organized for the purpose of holding agricultural fairs and encouraging agricultural pursuits, or for strictly educated purposes, or for purely public charity."

The statute requiring corporations to pay a franchise tax is a general statute.50 The statute copied above exempts certain types of corporations. In order for a corporation to avail itself of this exemption, it must clearly show that it comes within the exemption.51 Therefore, where it was shown that the terminal company received an income from its business, it is not exempt under the above statute.52

In 1927 the Legislature passed the following act regulating the payment of franchise taxes by closed state banks: "Hereafter no franchise tax shall be assessed against a State Bank after it has closed its doors and has gone into the hands of the Banking Commissioner for liquidation according to law, nor shall any such corporation be liable for any franchise tax while in the hands of the Commissioner for liquidation. The failure of the Commissioner to pay franchise taxes for any bank in his hands for liquidation shall not operate to revoke or forfeit the charter of such corporation. In Ross 

Amigos Oil Co. v. State59 the Supreme Court of Texas said: "A 

construction of the foregoing articles of the statutes resolves itself into one of legislative intent; which is to be determined from the language used and the purpose in view in enacting the law. 

When all the articles of this statute are considered together, and full effect given to the object sought to be attained therein, the conclusion is inescapable that this statute was enacted solely for the purpose of raising revenue. The clear purpose of this law is to levy a franchise tax on each and every corporation that is chartered in the State,—with certain exemptions, which are not involved here. The penalties imposed for failure to pay the franchise tax are heavy, and were evidently provided to hasten payment and to inflict a punishment on such corporations for failure to pay such tax. "The Oil Company could have made valid contracts, because the law does not expressly declare that contracts made by a corporation whose right to do business has been forfeited are void. 

Nor does the law declare that the business transacted during the time of such forfeiture is void. It is undisputed that the Oil Com-

The only right or privilege taken away from such corporation by the forfeiture of its right to do business by the Secretary of State was its right to sue and defend in the courts of this State. "It will be noted that the Attorney General brought no suit against the Oil Company to forfeit its charter, either for failure to pay the franchise tax or upon any other ground. The failure of a corporation to pay a franchise tax does not authorize the Secretary of State to declare a forfeiture of its charter. All that the law authorizes him to do is to forfeit the right of the corporation to do business, and it shall be denied the right to use the courts of this State. The law specifically places the burden on the Attorney General to effectuate a forfeiture of the charter of a corporation, by legal proceedings brought on behalf of the State for that purpose. "It is undisputed that after the forfeiture of the Oil Company's right to do business it exercised all the benefits and privileges conferred on a chartered corporation, except its right to sue and defend in the courts. It carried on its business, retained the proceeds derived therefrom, and up to the time it was finally dissolved it acted as though it had paid its franchise tax. To hold under these facts that a corporation could refuse to pay its franchise tax, and thereby defeat its obligation to pay same, would nullify the dominant purpose of this law and defeat the very purpose for which it was enacted." "Any corporation whose right to do business shall be thus forfeited shall be denied the right to sue or defend in any court of this state, except in a suit to forfeit the charter of such corporation."60 This statute is applied even though the cause of action asserted by the corporation arose prior to the time its permit to do business was forfeited.61 But is not applied where the cause

The Supreme Court has held that the payment at any time before suit is brought by the Attorney General68 to forfeit the corporation's charter, will relieve of such a forfeiture.

Because no prohibition is found in the statute which denies the Corporation the right to revive after the period stated and because the Secretary of State, pursuant to an opinion by the Attorney-General, has so construed the statute, after which the Legislature reenacted the statute in substantially the same form, the court concludes that the Legislature did not intend the period stated to be the time limit within which such revival right must be exercised.

§ 899. Corporation in Process of Liquidation 

Article 709779 provides that: "If a corporation is actually in process of liquidation, such corporation shall only be required to pay a franchise tax calculated upon the difference between the amount of stock actually issued and the amount of liquidating dividends actually paid upon such stock; provided, that the president and secretary of such corporation shall make affidavit as to the total amount of capital stock issued and as to the amount of liquidating dividends actually paid and that such corporation is in an actual bona fide state of liquidation."

State banks in the hands of the Banking Commissioner are exempted from the payment of this tax by statute.&

§ 920. Rights and Remedies in General 

Since theoretically a corporation is a legal person, separate and distinct from its stockholders, it owns the assets of the corporation unconditionally and in the same way as an individual holds title. Therefore, as a general rule, the rights and remedies of the creditors of a corporation are the same, both at law and in equity, 435

§ 

as the rights and remedies of the creditors of a natural person.¹ 

Of course, the rights of the corporation as a creditor are the same as an individual creditor. Therefore, if it sells machinery or materials, it may claim a lien for the purchase price, whether the lien is a conventional or legal lien, under the same circumstances as the individual creditor.2 The creditor of the company may sue the corporation at common law and recover a judgment against it, and may enforce the judgment by execution against the corporate assets the same as an individual creditor may enforce his claims against any defendant debtor. But the franchise to exist as a corporation cannot be sold voluntarily by the directors of the company nor under legal proceedings instituted by corporate creditors unless the statute specifically confers this right and specifies the mode such sale and transfer may be effected, any more than the creditors of an individual could sell the individual's right to life and liberty.*

court in overruling the special exceptions. This presents a very old, and often recurring, question in this state, which, it would seem, ought to have been settled long ago. In the President and 

Directors of Bank of Alabama v. Simonton, 2 Tex. 531, and in 

Holloway v. Memphis, E. P. & P. Ry. Co., 23 Tex. 465, 76 Am.Dec. 

68, the law of this state, as it then existed, was interpreted to the effect, that in a suit by or against a corporation in its corporate name, it was necessary to allege and prove that such party was a corporation. There was no question suggested in those cases that the mere allegation that the party was a corporation would be insufficient. Revised Civil Statutes 1879, Art. 1190, [now Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1999] provided that, 'In pleading the charter or act of incorporation of any corporation, public or private, organized under the laws of this State, it shall not be necessary to set out at length such charter or act of incorporation, but it shall be sufficient to allege that such corporation, if it be of the adverse party, was duly incorporated, and if it be of the party pleading it, or of a third party, the date and manner of incorporation shall be stated.' By Act approved April 17, 1883, Acts 1883, c. 101, p. 

103, the above was amended to read: 'In pleading the charter or act of incorporation of any corporation, public or private, it shall not be necessary to set out at length such charter or act of incorporation, but it shall be sufficient to allege that such corporation was duly incorporated, and such allegation by either party shall be taken as true, unless denied by the affidavit of the adverse party, his agent or attorney.' Obviously, this amendment wrought two changes in the pre-existing law: (1) it abolished the distinction between such a pleading as referable to the adverse party, and as referable to the party pleading; and (2) it obviated the necessity of the proof of the fact of incorporation, unless denied by the affidavit of the adverse party, his agent or attorney. "In Houston Water Works v. Kennedy, 70 Tex. 233, 8 S.W. 36, the plaintiff alleged that the defendant was a corporation, but did not allege how incorporated. The sufficiency of the petition was questioned by special exception as follows: 'Because it (the petition) fails to state by what authority this defendant was incorporated, or that it was incorporated by any authorized power.' 440

The action of the court in overruling the special exception, being presented as error, was disposed of by the Supreme Court with this statement: "This matter is regulated by statute, which does not require, when a corporation is defendant, that the petition should set out the charter, or allege by what authority the defendant was incorporated'-citing General Laws 1883, p. 103, being the amendment above quoted. In the light of the earlier judicial decisions, it seems clear to our minds that the Supreme Court simply recognized no distinction between an allegation that the defendant was a corporation and that it was duly incorporated. 

Upon this view this court in Texas & P. Ry. Co. v. Bufkin, Tex. 

Civ.App., 46 S.W.2d 712, having the question squarely presented, reached the conclusion that a pleading was not subject to special exception which alleged that a party was a corporation, but omitted to allege that it was duly incorporated. Woodson Mill & Elevator Co. v. Graham Mill & Elevator Co., Tex.Civ.App., 57 S.W. 

2d 943, and authorities cited. "It is believed that the correctness of said decisions is dependent upon the question of whether an allegation that a named party is duly incorporated presents for determination any issue not presented by an allegation that such company is a corporation. An allegation that a named party is a corporation is an allegation of a provable fact. An allegation that a party is a corporation, duly incorporated, if anything more, is an allegation of a conclusion of law, or, at least a conclusion of law and fact. "But, as applicable to the question here, if, in addition to the fact that a party is a corporation, there could be no issue of due incorporation, then it would seem certain that an allegation of due incorporation would neither add to, nor detract from, the allegation that a party is a corporation. Granted that a party is a corporation, then there could be no issue as to whether the party was duly incorporated except in a suit by the state brought to establish by judgment that a corporation was not duly incorporated. "It seems, therefore, it would be an unnecessarily strict construction of the law, which would impute to the Legislature the 441

§ 

intention that in lieu of an allegation of a fact the pleader must substitute an allegation of a conclusion of law, or of mixed law and fact, tendering no justiciable issue, as the condition upon which the pleader is to be relieved of the burden of proving the alleged fact in the absence of affidavit, etc. It is our view, as seems to have been held in the very early cases above mentioned that an allegation that a party is a corporation is sufficient and will relieve the pleader of the necessity of proving the allegation except under the conditions prescribed by the statute. If due incorporation be not an issue additional to the issue of the fact of incorporation, then the last-named fact implies due incorporation."15

The above authorities seem to settle the point in Texas to the effect that the above statutes apply where the allegation is that the association or company "is a corporation duly incorporated" or its "equivalent." Where the allegation is that the defendant. is "a state-wide mutual assessment life insurance company operating under article 4859f of the Revised Statutes" the burden is on the party making such allegation to prove the character of the plaintiff company even though the opposite party does not deny the truth of the allegation in a sworn plea.  § 922. Evidence of Incorporation 

The permit of a foreign corporation to do business in Texas is prima facie evidence of its due incorporation.18 

But even though the plaintiff alleges that it is a corporation and the defendant does not deny that allegation, the plaintiff is in no position to invoke the provisions of Vernon's Ann. Civ.St. arts. 1999 and 2010, where he agrees that certain testimony is admissible on the trial of the case and that evidence shows the plaintiff is neither a de facto or de jure corporation.19 

If the issue before the court is whether the company is incorporated, the testimony of a witness that he had examined the files in the office of the Secretary of State and had failed to find any record of a charter of the company, is relevant.20 The court in the Cobb-Bryan case, cited in the last note, also said that a witness could testify that he had never heard of such a corporation in the place where such corporation was alleged to have had its domicile.

Where the defendant corporation in the affidavit attached to its plea of privilege to be sued in a certain county admits that the defendant is a corporation, it is unnecessary for the plaintiff to prove that fact.21 And even though the plaintiff fails to allege that the defendant is a duly incorporated company, no error is committed where the plaintiff proves that the defendant is incorporated.22

§ 923. Rights of Creditors of a Corporation 

Like creditors of a natural person, creditors of a corporation may come into a court of equity and reach and subject equitable assets of the corporation to the satisfaction of their claims.27 

Creditors of a corporation may also attach the property of the corporation under the statutes, where the property of a natural person could be attached. A corporation is a "person" within the meaning of the attachment laws.28 

§ 924. Liability of Shareholders for Debts of the Corporation 

One of the business reasons for organizing a corporation is to escape personal liability on the part of the stockholders for the obligations of the company. In the absence of a statute, the stockholders are not liable for the debts of the company if they have fully paid for their stock.29 If they have not fully paid

 § 927. Assets of a Corporation as a "Trust Fund" for Creditors 

In most of the text-books and in a great number of the cases, it is said broadly and without qualification, that the capital stock and assets of a corporation constitute a "trust fund" for the payment of its creditors, and cannot be squandered or given away when necessary for the satisfaction of the debts of the corporation.56 And it is also said that if this is done the property may be followed in equity by the creditors of the corporation into the hands of any person other than a bona fide purchaser for value in accordance with the equitable rule by which trust funds may be followed.57 Late decisions, however, and a careful consideration of most of the cases in which this dictum is found, will show that in reality both the property of the corporation that was purchased with its "contributed capital stock" and its other assets so long as it is doing business-belong to the corporation itself, both in law and in equity, just as completely as does the property of a natural person belong to him, and these

The doctrine that the capital of a corporation contributed by the subscribers for its capital stock is a trust fund for creditors was first laid down by Mr. Justice Story in Wood v. Dummer.59 

In this case a bank had distributed part of its assets among its stockholders, leaving the debts unpaid, and nothing with which to pay them. It was said that the property so distributed was a trust fund for the payment of the debts of the corporation, and it vas held that the creditors could follow it in equity into the hands of the stockholders. The doctrine was thus stated: "It appears to me very clear upon general principles, as well as the legislative intention, that the capital stock of banks is to be deemed a pledge or trust fund for the payment of the debts contracted by the bank. The public, as well as the Legislature, have always supposed this to be a fund appropriated for such purpose. 

The individual stockholders are not liable for the debts of the bank in their private capacities. The charter relieves them from personal responsibility, and substitutes the capital stock in its stead. Credit is universally given to this fund by the public, as the only means of repayment. Why, otherwise, is any capital stock required by our charters? If the stock may, the next day after it is paid in, be withdrawn by the stockholders without payment of the debts of the corporation, why is its amount so studiously provided for, and its payment by the stockholder so diligently required? To me this point appears so plain upon principles of law, as well as common sense, that I cannot be brought into any doubt, that the charters of our banks make the capital stock a trust fund for the payment of all the debts of the corporation. The billholders and other creditors have the first claims upon it; and the stockholders have no rights, until all the other creditors are satisfied. They have the full benefit of all the profits made by the establishment, and cannot take any portion of the fund until all the other claims on it are extinguished. Their rights are not to the capital stock, but to the residuum after all demands on it are paid. On a dissolution of the corporation, the billholders and the stockholders have each equitable claims, but those of the billholders possess, as I conceive, a prior exclusive equity." This is the decision and the dictum upon which the so-called trust fund doctrine is based. But it requires no argument to show that the facts of the case did not render it necessary to hold that the assets of a corporation are a trust fund for creditors in the strict sense of the term. All that the case decided was that a corporation cannot distribute its assets among its stockholders, and thereby leave creditors unpaid-a transaction which is clearly a fraud upon existing creditors, just as a voluntary conveyance by a natural person is a fraud upon his existing creditors who are thereby prevented from collecting their claims. It is self evident that if a corporation releases subscribers from liability to contribute to the capital of the corporation, or distributes part of its assets to them, the transaction is a fraud upon prior and subsequent creditors who are ignorant of the transaction, and deal with it on the faith of its capital stock 454

being fully paid, and the transaction may be avoided by them on this ground. Many of the courts base the right of creditors to hold stockholders liable in these cases upon the ground that "the capital" contributed by the subscribers for its capital stock is a trust fund for creditors. And it is in these cases chiefly that we find the trust fund doctrine declared.6⁰ No such doctrine, however, is necessary. The stockholders are liable on the ground of fraud. Persons who deal with a corporation and become its creditors after such a transaction, and with knowledge of it, cannot complain, because they are not defrauded.61 If the capital were really a trust fund for creditors, they could complain.

The only consideration for the transfer was the assumption by the grantee of the grantor's debts. Clearly, it was unnecessary to resort to any trust fund theory to sustain this decision. The decision might be based on elementary principles of the law applicable to fraud.

The trust fund doctrine was ably repudiated by the Supreme 

Court of Minnesota in the case of Hospes v. Northwestern Mfg. & Car Co.

In that case it was held that the corporation owns both the legal and equitable title to all of its property, and that it may use and dispose of its assets, if not prohibited by its charter or governing statutes, the same as a natural person; that its property is not held in trust for creditors, except in the sense that there can be no distribution of it among stockholders without provision being first made for the payment of the corporate debts; and that, as in the case of a natural person, any disposition of it in fraud of creditors may be set aside by complaining creditors. "The phrase," said the court, "that "the capital of a corporation constitutes a trust fund for the benefit of creditors,' is misleading. Corporate property is not held in trust, in any proper sense of the term. A trust implies two estates or interests one equitable and one legal; one person, as trustee, holding the legal title, while another, as the cestui que trust, has the beneficial interest. Absolute control and power of disposition are inconsistent with the idea of a trust. The capital of a corporation is its property. It has the whole beneficial interest in it, as well as the legal title. It may use the income and profits of it, and sell and dispose of it, the same as a natural person. It is a trustee for its creditors in the same sense and to the same extent as a natural person, but no further."

In Sanger v. Upton,65 in the Supreme Court of the United 

States, the dictum of Wood v. Dummer66 was repeated. In that

case the court said: "The capital stock of an incorporated company is a fund set apart for the payment of its debts. It is a substitute for the personal liability which subsists in private copartnerships. When debts are incurred, a contract arises with the creditors that it shall not be withdrawn or applied, otherwise than upon their demands, until such demands are satisfied. 

The creditors have a lien upon it in equity. If diverted, they may follow it as far as it can be traced, and subject it to the payment of their claims, except as against holders who have taken it bona fide for a valuable consideration and without notice. 

It is publicly pledged to those who deal with the corporation, for their security. Unpaid stock is as much a part of this pledge, and as much a part of the assets of the company, as the cash which has been paid in upon it. Creditors have the same right to look to it as to anything else, and the same right to insist upon its payment as upon the payment of any other debt due to the company. As regards creditors, there is no distinction between such a demand and any other asset which may form a part of the property and effects of the corporation.' 19 This dictum is broad enough to imply that all the assets of a corporation constitute a trust fund in the strict sense for the payment of its debts, but it must be considered in connection with the facts before the court. Except as applied to them, it is mere dictum. In this case the assignee in bankruptcy of a corporation was seeking to compel stockholders to pay a balance due to the corporation-equitable assets of the corporation-and apply them to the payment of its debts. There was no necessity at all to resort to any trust fund doctrine. And the later decisions of the Supreme Court of the United States clearly show that they do not regard corporate assets as a trust fund for the payment of debts, and the trust fund doctrine has been repudiated by that court.67 and by other courts it has been held that persons who become creditors of a corporation, with knowledge that its stock has not been paid in full, and that it was issued under an agreement by which the stockholders are not bound as

As is shown in subsequent sections, under the Minnesota doctrine it is held that under certain circumstances a conveyance of its property by a corporation cannot be questioned by those who subsequently deal with it with knowledge of the true facts.69 Such rulings as these are inconsistent with the so-called trust fund doctrine. 

It may perhaps be said that the assets of a corporation representing its capital stock are trust funds for creditors who deal with it on the faith of its being fully paid, and that it is on this ground that they may compel its payment notwithstanding any contrary agreement by the corporation. It is not necessary, however, to rest their right in this respect on any trust fund theory, and to do so merely tends to confuse. Their right in such case may well be rested on the ground of fraud."

In Hollins v. Brierfield Coal & Iron Co.,73 the Supreme Court of the United States virtually repudiate the so-called trust fund doctrine. In that case the Court virtually said that, when it is said that the assets of a corporation constitute a trust fund for the benefit of creditors, it is not meant to convey the idea that there is any direct and express trust attached to the property of the corporation in favor of its creditors; that a corporation as against its creditors is entitled to hold its property, if it does not violate its charter, as absolutely, and as free from the claims of or interference by its creditors, as an individual can hold his property; that all that is meant by the trust fund doctrine is that when a court of equity takes into its possession the assets of an insolvent corporation it will administer them on the theory that they in equity belong to the creditors, if necessary in order to satisfy their claims, rather than to the corporation itself, or to its stockholders.
