Work is done for a limited company; no engagement is taken from them by way of security; no debenture or mortgage is granted by them; but the work is done simply on the credit of the company. The only remedy for a creditor in that case is to obtain his judgment and to take out execution; or it may be that he may have a power, if the case warrants it, of applying to wind up the company. But it is wholly unprecedented for a mere creditor to say, 'Certain transactions are taking place within the company, and dividends are being paid to shareholders which they are not entitled to receive, and therefore I am entitled to come here and examine the company's deed, to see whether or not they are doing what is ultra vires, and to interfere in order that, as by a bill quia timet, I may keep the assets in a proper state of security for the payment of my debt whensoever the time arrives for its payment.'" "The case must have occurred, of course, many years ago, before joint-stock companies were so abundant, but certainly within the last twenty or thirty years the money due to creditors must have been many millions, and the number of creditors must have been many thousands; yet I have never before heard-and I asked in vain for any such precedent-of any attempt on the part of a creditor to file a bill of this description against a company, claiming the interference of this court on the ground that he, having no interest in the company, except the mere fact of being a creditor, is about to be defrauded by reason of their making away with their assets. It would be a fearful authority for this court to assume, for it would be called on to interfere with the concerns of almost every company in the kingdom against which a creditor might suppose that he had demands, which he had not established in a court of justice, but which he was about to proceed to establish. If there is this power in any case, of course 466 

3 HILDEBRAND TEX.CORP.

Ch. § 928 

1 it would apply not only to the raising of money by debentures and to paying shareholders, but it would extend to an interference in every possible way with the dealings of the company." 

A similar decision was made by the Massachusetts court in 

Pond v. Framingham & Lowell Railroad Co.93 The bill alleged that the plaintiffs were creditors of the defendant corporation; that it owed large amounts to other creditors, one of whom had attached all its property; that it was about to execute a lease to the attaching creditor for 999 years, at a rental which would not pay the interest on its indebtedness; and that the lease would be injurious to its creditors and stockholders. The prayer was for an injunction to restrain it from further prosecuting its business and for a receiver. The court said: "The plaintiffs cannot maintain this bill, unless upon the ground that a creditor can maintain a bill in equity against an individual debtor upon like allegations. 

But there is no allegation of fraud or breach of trust, or any other ground of jurisdiction, which brings the case within the general equity powers of a court of chancery. The bill is an attempt by a creditor to restrain his debtor from making what is alleged to be an improvident contract. The rights of the parties are governed by the rules of the common law. The plaintiffs as creditors might by an attachment have obtained security which would take precedence of the contemplated lease; but if they could not, the court has no power to restrain the debtor from making a disposition of his property which is permitted by the common law, unless fraud or a breach of trust is alleged and shown. "The allegation that the defendant corporation is insolvent does not aid the plaintiffs. In the absence of any statute giving the power, this court has no authority to act as a court of insolvency for the liquidation of the affairs of an insolvent railroad corporation."

 § 929. Fraudulent Conveyances and Transfers 

If a corporation conveys or transfers its property fraudulently, with intent to hinder, delay or defraud its creditors in the enforcement of their claims, the creditors may come into a court of equity and set aside the transaction, as against any person other than a bona fide purchaser for value, and subject the property so disposed of to the satisfaction of their claims.94 They have such rights, and such rights only, in this respect, as creditors of a natural person would have under the same circumstances. The principles of law which govern are the same in both cases.95

The stockholders of a corporation cannot transfer the corporate property to themselves, directly or indirectly, and thereby defeat the rights of creditors of the corporation.96 The stockholders will be liable to the unpaid creditors of the corporation for the value of the corporate assets wrongfully received. It is a well established rule that a corporation may recover corporate assets which have been distributed among its stockholders even though the distribution was authorized by the stockholders as a body under the mistaken belief that sufficient assets remained to take care of the corporation's liabilities.""

A New York court has declared that where the stockholders are in actual possession and have under their immediate control the property of the corporation, they are trustees of the creditors of the corporation in respect to such property and will be liable to the creditors for any act done in disposing of the property which results in injury to them.98

Under these circumstances the majority of courts agree that the liability of the stockholders is co-extensive with the corporate assets received by them, or so much thereof as may be necessary to liquidate the outstanding indebtedness.99 

The stockholders cannot defeat the rights of creditors by forming a new corporation in which they are the principal stockholders, and transferring to it the property of the old company. Such a transfer is a fraud upon the creditors of the old company, and may be treated as void as to them, or the new corporation may be held liable for the debts of the old to the extent of the property received by it. well-settled rule of law that if an individual, being solvent at the time, without any actual intent to defraud future creditors, sells some of his property for an inadequate consideration, or even makes a voluntary conveyance of it, subsequent creditors cannot question the transaction, since they are not injured thereby. They should investigate his financial standing when they give credit to the debtor and they are presumed to have extended credit on his financial status at the time credit was given to him.¹ 

In Graham v. La Crosse & M. R. Co.,5 it was held that this principle applies to conveyances by a corporation; that the disposal by a corporation of any of its property cannot be questioned by subsequent creditors any more than a like disposition of property by an individual may be. It was contended in this case that a corporation debtor does not stand on the same footing as an individual debtor; that, while the latter has supreme dominion over his own property, a corporation is a mere trustee, holding its property for the benefit of its creditors and stockholders; and that if it fails to pursue its rights against third persons, whether arising out of fraud or otherwise, it is a breach of trust, and creditors may come into equity to compel an enforcement of the corporate duty. But on this issue the court said: "We do not concur in this view. It is at war with the notions which we derive from the English law with regard to the nature of corporate bodies. A corporation is a distinct entity. Its affairs are necessarily managed by officers and agents; but, in law, it is as distinct a being as an individual is, and is entitled to hold property (if not contrary to its charter) as absolutely as an individual can hold it. Its estate is the same, its interest is the same, its possession is the same. Its stockholders may call the officers to account, and may prevent any malversation of funds, or fraudulent

disposal of property on their part. But that is done in the exercise of their corporate rights, not adverse to the corporate interests, but coincident with them. "When a corporation becomes insolvent, it is so far civilly dead, that its property may be administered as a trust fund for the benefit of its stockholders and creditors. A court of equity, at the instance of the proper parties, will then make those funds trust funds, which, in other circumstances, are as much the absolute property of the corporation, as any man's property is his. 

We see no reason why the disposal by a corporation of any of its property should be questioned by subsequent creditors of the corporation, any more than a like disposal by an individual of his property should be so. The same principles of law apply to each." 

In general, the above quotation correctly states the law. But the courts should never forget that only the property owned by the corporation is liable for its debts. And since the stockholders virtually agreed to keep intact for the benefit of the creditors of the company assets equal to its capital stock no stockholder should be permitted to violate the above understanding. Therefore, if the stockholders by way of dividends are given some of the above safety fund they should be forced to return it to the corporation if needed to satisfy creditors." 

§ 931. — Effect of Fraudulent Conveyance-Remedy of Gen eral Creditors The statute & declares that conveyances made with intent to delay, hinder or defraud creditors are void. The Texas courts hold that a conveyance in violation of this statute is voidable at the option of the creditors and not void in the accurate sense of that term, i. e., null and without any effect, or incapable of ratification. In A. B. Frank Co. v. Berwind, Justice Fly said: "Under the Texas doctrine the trust relation does not arise between the directors of an insolvent corporation until it has ceased to do business. If there is no trust relation, the director should occupy the position of any other creditor, except, perhaps, that his acts would be scanned more closely, in order that fraud might not be perpetrated. If the director, as in this instance, advanced money in good faith to the corporation to tide it over its difficulties, he should be allowed to use the same means accorded any other creditor to collect his debt. This doctrine is founded upon common sense and justice, although it is denounced as infamous by Mr. Thompson in his 'Commentaries on the Law of Corporations' (sections 6498, 6499). Pages of that work are devoted to denunciations of what are styled 'the mouthings of judges upon the subject,' and yet in that same work (section 4068) it is, in the usual style, insisted that the doctrine must prevail that directors may enter into contracts with, and furnish money to, a corporation, take mortgage to secure the same, and enforce the same; but this seems to be lost sight of in the succeeding parts of the work, and courts are denounced that hold that, although insolvency may have supervened, the right to enforce is not lost. As long as the doctrine prevails in Texas that directors of corporations do not occupy the relation of trustees to creditors of insolvent corporations still engaged in business, just so long must the doctrine be recognized that a director can contract with the corporation, and that his right to enforcement of his contracts shall be the same as that of any other creditor. The expression in the opinion in Rogers v. East 

Line Lumber Co., 11 Tex.Civ.App. 

108, 33 S.W. 312, was not necessary in the decision of that case. There is no Texas case directly in point, but it has been held by the supreme court that a member of a corporation who is a creditor has the same right of action as any other creditor, and may even attach the property of the company. 

Henderson v. Railroad Co., 17 Tex. 560; City National 

Bank v. Cupp, 59 Tex. 268, 270.

Such transactions must be bona fide and will be scrutinized very closely by the courts.39 And after a petition to have a receiver appointed for the corporation on the ground of insolvency is filed no creditor can be given a lien on the property of the company if the court appoints the receiver as the appointment relates back to the presentation of the application for the appointment of the receiver to the judge. Nor can a creditor be given more than his share of the assets of the corporation after such application.40 be permitted to deal for his own advantage with the property or shares of the corporation. The case presented is one between outside creditors and a director, and it is sought to withhold from him the right to collect his debt from the corporation, merely because he is a director, and not because any fiduciary relation existed between him and the creditors."

Since in Texas the assets of the corporation become trust funds after the corporation has become insolvent and ceased to do business, the levy of an execution after that time does not create a lien, and, therefore, a sale under the execution is invalid.50 For It would be intolerable if a creditor of a corporation could interfere with the management every time he thought that the business of the company was being improperly conducted. this reason it is usually said that the creditors of a corporation have no more control over its business than those of an individual debtor. But the courts should always be mindful of the fact that the above statement is only a generality, and, therefore, has its limitations. In permitting individuals to incorporate the state has authorized them to conduct a business without personal liability. In consideration of this privilege the courts should insist that the statutory protection of creditors should never be violated. Therefore, it is proper to say that a corporation is virtually as free from interference by its creditors as an individual so long as it keeps intact for its creditors the safety fund provided for by the statute under which the corporation was organized.51 The Texas courts have too often lost sight of this principle. For instance, in Tweedie Footwear Corp. v. Fonville52 the Court of Civil Appeals cited with approval the federal case of Sweet v. Lang,53 in which the Circuit Court said: “A solvent corporation may deal with its assets and dispose of them in any way it wishes with the consent of its directors and stockholders, and creditors have no right to complain if the corporation is not thereby rendered insolvent." In that case the Court forgot that another principle was involved. Will the Texas Supreme Court permit stockholders to retain money given to them which should have been kept inviolate for creditors? The court was blinded by its adherence to the Texas "trust fund" doctrine. No corporation should be permitted to give away its assets where it impairs "the capital" of the company. To permit a company to return part of its assets in the form of dividends to its stockholders where such capital is needed to pay creditors shocks one's sense of justice and fair dealings even though such conduct is approved by all the stockholders and directors.

If the directors had attempted to defeat the suit on the ground that they received the $8,000 in the nature of a dividend, their position would have been without merit, since the plaintiff was a stockholder and he did not receive his share of the dividend. 

Therefore, it would seem more reasonable for our courts to say in those cases that the shareholders should not be permitted to tamper with those assets which should be kept intact in order to balance the assets and liabilities of the company-always remembering that the amount of the capital stock should appear on the liability side of the balance sheet. This should be done not only for the protection of the present creditors of the company who do not complain in many cases because of their ignorance of the manner in which the business is being conducted, but especially for future creditors. That should be the price exacted of the shareholders of a corporation for the privilege of conducting a business without personal liability on the part of the stockholders. In these cases the courts too often shut their eyes to the rights of future creditors and focus their minds too much on the rights and duties of the shareholders among themselves. 

In Landa v. Whitfield1 the stockholder who owned all the stock of the company paid Landa twenty-five thousand dollars for the latter's stock with company funds. It was not shown that the company was insolvent at the time. In fact the company was solvent at that time and carried on its business for eighteen months longer. After a receiver was appointed, he sued Landa for the return of the twenty-five thousand dollars. If the company's balance sheet justified the declaration of a twenty-five thousand dollar dividend when that amount was paid to Landa, no one could complain. And even though such dividend had been paid out of the capital stock as the company had not ceased to carry on its business, the shareholder would not have been forced to return the amount received if Temple Lumber Company-Pineland Naval Stores' case is followed. 

61. Tex.Civ.App., 131 S.W.2d 310, writ dismissed. 488

Ch. § 933 

 § 933. Contractual and Statutory Preferences 

Some of the Courts of Civil Appeals made a distinction between contractual and statutory preferences. Those courts held that a diligent creditor could obtain a statutory preference by attachment or garnishment even though the corporation was insolvent and had ceased to do business since the property of the corporation was not in custodia legis and that the "trust fund" doctrine was invoked only to prevent fraudulent preferences by the corporation itself.62 The Supreme Court, however, held that "after a corporation becomes insolvent and ceases to carry on its business, creditors cannot acquire a preference lien upon the assets by attachment or other judicial process."63 Thus the same rule obtains whether the preference asserted be contractual or statutory. The reasons for such a result are that: "The rights of all creditors in the fund are by law fixed, so soon as the conditions arise out of which the trust relation springs. After the trust attaches, no creditor can, by any act of diligence on his part, accomplish that which neither the corporation nor trustees could do by agreement with him. 

If one could secure an advantage by garnishment or attachment over other creditors, the equality of right created by law would be destroyed."64 * *

Even though the creditor is a director of the corporation, the latter may give the director-creditor a preference.65 In Zorn v. 

Brooks,66 the corporation after it became insolvent, but before it ceased to do business, conveyed part of its assets to its president who was also a director in payment of a $12,000.00 debt it owed him. It was contended that a corporation could not prefer one creditor as freely as an individual. In the opinion the court said: "It is urged that the transaction amounted to a preference of creditors and was therefore a nullity. The argument is that a corporation, unlike an individual, has no power under its charter and under the statutes to prefer a creditor. This is the rule in some jurisdictions, but in this State, a corporation, even though insolvent, which is still transacting its business in the usual way, may perfer one of its creditors."

Sav. Neither can creditors, when such conditions exist, obtain a preference by any form of legal process Our Supreme Court has further held that in such cases the appointment of the receiver relates back to the presentation of the application to the judge and his recognition of the same by setting it down for hearing."68 As a general rule, the corporation itself

§ 935. Dissolution of Corporation 

At common law, debts due to and from a corporation were extinguished by its dissolution. The reason usually given for this ancient rule was that after dissolution there is no one to sue or be sued.76 At least this was true so far as a right of action was concerned. This rule, however, very properly did not obtain in equity. A court of equity will recognize and enforce debts due to the corporation, and will lay hold of and apply its assets to the payment of its debts."7

By statutory enactment in Texas, upon the dissolution of a corporation, a trust attaches to the corporate property in favor of its creditors.78 Where the trustees after the corporation is dissolved sell some of the assets for a valuable consideration, as a general rule, the vendee is not liable for the debts of the dissolved

Ch. § 937 

This rule is based upon the established principle that in order to invoke the aid of a court of equity the complainant must show that there is no legal remedy or that the legal remedy, under the peculiar facts of his case, does not furnish a complete or adequate remedy.¹ Due to our blended system of law and equity and to expedite matters, a general creditor may bring a creditor's bill by alleging that the corporation does not possess sufficient assets to satisfy his claim.2 

In the Murphy case³ it was said, "Where law and equity practice is blended, it is not essential that the owner of a foreign judgment should establish the judgment in a Texas court before he can have the benefit of a creditor's bill." In each of the cases cited above, the creditor's bill was instituted to set aside a fraudulent conveyance of the property. In such a case it is established in Texas that an action against the directors for a misapplication of the funds can be joined with an equitable bill seeking to hold the transferees liable for the value of the property.4 

Similarly, the creditor may sue the corporation upon the indebtedness due him and in the same suit seek to set aside the conveyance made in fraud of his rights as a creditor. Such a proceeding is sustained upon the grounds that the remedy in equity is more adequate, and that the conveyance, unless removed, would be a cloud upon the title which would prevent the sale of the property at a fair valuation to satisfy the judgment rendered in favor of the creditor.5 Moreover, creditors may unite in the same suit an action to foreclose a mortgage and an equitable claim which they have as creditors against the shareholders where the property has been distributed among the shareholders."

The same cases, as well as others, appear to be applicable to the particular application as here made requiring notice thereof to be given to the parties affected." "These and other cases relied upon by appellees apply the rule to a going corporation, with managing officers and directors who are in actual charge of its affairs. The rule which inhibits minority stockholders, as such, from invoking the appointment of a receiver has for its reason that courts will not control the officers and directors of such a corporation or take the corporate property from their charge through the agency of a receiver, except upon gravest considerations of the conservation of the property in the interest of creditors and stockholders. But when, as in this case, the corporation has forfeited its right to do business, and has failed to elect officers, and has abandoned all corporate enterprises and its property, a stockholder, regardless of the extent or value of his holdings, may petition the court to take into its custody and control the assets of the corporation. The rule, as contended for by the appellees in this case, as well as the exceptions thereto, is thus stated in 23 R.C.L. 11: "As a general rule, a receiver is a purely ancillary remedy, and it cannot be maintained in a proceeding instituted solely for that purpose. Of course, if the statute authorizes it, and in some well-recognized exceptions to the general rule, the appointment of a receiver may be the main object and purpose of the suit or proceeding. Thus it has been held that the appointment of a receiver may be made the main purpose of an action where a corporation ceases to exist, or abandons its business and neglects to elect its officers and there is no

cured creditor may apply for a receivership in the following words: "A receivership can never be properly granted at the instance of a general creditor of a corporation until the point has been reached in its affairs at which the trust-fund doctrine may be invoked by the creditors, and when that point is reached the statute applies. We understand the law to be that, in all cases in which a receiver of property is applied for, the showing must be made either that the applicant has an actual interest in the property, or a lien thereon, or else the property constitutes a fund out of which he is entitled to the satisfaction of his claim. 

Beach on Rec. Sec. 7. This justified the distinction whereby a general creditor under our statute may successfully apply for a receiver of the property of an insolvent corporation, whereas none but a lien creditor would be entitled to the relief as against a partnership or natural person. New Birmingham Iron & Land 

Co.v. Blevins, 12 Tex.Civ.App. 410, 34 S.W. 828; Cahn v. Johnson, 12 Tex.Civ.App. 304, 308, 33 S.W. 1000; Carter v. Hightower, 79 Tex. 135, 137, 15 S.W. 223; San Antonio & G. S. Ry. Co. v. Davis, Tex.Civ.App., 30 S.W. 693. The distinction is referable to the trust-fund doctrine, which means that whenever a corporation voluntarily ceases business, or is otherwise practically dissolved, either by actual insolvency or its imminent pendency, its property becomes at once a trust fund in the hands of its officers for the benefit of creditors of every character, as well as the stockholders of the defunct concern. Lyons-Thomas Hardware Co. v. Perry Stove Mfg. Co., 86 Tex. 143, 156, 24 S.W. 16, 22

L.R.A. 802. Thus, when that point is reached in the affairs of a private corporation, the general creditor may maintain his bill for a receiver upon an otherwise proper showing; he being able to satisfy the general requirement that he has an actual interest in the fund. It is also true that when that point is reached (that is to say, when a corporation has become technically insolvent), no creditor can by legal process or contract secure an advantage over any other creditor which he did not theretofore have. 

Whether the point of insolvency is left open, to be ascertained as any other fact, or whether it is arbitrarily fixed by the date of the proceedings brought for the purpose, is perhaps an open question. In line with this principle it is held in this state that 505

Can it be justly said, in the light of the facts, that such a point is shown to have been reached in the history of this concern? We think not."

Venue of Suit against Receivers 

By statute suit may be filed against the receiver of a corporation in the county where the principal office of the corporation is located.49 It has also been provided that "Whenever in any law authorizing or regulating any particular character of action, the venue is expressly prescribed, the suit shall be commenced in the county of which jurisdiction may be so expressly given." 50 It is to be noticed that the statute authorizing a suit against the receiver in the county where the principal office is located is couched in permissive language,51 and therefore is not controlling. The receiver can be sued in any county where the court has jurisdiction under the venue statutes, and the plaintiff is not compelled to sue the receiver at the principal place of the business of the corporation.52 In Bowles v. Mitchell, cited in the last note, the 

Commission of Appeals said: "We think, after mature consideration, that his construction of these two articles of the statutes (Rev.St. arts. 2146 and 2147, Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. arts. 2310, 2311) is correct, and that the Court of Civil Appeals in the in-

See, Mitchell v. Hancock, Tex.Civ. 

App., 196 S.W. 694, holding under Texas statute suits against receivers are not limited to the county where the principal place of the corporation is located. 511

§ 

Ch. 21 stant case is in error. The latter court holds, briefly, that prior to 1887 a receiver could only be sued with the permission of the court appointing him; that in 1887 the Legislature passed article 

2146, which merely grants general permission to sue receivers without permission of the court appointing them, and also enacted, at the same time, article 2147, fixing the venue of suits against the receiver of a corporation in the county of its principal office. In other words, the Court of Civil Appeals, in the instant case, holds that a receiver cannot be sued anywhere except in the county where the principal office of the corporation is located. These articles of the statutes are quoted by Judge 

Conner, as shown herein. The Amarillo Court, in effect, concedes that article 2147, standing alone, would be merely permissive, and would not fix venue in one county only. But they say that, taken in connection with article 2146, it must be so construed. If the only purpose of the Legislature in enacting article 

2146 was to authorize suits against receivers without permission of the courts appointing them, then nearly all the language of said article is mere surplusage, and meaningless. The article provides that the suits may be brought 'without first obtaining leave of the court appointing such receiver.' If that was the sole purpose, then why does the article go further, and say that the receiver may 'be sued in any court of this state having jurisdiction of the cause of action'? To us the answer is clear. The 

Legislature intended to provide, as its plain language imports, that receivers could be sued in any court of this state where such court would otherwise have jurisdiction of the cause of action. 

On the other hand, by article 2147 the Legislature permitted suits, at the option of any given plaintiff, against the receiver in the county of the corporation's principal office, limited only, of course, by any mandatory provision contained in other articles of the venue statutes. "If the Legislature had intended the statutes to have the effect given them by the Amarillo court, they could much more simply have provided that receivers of corporations may sue or be sued without first obtaining the permission of the courts appointing them, but only in a court in the county of the principal 512

Ch. § 942 

office of the given corporation. But, the Legislature did not so provide. By enacting the two articles now under consideration, it expressly, in our opinion, disavowed any intention to show any such partiality to receivers, but made them subject to the venue laws of our state, just as others, including the corporations themselves, are."

It has been held that a receiver may be sued in the county where the corporation has contracted in writing to perform an obligation, but that the debt and lien can only be fixed by this court and such action must be certified to the court appointing the receiver, which court is free to marshall the assets of the receivership and to determine the classification and priority of such debt and lien.53 In other words, subject to venue statutes the rule that a suit may be brought against the receiver in his official capacity in any court having competent jurisdiction of the subject-matter, is subject to the limitation that no court, other than the one in which the receiver is appointed, may make any order or take any action in such suit that will disturb the possession, control, and management of the assets of the receivership.

'Mortgage Action' must have some relation to the appointment of the receiver, and the action to foreclose a mortgage being the basis for the appointment of a receiver that proceeding is within the meaning of the statute 'mortgage action.' The law gives to the mortgage creditor the full benefit of the mortgage by subjecting the corpus of the property to his debt, but refuses to carry on the business for his benefit. By his action the mortgage creditor destroys the means of paying other creditors, and, choosing his remedy, he must abide his choice. acted in pursuance and furtherance of what was evidently considered to be a wise public policy. In other words, it was thought desirable to provide that where persons holding a lien upon the property of a corporation took the initiative and secured the appointment of a receiver that it should not share in the earnings of the property of its plant during the receivership. The effect of this would be, of course, to certainly discourage if it did not absolutely prevent collusive receiverships in which the creditor holding a lien might successfully delay the payment of an unsecured creditor, and, if ultimately the property was sold, secure the proceeds of a sale of the corpus of its estate and at the same time share in the earnings of the plant while operated by the receiver. 

It could, we think, have no application to a case where a receiver was appointed, not at the instance of the mortgage holder, and not as a result of a mortgage action, but without the concurrence, co-operation, or consent of the mortgage holder. If it should be held that this statute applied and would defeat the participation by the mortgage holder in the earnings of the property during receivership where such receivership had been brought about by the action of the unsecured creditor, this would constitute an invitation if not an encouragement to receiverships of corporations by unsecured creditors who in this way could impound the property of such companies, secure their operation by a receiver and, to the exclusion of the mortgage holder, apply the earnings of such properties to the payment of their debts. 

In this case the bank held a mortgage on a part only of the property of the companies in question. It had taken no action until forced to do so by proper intervention after the grant of a receivership. In such a case we think a true interpretation of the statute in question should entitle it to share in such earnings and that it is not to be excluded therefrom, for the reason that in such case its suit was not a mortgage action within the contemplation of the statute." 57

 § 944. Operating Expenses-Priorities-Receivers Certificates 

Where a lienholder procures the appointment of a receiver with the power to operate the property, which is subject to his lien, it is only just that the consequent expenses should take precedence over his lien, since it must be anticipated that such operation will be attended with cost, and possibly in excess of the income.60 The same rule should be applied to a party who, while not directly the applicant upon whose petition the receiver is appointed, is privy to the action which results in the appoint- 

60. Craver v. Greer, 179 S.W. 862, 107 Tex. 356. In this case Judge 

Phillips said: "Upon the other questions, it is hardly necessary to restate the general rule, that a receivership is always subject to vested rights. As broad as are the powers of a court of chancery, it is without authority to impair the force of contracts. Where the court takes charge of railroads or other corporations affected with a public use, and undertakes to operate them through a receiver, the necessary debts of such operation may, as against all parties to the suit, be made a prior lien upon the income, and, if that be insufficient, upon the property itself. 

But, as has been frequently stated, this is an extraordinary power; and it is exercised only because of the public duty resting upon such corporations and the public interest accordingly involved in the continuance of their operation. On the other hand, the conduct of the business of an insolvent private corporation, or an insolvent person, is no part of the duty of a court of equity; and the authority, if it exists, for the displacement in such receiverships of a vested lien for indebtedness incurred through an operation of the business by the court, must be found in an estoppel which is justly enforceable against the owner of the lien. The distinction which governs the question, according to whether the property is impressed with a public use or is purely private in its nature, is generally recognized, and is announced in the decision of this court in Clint v. Houston Ice & 

Brewing Co., 106 Texas, 508, 169 S. 

W. 411. "Where a lienholder procures the appointment of a receiver with the power to operate the property which is subject to his lien, in a continuance of the business to which it is devoted, it is only just that the consequent expenses should take precedence over his lien, since it must be anticipated that such operation will be attended with cost, and possibly in excess of the income. Heisen v.

 § 946. Levy on Shares of Stock to Satisfy Individual Creditor of 

Stockholder

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 3795, provides that, "A levy on the stock of any corporation or joint stock company is made by leaving a notice thereof with any officer of such company." 

Article 3798 provides that, "Shares of stock in any joint stock or incorporated company may be sold on execution against the person owning such stock."

Article 4080 provides: "Where it appears from the plaintiff's affidavit that the garnishee is an incorporated or joint stock company, in which the defendant is the owner of shares, or is interested therein, the writ of garnishment shall further require the garnishee to answer upon oath what number of shares, if any, the defendant owns in such company, or owned when such writ was served, and what interest, if any, he has in such company, or had when such writ was served." 

Article 4084 provides: "From and after the service of such writ of garnishment, it shall not be lawful for the garnishee to pay to the defendant any debt or to deliver to him any effects; nor shall the garnishee, if an incorporated or joint stock company in which the defendant is alleged to be the owner of shares or to have an interest, permit or recognize any sale or transfer of such shares or interest; and any such payment or delivery, sale or transfer, shall be void and of no effect as to so much of said debt, effect, shares, or interest as may be necessary to satisfy the plaintiff's demand.”

Article 4091 provides: "Where the garnishee is an incorporated or joint stock company, and it appears from the answer, or otherwise, that the defendant is, or was when the writ of garnishment was served, the owner of any shares of stock in such company, or any interest therein, the court shall render a decree, ordering the sale under execution, in favor of the plaintiff against the defendant, of such shares or interest of the defendant in such

Article 4092 provides: "The sale so ordered shall be conducted in all respects as other sales of personal property under execution; and the officer making such sale shall execute a transfer of such shares or interest to the purchaser, with a brief recital of the judgment of the court under which the same was sold."

Article 4093 provides: "Such sale shall be valid and effectual to pass to the purchaser all right, title and interest which the defendant had in such shares of stock, or in such company; and the proper officers of such company shall enter such sale and transfer on the books of the company in the same manner as if the same had been made by the defendant himself. 

Under these statutes the individual creditor of a stockholder has a choice of one of two remedies when attempting to satisfy his debt out of shares that belong to the debtor. But a levy of execution not in compliance with the statute is invalid." In a recent case the Commission of Appeals in construing the above articles modified several previous Texas cases.11 In this case the court said: "These answers were in no manner contested. It will be noted that the article above quoted does not make it a condition precedent to the discharge of the garnishee that the answer must show that garnishee has no knowledge that other persons have in their possession effects belonging to the defendant or judgment debtor. The express language of the article is that the garnishee shall be discharged if the answer contains the matters therein mentioned, regardless of what may or may not be shown concerning the inquiry about the effects in the hands of other persons. This article must be given effect if possible, and such construction must be given all other articles as will make them in harmony with this article, if this can reasonably be done. "There are expressions in previous cases to the effect that if the garnishee fails to make answer to any one or more of the

"Prior decisions, however, must be construed as clearly establishing the rule that if the answer filed does not contain responses to all inquiries required to be answered in order to furnish the basis for discharge, as provided by Article 4086, then the answer may be regarded as insufficient, even in absence of exceptions or a controverting affidavit, and judgment by default may be entered against the garnishee. It appears to us that if an answer which fails to make response to each and all of the inquiries provided for in article 4081, is to be regarded as no answer at all, thus preventing a discharge, even if the answer contains all that is mentioned in article 4086, such holding would make this latter article accomplish no useful purpose. "If a garnishee files answer which complies with article 4086, it seems to us but a fair and just rule to require the plaintiff to call to the attention of the court by proper exceptions or objections the fact of any insufficiency in the answer, thus affording the garnishee an opportunity to supply a complete answer, and also affording the court an opportunity to prevent injustice and to do justice by all parties." 

When the writ of garnishment is properly served on the corporation a lien is fixed upon the shares of stock owned by the defendant from the date of the service of the writ. The rights of other creditors who subsequently serve similar writs are subordinate to the rights of the plaintiff who served the first writ, even though the subsequent creditors obtain judgments before the first creditor reduces his claim to a judgment.12 A judgment creditor of a corporation may by garnishment compel the shareholders to pay the balance of their unpaid subscriptions to its capital stock.13

No principle of law is violated by their forming the new organization; and no right of the creditors of the old organization is injured, provided its assets are lawfully acquired by the new one. If they are not lawfully acquired, the creditors have the same right to pursue the assets as they would have if any other person had unlawfully acquired them; and it is difficult to find any basis for any other equity which they could claim as inuring to them from the transaction. The stockholders of an insolvent corporation are not bound to maintain the corporation in a hopeless struggle.

§ 981. Consolidation-Definition 

"Accurate logicians very properly distinguish between the meanings of 'consolidation' and 'merger.' Strictly speaking, a consolidation means the unifying of two or more corporations into a single new corporation, having the combined capital, franchises, and powers of all of its constituents. And strictly speaking, a merger means the absorption of one corporation by another which retains its name and corporate identity, with the added capital, franchises, and powers of the merged corporation." 1 

However, it appears that the terms "merger" and "consolidation" have been used by the courts interchangeably, and without a definite legal meaning. Some courts speak of consolidation and amalgamation in the same breath.3 The term "consolidation" 2

has been used by other Texas courts to describe various types of arrangements between corporations.¹ 

The Texas Supreme Court indicates that a new corporation can be created in the case of a consolidation or merger, if such is the intention of the parties. To demonstrate the lack of any uniform use or a fixed meaning of the term "merger," we need only to read an excerpt from a Texas Civil Appeals opinion; namely, "Union may mean different degrees of relationship. It may mean a confederacy, a merger of two into one, or an absorption of one by another. In a confederation the legal identity of the confederating bodies is maintained; but all become subordinate to a third, which is the outgrowth of the confederating compact. A merger of two or more into one may sometimes destroy the legal identity of both, resulting in the formation of a third, possessing such powers, rights, and franchises as the contract of merger may provide for, but where there is an absorption of one by another, there is necessarily a complete destruction of the legal identity of the absorbed association or corporation." 6 "The word 'successor', employed in contracts and statutes, has no fixed company, under an arrangement by which the shares of the latter company are issued to them in exchange. * Therefore, it may be considered that, the instant the consolidation of these two corporations was effected, the First National Bank of Eagle Pass, though its name remained unchanged, became, in effect, new corporation, having as its stockholders not only its former ones, but those of the Simpson National Bank, which had been amalgamated with it, with the franchises, property, and liabilities held and incurred by each before the act of consolidation." § 982. Merger-Definition 

A federal court described "merger" as follows: "As applied to corporations, the terms 'merger' and 'consolidation' have well known legal meanings. While the result is practically the same in either event, there is this difference. In a merger one corporation absorbs the other and remains in existence while the other is dissolved. In a consolidation a new corporation is created and the consolidating corporations are extinguished. In either event, the resulting corporation acquires all the property, rights, and franchises of the dissolved corporations, and their stockholders become its stockholders." 8 "The results of a merger are entirely different from those of a consolidation. Ordinarily, when corporations of two or more states 'consolidate', in the technical sense of the term, the old corporations are dissolved and a new corporation comes into being in each state. However, when two corporations unite by way of merger, the one is absorbed by the other; and when we come to apply the true test as to whether, under a given statement of facts, there has been a merger, it becomes necessary to ascertain whether the existence of one of the corporations, as such, has been preserved, and the other has ceased to exist." Whether the parties, by their agreement, intended to effect a consolidation or merger depends on the instrument of agreement; and if the instrument uses both terms, the court will construe the agreement to create a merger where it

Ch. § 983 

provides that a new corporation shall not be created.10 In the final analysis, "whether a particular transaction is in reality a sale, conversion, consolidation, or merger, to a great extent depends on the circumstances surrounding that particular case.” 11 

There is a decided distinction between "dissolution" and "consolidation" or "merger," and consequently a state statute dealing with dissolution of corporations cannot be used as statutory authority for either "consolidation" or "merger." 12 

§ 983. Sale Distinguished 

Merger or consolidation must be distinguished from a sale of its property by one corporation to another. "While the transaction has some of the features, it is wanting in the essential elements of a sale. A sale implies a vendor and a vendee, and by it the former sells and transfers a thing that he owns to the latter for a price paid or to be paid to himself. The vendor parts with nothing but his property, and for it receives a quid pro quo. Such is not the case where companies are consolidated under this statute. It is true that the owner of each constituent road parts with its property. But it does much more; it not only parts with its property, but ceases to be a juristical entity, capable of owning or acquiring property. It does not, and could not receive any consideration for the transfer, because it is extinguished and dissolved by the act of its stockholders in assenting to the proposed agreement. It is futile to urge that the consideration is received by the stockholders. They are not the corporation, nor do they 

10. Chicago & E. I. R. Co. v. Doyle, 100 N.E. 278, at page 281, 256 Ill. 

514. This court made a very sensible statement, to wit: "Much is said in the argument about the terms 'merger' and 'consolidation' and distinctions are sought to be drawn between the two forms of contract. 

We do not attach great importance to this line of argument. While there appears to be a distinction recognized by most of the authorities between a 'merger,' strictly speaking, and a 'consolidation,' still the terms are not always used with strict accuracy. Besides, the agreement under consideration employs both terms, so that the true intent of the agreement cannot be determined by recourse to the dictionaries."

All that the stockholders of either of the old companies receive, is stock in the new company in exchange for what they held in the former company." 13 

Furthermore, "a purchase by definite contract by one corporation of the assets of another, and the assumption of debts specified in the contract, does not constitute a merger or consolidation, and does not, in the absence of fraud, make the purchasing corporation liable for the debts of the selling corporation." 14 If a corporation purchases the assets of another corporation at execution sale, there is neither a merger nor consolidation, and the purchaser takes the property free from all liability for its former indebtedness not secured by prior lien.15

Necessarily by this combination or arrangement the holding company in the fullest sense dominates the situation in the interest of those who were stockholders of the constituent companies; as much so, for every practical purpose, as if it has been itself a railroad corporation which had built, owned, and operated both lines for the exclusive benefit of its stockholders. Necessarily, also, the constituent companies ceased, under such a combination, to be in active competition for trade and commerce along their respective lines, and have become, practically, one powerful consolidated corporation, by the name of a holding corporation, the principal, if not the sole, object for the formation of which was to carry out the purpose of the original combination, under which competition between the constituent companies would cease." 20

Ch. § 984 

 § 984. Lease Distinguished 

There is a clear distinction between a consolidation of two or more corporations and the acquisition by one corporation of the property of another corporation by means of a lease; consequently a statutory or constitutional provision which prohibits a consolidation of specified types of corporations does not prohibit the use of the property of one corporation by another corporation by means of a lease contract.22 

22. In State v. Montana R. Company, 53 P. 623, 21 Mont. 221, 243, 45 

L.R.A. 271, 282, the court was confronted with the problem of determining the validity of a ten year lease involving the property of railway corporations. The court in the opinion said: "Ordinarily no idea of a lease would ever enter into any explanation of what constituted a consolidation, unless such contract of lease was for so long a period of time, or by its terms was such as to make it a practical merger of one corporation into another. Lease does not imply consolidation, nor consolidation lease. The power to consolidate, as has been seen, is a power to make two corporations one; the power to lease carries with it no power to pass anything except the right to use the property leased. In the lease under consideration there is no merger of ownership, no communion of interest, no distribution of receipts based upon a contingent measure of profits, no common ownership of shares of stock, no joint management, and no yielding up of an independent corporate existence by the lessor to the lessee. "As was said in State v. Vanderbilt, 37 Ohio St. 590: 'Power to lease does not imply the power to consolidate, nor er to consolidate the power to lease. They are distinct and independent powers.

Nothing passes under the lease except the right to use. The lessor retains its existence, and its right to consolidate with connecting lines. 

There can be no consolidation except as to connecting lines. These connecting lines belong to the lessor companies, but these have not entered into the consolidation.'' 

See, also, Missouri Pac. Ry. Co. v. 

Owens, 1 White & W.Civ.Cas.Ct.App. 

§§ 384-386.

 § 985. Authority to Consolidate or Merge 

Corporations have the power to consolidate or merge only if that power has been bestowed by the sovereignty which authorized the creation of the corporations concerned.23 Consequently, corporations desiring to consolidate or merge can lawfully do so only if the legislature has expressly authorized such action either by statute or charter. In Texas there are various constitutional and statutory provisions authorizing the consolidation and merger of private corporations. The Texas Constitution prohibits consolidation of railroad corporations which have parallel or competing lines.25 A statute, Article 513,26 regulates the bank-

Article 1316,45 expressly provides for consolidation of private corporations. The wording of this statute seems to refer to the types of private corporations enumerated in the preceding article, i. e., 1315.46 The types of corporations there enumerated are "corporations created for the support of benevolent, charitable, educational or missionary undertakings, the support of any literary or scientific undertaking, the maintenance of a library, or the promotion of painting, music, or fine arts." The commercial private corporations are conspicuously absent in this enumeration. However, the Texas courts have not been overawed by the wording of article 1316 7 and have, therefore, applied it to consolidations of commercial private corporations.48 

The power of one corporation to consolidate with another corporation is very strictly construed in Texas. The court, in Morrill v. Smith County,49 said: "It does not follow that because the charter of a railway company empowers it, in general language, 'to consolidate with any other railroad company', these words should be construed as conferring the power upon any other company to consolidate with it. They reasonably admit of the construction that the company named is empowered only to unite with any other company which has a like power, and it would seem that, under the general rule previously announced, the construction least favorable to the corporation should control." Where an agreement to consolidate or merge is executed, three conditions may arise, to wit, "(1) An agreement or consolidation may be effected of two or more corporations and the corporate existence of each of the constituent companies continued; (2) the agreement may result in the merger of one or more corporations into another and provide for the continuance in existence of only one of the companies and the extinguishment of the others; (3) the consolidation may result in the extinction, at the same time, of all the constituent companies and the formation of a new corporation as the successor of all the contracting parties. In determining which of these results follows in any given case it is necessary to consider the true intent and purpose of the contracting parties as expressed in the agreement, in the light of the statute under which the union is effected." 66 However, if the intention of the parties, as construed, is such that it can be enforced only by going beyond the authorization of the statute, it will not be given effect.  § 989. Effect of Consolidation or Merger on Liens, Debts, and

The new corporation chartered to take over the assets of the corporation whose charter has expired may buy goods and create debts which will be guaranteed by a guaranty contract executed before the charter of the old corporation expired.79 When a lien has attached to the property of a corporation, the lien will be preserved regardless of whether there is a merger, consolidation or a sale of the assets by one corporation to another. 80 

This rule applies to judgment liens as well as to mortgage liens.$1

There is a difference of opinion in the decisions on the question of the extent of the liability of the corporation, i. e., whether the liability extends only to the amount of property received from the constituent corporation or extends beyond such an amount. A Mississippi court has held that a consolidated corporation is liable on the claims against the constituent corporations without regard to the amount of property received from them.93 Other courts use language which indicates that the liability of the continuing or consolidated corporation is limited to the amount of assets received from the constituent corporations.94 In the case of a merger, the continuing corporation is liable for the debts of the merged corporations, at least to the extent of the property received from the merged corporations.95 

An attempted consolidation of two corporations is a nullity if there is no authority to consolidate in the charters of the corporations or in the statutes of the states creating the corporations.96 

The cases seem to be in more accord on the question of liability of the purchasing corporation for the debts of the selling corporation after there has been a sale and transfer of the assets by one to the other corporation. The rule appears to be well settled that in the case of a sale, in the absence of an express or implied assumption of the debts, the transferee corporation is not liable for the debts or liabilities, contract or tort, of the assignor corporation."  § 990. Unauthorized Consolidation or Merger-De Facto Consoli dation The problem of determining whether a de jure or de facto consolidation or merger has been effected is analogous to the problem of determining the existence of a de jure or de facto corporation. There can be no de facto corporation unless there is a law under which a de jure corporation might be created; similarly, there can be no de facto consolidation or merger unless there is a law under which a de jure consolidation or merger can be· effected. Consequently, if there is no law authorizing the particular consolidation, neither a de jure nor a de facto consolidation can exist.¹ As a general rule, a stockholder cannot complain, question or attack the validity of a consolidation or merger if he has expressly consented or if he has acquiesced in the union.5 

But a mere refusal on the part of a stockholder to vote for a union of the corporations does not amount to a consent on his part, and he may enforce rights of a dissenting stockholder." 

And when the corporation is sued on a debt, neither the corporation nor a stockholder can set up any invalidity of the procedure of consolidation or merger in an attempt to evade or defeat the payment of the debt. In the case of fraud a dissenting stockholder may attack a consolidation, i. e., if the officers of the corporation have been guilty of misrepresentations or other fraudulent action. § 1001. Definition and Purpose 

"The term 'reorganization' is commonly applied to the formation of a new corporation by the creditors and shareholders of a corporation which is in financial difficulties, for the purpose of purchasing the company's works and other property, after the foreclosure of a mortgage or judicial sale. The result of a transaction of this kind is to form a new corporation to carry on the business of the old company upon a new basis, free from its debts and obligations, except to the extent that they have been expressly assumed." 1 As a general rule, reorganization involves the cre-

The purpose of reorganization is to rearrange the financial structure of the corporation so that it will not have to be dismantled and sold and thereby completely wipe out the equity which the stockholders have left in the corporate assets.3 The United 

States Supreme Court definitely has held that a federal equity court does not have jurisdiction or power to help a corporation to reorganize in order to scale down its fixed charges, so long as the corporation is solvent and where there is no definite proof that it will become insolvent. Notwithstanding the fact that the purpose of reorganization and dissolution is the same, namely, to conserve the corporate assets for the benefit of the stockholders and creditors, the legal result is different.5 

The reason for reorganization is to continue the business, whereas the dissolution of a corporation is its complete destruction and the liquidation and distribution of its assets. In reading the cases, the term "reincorporation" will be encountered; that term is not synonymous with reorganization, nor are the legal consequences the same. Also, "reorganization," "merger", and "consolidation" are not synonymous terms; each of these three types of corporate action has its own legal consequences and each is distinguishable from the others. The fact that a corporation is chartered for the purpose of taking over the assets and liabilities of another corporation does not mean that there is a reorganization of the transferor corporation.10 "It is held in a long line of authorities that, where a new corporation is organized by the officers and stockholders of an existing corporation who are retained as officers of the new corporation, where the stock in the new corporation is exchanged for stock in the old corporation, where the new corporation succeeds to the franchise and acquires the property and assets of the old corporation, and the new corporation continues to do business at the same place as the old corporation, under such circumstances the new corporation was not a purchaser of the assets and property of the old corporation, but that such acts amounted simply to a reorganization and a continuation of the old business under a new name, and consequently the new organization becomes responsible for the debts and obligations of the old corporation.” 11 § 1002. Authority to Reorganize

Furthermore, if the directors attempt a reorganization without the consent of at least the majority of the stockholders, a stockholder has the right to enjoin the directors' attempt to reorganize.13 There are early decisions which limited the power of the courts to compel a reorganization.14 And, too, in the early decisions the courts took the position that a court had no power to determine the propriety of a plan of reorganization, nor did the court have the power to force recalcitrant stockholders to comply with a fair plan of reorganization. Of course, the view of the courts in this respect existed primarily in cases not involving a foreclosure of the securities.15 However, the later cases show a change of viewpoint on the part of the courts with regard to the powers of a court in reorganization proceedings. 

The foregoing statement is well illustrated by the following language of a federal court, to-wit: "At the threshold lies the question of the relation of a court which appoints receivers of a railroad to a reorganization thereof by the security holders. There is no doubt but that bondholders have a right, upon default, to a strict foreclosure and sale according to the terms of their mortgages and the applicable statutes, and to leave the holders of junior securities, unsecured creditors, and stockholders to protect themselves as best they can. But in practice, on a large scale, and except in cases of utter insolvency, that is rarely done in these days. If the financial difficulties resulting in receivership are not mortal, but are mere embarrassments, which may be relieved by time and readjustment, the custom is a reorganization, embodying a recognition of all interests-bonds and other lien debts, general debts, and stocks-as far down the scale of preference as the value of the property and sound business judgment reasonably justify.

Ch. § 1002 

REORGANIZATION 

"The considerations which have led to such reorganizations in place of strict insistence upon contractual and legal rights are not important here. It has sometimes been claimed that plans of reorganization formulated by bondholders and stockholders of a railroad in the hands of receivers are exclusively of private concern, free from judicial action or interference. But for various reasons the view cannot be sustained in principle. 

After all that can be said from the standpoint of theory and strict right, the fact remains that many railroad receiverships, and the one here is typical of them, are but instruments for consummating plans of reorganization, and courts have come to realize that such use of their jurisdiction and processes entails a correlative duty to those affected by the result. Generally, in such cases, the principal parties to the suits are adversary only in name, and the existence of the collateral agreement or understanding sought to be consummated is suggested by the face of the pleadings. The relation between the receivership which ensues and the plan of reorganization agreed upon is close and intimate. So far as properly can be, the judicial proceeding is conducted in harmony with the plan, and the success of the agreed readjustment is promoted by the orders of the court and the acts of its receivers. Generally the judicial course would not be different if the court were carrying out a plan of reorganization of its own making or one affirmatively adopted by judicial order or decree. It is not meant by this that a court should insist on engaging with the security holders in formulating the terms of readjustment, but that the plan put out by them may and usually does have such relation to and dependence upon its judicial action that it is its duty to take cognizance of it and act accordingly. While it is the settled doctrine that reorganizations will be encouraged, yet, on the other hand, a court of equity will not lend its aid to one that is inequitable or oppressive." 16

§ 1003. Voluntary Reorganization 

The reorganization of a corporation may be consummated by voluntary agreement and the readjustment of the financial structure may be for the benefit of the bondholders alone, or bondholders and other creditors, or the stockholders, bondholders and other creditors. The purpose of such a voluntary readjustment of the corporate financial structure is to prevent a judicial foreclosure with its attendant expenses and to make it possible for the corporation to continue business.22 The transfer of the corporate assets to the new or reorganized corporation is generally the result of a foreclosure of corporate mortgages; however, the reorganization can be brought about without legal proceedings of any kind, and without a judicial sale of the corporate properties securing the mortgages.23 A reorganization may be under the guise of a foreclosure sale, and yet the court, as did the United States Supreme Court, may hold that the reorganization was in reality the result of an agreement between the mortgagor (the corporation-in the last analysis the stockholders) and the mortgagees (the bondholders) and that the judicial sale was a "mere form". § 1006. 

Committees

The purpose of the protective or reorganization committees is to collect the stocks and securities of the corporation which is under reorganization, and also to protect rights of the various classes of stockholders, security holders, and other creditors.56

§ 1007. 

Who May Participate 

As a general rule the stockholders have no legal right to participate in the reorganization of their corporation;66 however, a statute or the reorganization agreement frequently gives them the right to participate provided they do so under specified conditions.67 But in compliance with the principle of the Boyd case, both the secured and unsecured creditors must be protected in the final reorganization plan, and any creditor who has not been given adequate protection has recourse against the reorganized or new corporation.68 In order to get this protection the creditor must be diligent and keep himself posted with regard to the court orders involving the fixing of the dates within which the creditors must present their claims; the court has complete authority to set the dates after which the creditors of the old corporation will not be permitted to file their claims either against the old or reorganized corporation.69 The same time limit within which the creditors must present their claims can also be legally imposed by the reorganization agreement.70 The mere deposit by the owner of his stocks or securities with the designated committee has been held to be an agreement by the depositor to be bound by the reorganization agreement." 71 But neither a bondholder, other creditor, nor a stockholder can be forced into a reorganiza-

§ 1008. Foreclosure and Sale 

In connection with the reorganization of an insolvent corporation, the foreclosure and sale for the purpose of effecting a reorganization can be had only by the agreement of all the parties in interest.74 The foreclosure and sale of the corporate mortgages of large corporations has been said to be a "mere step” in the reorganization procedure, because as a general rule the reorganization is based on the foreclosure and sale of the corporate mortgages.75 The practice generally followed in the federal courts is to fix an "upset" price, which is the price the purchasers at foreclosure will have to pay for the corporate assets before the court will even consider a confirmation of the sale. The upset price is merely a designated amount below which the court will not consider a confirmation.76 The bondholders alone or the

It is likewise true that the court cannot be required to make an anticipatory ruling as to the adequacy of a bid until it is formally before the court for action and is considered in all of its aspects. The decree requires bidders who present a plan of reorganization to submit the plan with their bids, and the adequacy of a bid as furnishing a basis for determining the distributive shares of those bondholders who elect not to participate in the reorganization must be viewed in the light of all of the elements of the proposed plan. 

It is not for the court to instruct prospective bidders with reference to their bids. Bidders must exercise their Own independent judgment.

A trustee named in a corporate mortgage or deed of trust holds a fiduciary position and therefore he is not permitted to buy the corporate property at the foreclosure sale; if he does buy the corporate property at such a sale any party in interest can compel him to account for any profit he may have made or the sale may be set aside.84 Notwithstanding that a mortgage trustee holds a fiduciary position, he has the implied power to bid at the foreclosure sale in order to protect the bondholders who are secured by the mortgage which is in the process of foreclosure.85 

There is no question about the power of the mortgage trustee to bid in the property at the foreclosure sale where the mortgage or deed of trust expressly authorizes him to bid in the property for the benefit of the bondholders secured by the particular mortgage.86 If the mortgage trustee willfully or carelessly disregards the rights of a bondholder, the trustee will be liable to the injured bondholder to the extent of the injuries or loss caused him.87

§ 1009. Rights and Liabilities 

The majority of the stockholders do not have the right to acquire the corporate property for themselves to the exclusion of the minority stockholders; especially is this true where the majority attempt to do so in breach of trust or through fraudulent means.95 If the foreclosure and sale are fairly conducted and there is no taint of fraud, the rights of the nonassenting stockholders in the old corporation are extinguished by the reorganization; of course, the nonassenting stockholders are paid their distributive share realized from the foreclosure sale.96 The statutes of some of the states require that the nonassenting stockholder to the reorganization plan must be paid his share in cash.⁹7

The nonassenting or assenting stockholders have an equitable remedy, if the legal remedy is inadequate, when they discover that the reorganization resulted from fraudulent, unjust or unfair acts of those parties who effected the reorganization.¹ The minority and nonassenting stockholder will not be given the equitable remedy of injunction for the purpose of enjoining the execution of the reorganization plan favored by the majority; the minority stockholder does not have to participate in the organization, but he cannot hinder the reorganization if the plan protects his rights. § 1010. 

Rights of General Creditors 

There are numerous complicated problems that beset the reorganizers of a corporation which has general or unsecured creditors. The most perplexing problems arise in connection with the involuntary reorganization brought about through a foreclosure and sale. If the reorganization is brought about without a foreclosure and judicial sale, the rights of the unsecured creditors must be protected when the assets of the old corporation are transferred to the reorganized corporation." The general or unsecured creditor must find solace in the fact that his only right is that he can insist on the payment of his claim with the surplus of the corporate assets, if any, after the secured claims have been satisfied.12 In the case of a large corporation with vast properties, it is essential that the bondholders and stockholders work in harmony with each other so that the interest of all the interested parties, including the general creditors, will be protected; such a course seems to be the only practical and feasible one

Ch. § 1011 

REORGANIZATION § 1011. Rights and Liabilities of the Old and New Corporations 

The new or reorganized corporation, as transferee of the corporate assets of the old corporation, will acquire only such rights and titles in the properties as was enjoyed by the old corporation.22 If the reorganized corporation obtains property from the old corporation for which the latter has not paid at the time of the reorganization, the reorganization proceedings, including a foreclosure sale, will not defeat the former owner's right to be paid for the property, and he can enforce his right against the reorganized corporation.23 The reorganized corporation acquires the rights and liabilities under contracts owned by the old corporation, and if the old corporation is precluded from recovering on the contracts, the new corporation with notice of the facts will have no greater rights.24 In accordance with statutory authorization, the reorganized corporation may issue bonds for property which it has actually received.25 

The reorganized corporation will not be liable on a debt of the old corporation unless the creditor can prove express or implied assumption of the debt, or that the "new" corporation is in reality nothing more than a continuation of the "old" corporation.26 

Irrespective of whether the reorganization was voluntary or involuntary, the new corporation is liable for the debts of the old corporation where the facts show that the reorganized corporation expressly or impliedly assumed the payment of those debts.27

1031. In General

The law-making bodies have attempted to safeguard the public welfare by imposing additional liability upon the stockholders in certain types of corporations. This added liability is imposed to aid the creditors of such corporations in the collection of their claims against the insolvent concern. The litigation, that has arisen thus far, has in every case involved the liability of stockholders in a banking corporation. The liability of stockholders in 592

Ch. § 1032 

state banks is fixed by the Constitution.¹ The liability imposed upon shareholders in a trust, guaranty or surety company is fixed by statute.2 

§ 1032. Constitutional and Statutory Provisions 

The Constitution of the State of Texas makes specific provision for the incorporation of banks and discounting agencies and provides for a system of State supervision and control as follows: "The Legislature shall by general laws, authorize the incorporation of corporate bodies with banking and discounting privileges, and shall provide for a system of State supervision, regulation and control of such bodies which will adequately protect and secure the depositors and creditors thereof. "Each shareholder of such corporate body incorporated in this State, so long as he owns shares therein, and for twelve months after the date of any bona fide transfer thereof, shall be personally liable for all debts of such corporate body existing at the date of such transfer, to an amount additional to the par value of such shares so owned or transferred, equal to the par value of such shares so owned or transferred. "No such corporate body shall be chartered until all of the authorized capital stock has been subscribed and paid for in full in cash. Such body corporate shall not be authorized to engage in business at more than one place which shall be designated in its charter. "No foreign corporation, other than the national banks of the United States, shall be permitted to exercise banking or discounting privileges in this State." 3

In accordance with the above constitutional provision, the Legislature of Texas passed a statute, quoted below, which fixed the liability of an ordinary shareholder in a banking corporation until

§ 1033. Corporate Liabilities to which Statutory or Constitutional

Under the existing Texas statutes, the corporation must, on demand of the Banking Commissioner, make good any deficiency in the required capital stock, which has occurred through impairment or otherwise below the amount required by law." It is true that this statute provides that the corporation must make up this deficiency brought about by impairment of its assets, but it has been held that such deficiency must be paid by the stockholders, when a call is made on them by the Banking Commissioner, it being said: "The duty of making good the deficiency devolves on the stockholders as the real owners of the corporation." 8 

Under the earlier cases before the enactment of the present law, which was passed by the Second Called Session of the Legislature of 1923, the person intrusted with the enforcement of the liability of banking corporations and their stockholders was called "Commissioner of Insurance and Banking." The act above referred to designated this enforcing officer as the "Banking Commissioner." So in the earlier cases the reference to the Banking and Insurance Commissioner carries the same significance as the designation in the later cases of Banking Commissioner.
