§ 1035. Who are Liable as Shareholders 

The real owner of the bank stock at the time of the failure of the bank, though he is not the record holder, is liable for assessment on the stock.17 The shareholder who transferred the stock is not liable for assessments even though he made a misrepresentation to the purchaser,18 and so it follows that the purchaser who acquires bank stock through a sale, though induced by misrepresentation to purchase it, is liable on assessments on the stock, if the bank is not a party to the fraud.19 

It is held under R.S.1911, Article 552,20 that the liability fixed by statute is not extended past the limits fixed by the Constitution, article 16, section 16, in that "each shareholder" as used in the Statute means the owner of the stock at the time of default in payment by the bank.21

§ Ch. 24 

Although an increase is made in the capital stock of a bank, over the protest of one of the stockholders, by the majority of the stockholders, the minority stockholder is still liable on his original stock, held before the increase, for assessments levied by the 

Banking Commissioner.22 

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 500 provides: "Any banking corporation doing business in this State may at any time reduce its capital stock to any sum not less than the minimum sum provided by law. No reduction of such stock shall be made except upon the written consent of the owners of not less than two-thirds of the stock of such corporation. Notice of the intention to reduce the capital stock shall be published for thirty days in some daily newspaper in the city or county where such bank is located, or in a weekly paper for four insertions before the time when such reduction shall be effected, and the last insertion of such notice shall be at least ten days before the date of the reduction. A statement of such reduction of the capital stock duly acknowledged by the officers of the corporation shall be recorded and filed in the same manner as provided for the original articles of agreement." 

The Supreme Court of Texas held that the above article must be strictly complied with in reducing the capital stock of a state bank.23 In the case cited in the note the defendant originally owned 18 shares of the stock of the bank. The stockholders attempted to reduce the capital stock by obtaining the written consent of all the stockholders and a written waiver by such stockholders of the publication of intention to decrease said capital stock. The Banking Commissioner sued the defendant for the number of shares that the defendant claimed had been cancelled on account of the reduction of the Bank's capital. The Court held that the defendant was liable, as no notice by publication was made in a daily newspaper as is provided in the above article. 

The general rule is stated to be that any person holding himself out as the owner of shares, by letting himself appear on the

If a person is to be held liable on assessment on bank stock, he must be a stockholder by agreement, express or implied, at the time the bank failed.25

Shareholders of bank stock where they are on the bank's books as such holders are liable to assessment equal to the par value of the stock at the time of the bank's failure; if they are holders by transfer, their liability is determined by the date of the transfer on the books of the bank,26 but the original holders of the stock can be assessed at any time within twelve months of the transfer, if the transfer was made when the bank was insolvent. This being true, it follows that where the bank is solvent at the time of the transfer, the original shareholder is not liable thereafter for assessments on the bank stock.28 

A shareholder of bank stock cannot be relieved from liability except by a transfer to one who is legally bound to pay assessments when levied,29 though such transferee does not need to be

It seems to be well settled in Texas that where stock is held purely for collateral or security purposes the holder of such collateral, though the stock be in his name, is not liable for assessments on the stock.31

It is held that where a private bank is concerned, the shareholders of such bank are liable individually to the depositors for any money that is deposited in the bank.32 This is a departure from the rule adopted where an incorporated bank is concerned, for there the shareholders are only liable to creditors, as previously pointed out.

A partnership may own bank stock and its members may be held liable where an assessment is levied.33

 § 1036. Who are Shareholders 

The basis for the imposition of the additional liability is the ownership of shares in a banking corporation.36 Mere reference to certain persons as owners of shares made in the certificate of the banking commissioner, stating that a banking corporation has been legally created or that the capital of the corporation has been increased, is not conclusive evidence of such ownership, but is subject to collateral attack.37

In Thompson v. First State Bank 38 the Commissioner of In surance and Banking brought suit on behalf of creditors of the insolvent bank against Thompson on his note given in payment for bank stock. Thompson based his defense upon article 12, section 6 of the Constitution, which provides that no corporation shall issue stock except for money, labor or property and that all fictitious increase of stock shall be void. The court held that this was not a fictitious increase, that as between Thompson and the bank, the transaction was illegal, but that where the rights of creditors were involved, Thompson was estopped to assert the illegality, and, therefore he was held liable on the note. 

In Furr v. Chapman 39 the Commissioner of Insurance and 

Banking sued Furr to enforce alleged liability of a stockholder in a defunct bank. The bank had purported to increase its capital stock and some of these shares were delivered to Furr. He ac- cepted them either as a gift or in order to qualify as a director and to assist in salvaging the bank. The Commission of Appeals

Ann.Civ.St. art. 378 served to prevent the bank from acquiring a legal existence in Shaw v. Kopecky,42 by the same reasoning the bank in Thompson v. First State Bank,43 never acquired a legal existence.

It is to be remembered that the Thompson case established the doctrine that creditors of a corporation may enforce the payment of a note given as payment for stock. Thompson predicated his defense on Article 12, section 6 of the Constitution and Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1353.44 The court's attention was not directed to article 16, section 16 of the Constitution or to article 378, and the court in its opinion makes no reference to these provisions, but bases its conclusion upon the provisions applicable to corporation generally.

The Supreme Court since the Thompson case adopted the judgment in Furr v. Chapman and refused a writ of error in Shaw v. Kopecky. It is felt that the distinction suggested in Furr v. 

Chapman that article 12, section 6 of the Constitution renders void a gratuitous issuance of stock is not a sound distinction and is contra to the weight of authority and other Texas cases.45

In the old article the stockholder was made liable "to an amount double the par value of such shares." To make the above phrase explicit, the amendment provided that the stockholder was liable "to an additional amount equal to the par value of such shares." Before the 1929 amendment the by-laws of many banking corporations provided that the shares "shall be transferable only on the books of the corporation." Since the amendment of 1929, such a provision in the by-laws is unnecessary. In a fairly recent case by the Supreme Court of Texas, which arose before the 1929 amendment, it was held that a provision in the by-laws has the same effect as the amendment of 1929.57 In this recent case it was stated: "Article 535 of the Revised Civil 

Statutes of 1925, prior to its amendment in 1929 (Chapter 60, § 1, Acts First Called Session, 41st Legislature, page 159 (Vernon's 

Ann.Civ.St. Art. 535), by its terms imposed the added liability upon each stockholder of a bank only so long as he owned shares therein and for twelve months after the date of the transfer thereof and did not provide that shares of stock in a banking corporation should be transferable only on the books." "It is well settled by the decisions in this state, in cases arising prior to the amendment of article 535 in 1929, that, when the by-laws of the bank provide that the stock is transferable only on the books of the bank, the Banking Commissioner may enforce the stockholder's liability under that article of the statutes against one who, though not a real owner, allows the stock to stand in his name on the books of the bank.58 These

§ 1038. Time When Liability is Fixed-Statute of Limitations 

The Constitution limits the transferor's liability to debts existing at the time of the transfer. This liability is said to extend for twelve months after transfer. Is this a statute of limitations?

By these provisions, the liability is limited to those who are creditors at the time of the transfer, and, if that liability were intended to be fixed at any time within the ordinary period for bringing actions, the clause "for twelve months after the date of any bona fide transfer" would be meaningless. That clause can have but one significance, and that is its obvious one-namely, that at any moment within the specified period there exists a liability from the transferring stockholder to each and all of the defined class of creditors.

The purpose of this provision was to afford adequate protection to both the transferring stockholder and creditors of the bank. The stockholder fearing that the bank may be insolvent

The framers of the Constitution doubtless felt that there should be some period beyond which this contingent liability should not attach-and fixed the term at twelve months. The legislature has given the banking commissioner the sole authority to enforce this added liability on the stockholders by assessment. His judgment, as to the necessity for making the assessment, is conclusive.64 By levying the assessment the liability of the stockholder has been changed from a remote or contingent one to a definite or fixed one. Is it essential that the commissioner not only assess the transferring stockholder within the twelve months' period but also file suit thereon in order to enforce this liability? It is felt that the purpose of the framers of the constitution is best served by holding that when notice of assessment is given the transferring stockholder within the twelve months' period, his liability is fixed,65 and that the statute of limitations begins to run, as is the case on other assessments, from the date the assessment is due.66

That legal assessment of a bank stockholder can only be made after the bank has been taken over for liquidation, seems to be a well settled rule of law.90 This was the established rule prior to the time the Commissioner was given authority to levy assessments to make up the deficiency when the capital of a going concern has become impaired."1 Obviously, such rule would have no application in the latter situation. 

The district court of the county, where an insolvent bank is located, has exclusive jurisdiction and venue of all suits to enforce claims against such bank, when its assets are being liquidated by the State Banking Commissioner. There is nothing in the state banking law which can be construed as relating to the jurisdiction or venue of actions by the Commissioner. Thus, where the Commissioner files suit to enforce an assessment against a stockholder, the stockholder may assert the privilege vouchsafed a citizen under the general venue statutes to be sued in the county of his residence, unless by an agreement in writing the stockholder has promised to pay at some other place.9%

§ 

Ch. 24

This question has not as yet been presented, and consequently there has been no court decision or departmental ruling determinative thereof.

It would seem that the "double liability" of stockholders in trust, guaranty and surety companies was not thereby removed. 

Both Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. article 535 and article 1344 are derivative from article 552, R.S.1911, which provided: "If default shall be made in the payment of any debt or liability contracted by any bank, trust company, surety and guaranty company, (or) savings bank, each stockholder of such corporation, as long as he owns shares therein, and for twelve months after the date of a transfer thereof, shall be personally liable for all debts of such corporation existing at the date of such default, to an amount additional to the par value of such shares so owned or transferred, equal to the par value of such shares so owned or transferred." And it might well be argued that the policy or reason behind the "double liability" in both instances was the same, and consequently, that when the legislature removed double liability in one case it intended to remove also the double liability in the other. But however logical this argument may be, it is not applicable under the ordinary rules of statutory construction. An amendment or repeal of one article of the statutes does not operate as an amendment or repeal of another article unless expressly so provided or unless necessarily implied. In the present situation there is no express language of amendment or repeal of article 1344, and under no construction can it be said that there is a necessary implication of amendment or repeal of the article about stockholders in trust, guaranty and surety companies. Regardless of how just or expedient it may be that the double liability of stockholders in trust, guaranty and surety companies should be removed, it is the function of the Legislature to remove that double liability, and it seems that the statute does not include those companies.

The Joint Resolution providing for the amendment of Section 16, Art. 16, of the Texas Constitution is printed on pages 1495 and 

1496 of the Acts of the 45th Legislature 1937. It proposed "an 622

Ch. 

§ 1046 amendment to the Constitution relieving stockholders in state banks of double liability." It did not purport to determine the liability of the stockholders in any company except the "state bank." In fact, Art. 16, Sec. 16, of the Texas Constitution, before the above amendment, was adopted, provided for double liability of stockholders in "corporate bodies with banking and discounting privileges." The double liability of stockholders in those corporations was specifically set forth in the Texas Constitution. The amendment of 1937 omitted the second para graph of Art. 16, Sec. 16, of the Texas Constitution. The liability of stockholders in trust, guaranty and surety companies is determined by Art. 1344 of Vernon's Ann. Civ.St. and not by the

Texas Constitution. It would therefore seem evident that stockholders in those latter companies are still liable "to an amount double the par value of such shares", although many business men in Texas are of the opinion that the amendment to the Texas Constitution and the charge of double liability of stockholders in national banks by Congress relieved all shareholders of any personal liability where they had paid par for their stock.
